Nay, but this dotage of our general's / O'erflows the measure: those his goodly eyes, / That o'er the files and musters of the war / Have glow'd like plated Mars, now bend, now turn, / The office and devotion of their view / Upon a tawny front: his captain's heart, / Which in the scuffles of great fights hath burst / The buckles on his breast, reneges all temper, / And is become the bellows and the fan / To cool a gipsy's lust.

No, this infatuation of our general's goes too far. Those fine eyes of his, which used to blaze like Mars in armour over the ranks and parades of war, now bend and turn all their attention and devotion onto a dark-skinned face. His soldier's heart, which in the struggles of great battles has burst the buckles of his breastplate, has given up all self-control and become the bellows and the fan that cool a gypsy's lust.
Look where they come: / Take but good note, and you shall see in him / The triple pillar of the world transform'd / Into a strumpet's fool: behold and see.
Look, here they come. Just watch carefully, and you'll see in him one of the three pillars that hold up the world turned into a whore's plaything. Look and see.
If it be love indeed, tell me how much.
If it's really love, tell me how much.
There's beggary in the love that can be reckon'd.
Love that can be counted is a poor, beggarly love.
I'll set a bourn how far to be belov'd.
I'll set a limit on how far I'm to be loved.
Then must thou needs find out new heaven, new earth.
Then you'll have to find a new heaven and a new earth.
News, my good lord, from Rome.
How annoying. Just give me the summary.

Nay, hear them, Antony: / Fulvia perchance is angry; or who knows / If the scarce-bearded Caesar have not sent / His powerful mandate to you:  'Do this or this; / Take in that kingdom and enfranchise that; / Perform't, or else we damn thee.'

No, listen to them, Antony. Maybe Fulvia is angry. Or who knows if that barely-bearded boy Caesar has sent you his mighty orders: 'Do this, or this; conquer that kingdom and free that one; do it, or we'll condemn you.'
What do you mean, my love?

Perchance! Nay, and most like:-- / You must not stay here longer,--your dismission / Is come from Caesar; therefore hear it, Antony.  -- / Where's Fulvia's process?--Caesar's I would say?--Both?-- / Call in the messengers.--As I am Egypt's queen, / Thou blushest, Antony; and that blood of thine / Is Caesar's homager: else so thy cheek pays shame / When shrill-tongu'd Fulvia scolds.--The messengers!

Maybe! No, very likely. You mustn't stay here any longer; Caesar has sent your dismissal, so listen to it, Antony. Where's Fulvia's summons? Caesar's, I mean. Or both? Call in the messengers. As I'm Queen of Egypt, you're blushing, Antony, and that blood of yours bows to Caesar. Or else your cheeks pay the price of shame when shrill-voiced Fulvia scolds you. The messengers!

Let Rome in Tiber melt, and the wide arch / Of the rang'd empire fall! Here is my space. / Kingdoms are clay: our dungy earth alike / Feeds beast as man: the nobleness of life / Is to do thus [Embracing]; when such a mutual pair / And such a twain can do't, in which I bind, / On pain of punishment, the world to weet / We stand up peerless.

Let Rome melt into the Tiber, and the great arch of its well-ordered empire fall! This is my place. Kingdoms are just dirt; this dung-heap earth feeds animals and men alike. The noblest thing in life is to do this [he embraces her], when a pair so matched in love can do it. And I order the world, on pain of punishment, to recognise that we have no equals.
Excellent falsehood! / Why did he marry Fulvia, and not love her?-- / I'll seem the fool I am not; Antony / Will be himself.
What a beautiful lie! Why did he marry Fulvia if he didn't love her? I'll pretend to be the fool I'm not. Antony will always be himself.

But stirr'd by Cleopatra.-- / Now, for the love of Love and her soft hours, / Let's not confound the time with conference harsh: / There's not a minute of our lives should stretch / Without some pleasure now:--what sport to-night?

Yes, when Cleopatra moves him. Now, for the love of Love and her sweet hours, let's not waste time in harsh arguments. There shouldn't be a single minute of our lives now without some pleasure. What fun shall we have tonight?

Fie, wrangling queen! / Whom everything becomes,--to chide, to laugh, / To weep; whose every passion fully strives / To make itself in thee fair and admir'd! / No messenger; but thine, and all alone / To-night we'll wander through the streets and note / The qualities of people. Come, my queen; / Last night you did desire it:--speak not to us.

Oh, you quarrelsome queen! Everything suits you: scolding, laughing, crying. Every mood you have strives to become beautiful and admired in you! No messengers but yours. Tonight, just the two of us, we'll wander through the streets and watch the people. Come, my queen; you wanted to last night. Don't speak to us.
Is Caesar with Antonius priz'd so slight?
Does Antony think so little of Caesar?
Sir, sometimes when he is not Antony, / He comes too short of that great property / Which still should go with Antony.
Sir, sometimes, when he isn't really himself, he falls short of the greatness that should always belong to Antony.
I am full sorry / That he approves the common liar, who / Thus speaks of him at Rome: but I will hope / Of better deeds to-morrow. Rest you happy!
I'm very sorry that he proves the gossips in Rome right about him. But I'll hope for better behaviour tomorrow. Goodbye!

Lord Alexas, sweet Alexas, most anything Alexas, almost / most absolute Alexas, where's the soothsayer that you praised so / to the queen? O that I knew this husband, which you say must / charge his horns with garlands!

Lord Alexas, sweet Alexas, most wonderful Alexas, almost perfect Alexas, where's the fortune-teller you praised to the queen? Oh, I wish I knew this husband of mine, who you say will wear garlands on his cuckold's horns!
Is this the man?--Is't you, sir, that know things?
Is this the man? Are you the one, sir, who knows things?
In nature's infinite book of secrecy / A little I can read.
I can read a little in nature's endless book of secrets.
Bring in the banquet quickly; wine enough / Cleopatra's health to drink.
Bring in the dessert quickly, and enough wine to drink Cleopatra's health.
Good, sir, give me good fortune.
Good sir, give me a good fortune.
I don't make fortunes; I only foresee them.
Then please foresee one for me.
You shall be yet far fairer than you are.
You'll be even fairer than you are now.
No, you shall paint when you are old.
No, he means you'll wear make-up when you're old.
Vex not his prescience; be attentive.
Don't annoy him while he's seeing the future. Pay attention.
You shall be more beloving than beloved.
You'll love more than you're loved.
I had rather heat my liver with drinking.
I'd rather heat my liver with drink than with love.

Good now, some excellent fortune! Let me be married to three / kings in a forenoon, and widow them all: let me have a child at / fifty, to whom Herod of Jewry may do homage: find me to marry me / with Octavius Caesar, and companion me with my mistress.

Come on, give me a wonderful fortune! Let me marry three kings in one morning and outlive them all. Let me have a baby at fifty that Herod of Judea will bow down to. Fix it so I marry Octavius Caesar, and become my mistress's equal.
You shall outlive the lady whom you serve.
You'll outlive the lady you serve.
O, excellent! I love long life better than figs.
Oh, excellent! I like a long life better than figs.
You have seen and prov'd a fairer former fortune / Than that which is to approach.
You've already seen and enjoyed better times than the ones to come.
Then belike my children shall have no names:--pr'ythee, how many / boys and wenches must I have?
Then I suppose my children will be born out of wedlock. Please, how many boys and girls will I have?
If every of your wishes had a womb, / And fertile every wish, a million.
If each of your wishes had a womb, and every wish were fertile, a million.
Out, fool! I forgive thee for a witch.
Get away, fool! I'll let you off because you're a wizard.
You think none but your sheets are privy to your wishes.
You think only your bedsheets know what you wish for.
Mine, and most of our fortunes, to-night, shall be-- / drunk to bed.
Mine, and most of ours, tonight, will be to go to bed drunk.
There's a palm presages chastity, if nothing else.
Here's a palm that predicts chastity, if nothing else.
E'en as the o'erflowing Nilus presageth famine.
Just as the flooding Nile predicts famine.
Go, you wild bedfellow, you cannot soothsay.
Go on, you wild bedfellow, you can't tell fortunes.
Nay, if an oily palm be not a fruitful prognostication, I cannot / scratch mine ear.--Pr'ythee, tell her but worky-day fortune.
Well, if a sweaty palm doesn't mean you'll have lots of children, I can't scratch my own ear. Please, just tell her an everyday fortune.
But how, but how? give me particulars.
But how? How? Give me details.
Am I not an inch of fortune better than she?
Isn't my fortune even an inch better than hers?
Well, if you were but an inch of fortune better than I, where / would you choose it?
Well, if your fortune were an inch better than mine, where would you want that inch?

Our worser thoughts heavens mend!--Alexas,--come, his fortune! / his fortune!--O, let him marry a woman that cannot go, sweet / Isis, I beseech thee! And let her die too, and give him a worse! / and let worse follow worse, till the worst of all follow him / laughing to his grave, fiftyfold a cuckold! Good Isis, hear me / this prayer, though thou deny me a matter of more weight; good / Isis, I beseech thee!

Heaven correct our dirty thoughts! Alexas, come on, his fortune, his fortune! Oh, let him marry a woman who can't walk, sweet Isis, I beg you! And let her die too, and give him a worse one! And let worse follow worse, until the worst of all follows him laughing to his grave, a cuckold fifty times over! Good Isis, hear this prayer, even if you refuse me something more important. Good Isis, I beg you!

Amen. Dear goddess, hear that prayer of the people! for, as it is / a heartbreaking to see a handsome man loose-wived, so it is a / deadly sorrow to behold a foul knave uncuckolded: therefore, dear / Isis, keep decorum, and fortune him accordingly!

Amen. Dear goddess, hear the people's prayer! It breaks your heart to see a handsome man with an unfaithful wife, and it's terrible to see an ugly rogue whose wife is faithful. So, dear Isis, do what's proper and give him the fortune he deserves!
Lo now, if it lay in their hands to make me a cuckold, they would / make themselves whores but they'd do't!
Look at that! If it were up to them to make me a cuckold, they'd turn themselves into whores just to do it!
It's not him; it's the queen.
He was dispos'd to mirth; but on the sudden / A Roman thought hath struck him.--Enobarbus,--
He was in a cheerful mood, but suddenly a Roman thought struck him. Enobarbus!
Seek him, and bring him hither.--Where's Alexas?
Find him and bring him here. Where's Alexas?
Here, at your service.--My lord approaches.
Here, at your service. My lord is coming.
We will not look upon him: go with us.
We won't look at him. Come with us.
Fulvia thy wife first came into the field.
Your wife Fulvia was the first to take to the battlefield.
Ay: / But soon that war had end, and the time's state / Made friends of them, jointing their force 'gainst Caesar; / Whose better issue in the war, from Italy / Upon the first encounter, drave them.
Yes. But that war soon ended, and events made them friends, joining their forces against Caesar. He won the war and drove them out of Italy at the first battle.
The nature of bad news infects the teller.
Bad news makes the person who brings it hated.
When it concerns the fool or coward.--On:-- / Things that are past are done with me.--'Tis thus; / Who tells me true, though in his tale lie death, / I hear him as he flatter'd.

Only when the listener is a fool or a coward. Go on. What's past is done with as far as I'm concerned. This is how it is: if someone tells me the truth, even if his story means death, I listen as if he were flattering me.
Labienus,-- / This is stiff news,--hath, with his Parthian force, / Extended Asia from Euphrates; / His conquering banner shook from Syria / To Lydia and to Ionia; / Whilst,--
Labienus (this is hard news) has, with his Parthian army, seized Asia from the Euphrates. His conquering flag has flown from Syria to Lydia and Ionia, while...
While Antony, you mean to say...

Speak to me home, mince not the general tongue: / Name Cleopatra as she is call'd in Rome; / Rail thou in Fulvia's phrase; and taunt my faults / With such full licence as both truth and malice / Have power to utter. O, then we bring forth weeds / When our quick minds lie still; and our ills told us / Is as our earing. Fare thee well awhile.

Speak plainly to me; don't tone down what everyone's saying. Call Cleopatra what they call her in Rome. Abuse me in Fulvia's words, and mock my faults as freely as truth and spite can. We grow weeds when our lively minds lie idle, and hearing our faults is like ploughing them up. Goodbye for now.
From Sicyon, ho, the news! Speak there!
The news from Sicyon! Bring it in!
The man from Sicyon--is there such an one?
The man from Sicyon! Is there such a man here?
Let him appear.-- / These strong Egyptian fetters I must break, / Or lose myself in dotage.--
Let him come in. I must break these strong Egyptian chains, or lose myself in infatuation.
In Sicyon: / Her length of sickness, with what else more serious / Importeth thee to know, this bears. [Gives a letter.]
In Sicyon. This letter tells you how long she was ill, and other more serious things you need to know. [He gives a letter.]

There's a great spirit gone! Thus did I desire it: / What our contempts doth often hurl from us, / We wish it ours again; the present pleasure, / By revolution lowering, does become / The opposite of itself: she's good, being gone; / The hand could pluck her back that shov'd her on. / I must from this enchanting queen break off: / Ten thousand harms, more than the ills I know, / My idleness doth hatch--ho, Enobarbus!

There's a great spirit gone! And I wished for it. What we throw away in contempt we often want back again. A present pleasure, as time turns, becomes its own opposite. She seems good now she's gone. The hand that pushed her away would pull her back. I must break away from this enchanting queen. My idleness is hatching ten thousand harms, beyond the troubles I already know about. Hey, Enobarbus!
I must with haste from hence.
Why, then we kill all our women: we see how mortal an unkindness / is to them; if they suffer our departure, death's the word.
Well, then we'll kill all our women. We know how deadly any unkindness is to them. If they have to put up with our leaving, they'll die.

Under a compelling occasion, let women die: it were pity to cast / them away for nothing; though, between them and a great cause / they should be esteemed nothing. Cleopatra, catching but the / least noise of this, dies instantly; I have seen her die twenty / times upon far poorer moment: I do think there is mettle in / death, which commits some loving act upon her, she hath such a / celerity in dying.

If there's an urgent reason, let the women die. It would be a shame to throw them away for nothing, though compared with a great cause they're worth nothing. Cleopatra, if she hears even a whisper of this, will die on the spot. I've seen her die twenty times for much less reason. I think death must have some special power that makes love to her, she dies so readily.
She is cunning past man's thought.
She is more cunning than anyone could imagine.

Alack, sir, no: her passions are made of nothing but the finest / part of pure love: we cannot call her winds and waters, sighs and / tears; they are greater storms and tempests than almanacs can / report: this cannot be cunning in her; if it be, she makes a / shower of rain as well as Jove.

No, sir. Her passions are made of nothing but the purest love. We can't call her storms of feeling mere sighs and tears. They're greater storms and tempests than any calendar can predict. This can't be cunning. If it is, she makes rain as well as Jupiter does.
Would I had never seen her!
I wish I'd never seen her!
O sir, you had then left unseen a wonderful piece of work; which / not to have been blest withal would have discredited your travel.
Oh sir, then you'd have missed a marvellous masterpiece. Not to have been blessed with that would have made your travels worthless.

Why, sir, give the gods a thankful sacrifice. When it pleaseth / their deities to take the wife of a man from him, it shows to / man the tailors of the earth; comforting therein that when old / robes are worn out there are members to make new. If there were / no more women but Fulvia, then had you indeed a cut, and the case / to be lamented: this grief is crown'd with consolation; your old / smock brings forth a new petticoat:--and, indeed, the tears live / in an onion that should water this sorrow.

Well, sir, make a sacrifice to the gods in thanks. When the gods take a man's wife from him, it shows him they're the tailors of the world: when old clothes wear out, there's material to make new ones. If there were no women except Fulvia, then you would have had a real blow and something to grieve about. But this grief comes with a consolation: your old smock produces a new petticoat. And really, the only tears for this sorrow would come from an onion.
The business she hath broached in the state / Cannot endure my absence.
The trouble she started in the state can't do without me there.
And the business you have broached here cannot be without you; / especially that of Cleopatra's, which wholly depends on your / abode.
And the trouble you've started here can't do without you, especially Cleopatra's, which depends entirely on your staying.

No more light answers. Let our officers / Have notice what we purpose. I shall break / The cause of our expedience to the queen, / And get her leave to part. For not alone / The death of Fulvia, with more urgent touches, / Do strongly speak to us; but the letters too / Of many our contriving friends in Rome / Petition us at home: Sextus Pompeius / Hath given the dare to Caesar, and commands / The empire of the sea; our slippery people,-- / Whose love is never link'd to the deserver / Till his deserts are past,--begin to throw / Pompey the Great, and all his dignities, / Upon his son; who, high in name and power, / Higher than both in blood and life, stands up / For the main soldier: whose quality, going on, / The sides o' the world may danger: much is breeding / Which, like the courser's hair, hath yet but life / And not a serpent's poison. Say, our pleasure / To such whose place is under us, requires / Our quick remove from hence.

No more joking. Let our officers know what we're planning. I'll tell the queen why we must hurry, and get her permission to leave. It's not just Fulvia's death and more urgent matters that call me; letters from many friends working for us in Rome are begging me to come home. Sextus Pompeius has challenged Caesar and controls the sea. Our fickle people, who never love a man until his great deeds are over, are starting to transfer all the honours of Pompey the Great onto his son. He's grown so powerful in name and strength, and even more in spirit and energy, that he stands as the greatest soldier of all. If his power keeps growing, the whole world may be in danger. Much is brewing, like the horse's hair that was said to come alive in water: it has life, but not yet a serpent's poison. Tell those who serve under us that we wish to leave here quickly.
I did not see him since.
See where he is, who's with him, what he does:-- / I did not send you:--if you find him sad, / Say I am dancing; if in mirth, report / That I am sudden sick: quick, and return.
Find out where he is, who he's with, and what he's doing. Don't say I sent you. If you find him sad, say I'm dancing. If he's cheerful, report that I've suddenly fallen ill. Quick, and come back.
Madam, methinks, if you did love him dearly, / You do not hold the method to enforce / The like from him.
Madam, I think if you love him so much, you're not going the right way about making him love you the same.
What should I do, I do not?
What should I be doing that I'm not?
In each thing give him way; cross him in nothing.
Give in to him in everything. Never cross him.
Thou teachest like a fool,--the way to lose him.
You're teaching like a fool. That's the way to lose him.
Tempt him not so too far; I wish, forbear; / In time we hate that which we often fear. / But here comes Antony.
Don't push him so far. I wish you'd hold back. In time we hate what we often fear. But here comes Antony.
I am sorry to give breathing to my purpose,--
I'm sorry to have to tell you my plans...
Help me away, dear Charmian; I shall fall; / It cannot be thus long, the sides of nature / Will not sustain it.
Help me out of here, dear Charmian, I'm going to faint. It can't last like this; my body can't bear it.
Pray you, stand farther from me.
Please stand further away from me.

I know by that same eye there's some good news. / What says the married woman?--You may go. / Would she had never given you leave to come! / Let her not say 'tis I that keep you here,-- / I have no power upon you; hers you are.

I can tell by that look in your eye there's good news. What does your wife say? You may go. I wish she'd never given you permission to come here! Don't let her say it's me keeping you here. I have no power over you. You're hers.
O, never was there queen / So mightily betray'd! Yet at the first / I saw the treasons planted.
Oh, there was never a queen so badly betrayed! Yet from the beginning I saw the seeds of treachery.

Why should I think you can be mine and true, / Though you in swearing shake the throned gods, / Who have been false to Fulvia? Riotous madness, / To be entangled with those mouth-made vows, / Which break themselves in swearing!

Why should I believe you can be mine and faithful, even if you swear so hard you shake the gods on their thrones, when you've been unfaithful to Fulvia? It's insane to be caught up in vows made only with the mouth, which break even as they're sworn!

Nay, pray you, seek no colour for your going, / But bid farewell, and go: when you su'd staying, / Then was the time for words: no going then;-- / Eternity was in our lips and eyes, / Bliss in our brows' bent; none our parts so poor / But was a race of heaven: they are so still, / Or thou, the greatest soldier of the world, / Art turn'd the greatest liar.

No, please, don't look for excuses to go. Just say goodbye and go. When you begged to stay, that was the time for words. There was no talk of going then. Eternity was in our lips and eyes, bliss in the arch of our brows. No part of us was so poor that it wasn't heavenly. They still are, or else you, the greatest soldier in the world, have become the greatest liar.
I would I had thy inches; thou shouldst know / There were a heart in Egypt.
I wish I had your size; then you'd find out there's a brave heart in Egypt.

Hear me, queen: / The strong necessity of time commands / Our services awhile; but my full heart / Remains in use with you. Our Italy / Shines o'er with civil swords:  Sextus Pompeius / Makes his approaches to the port of Rome; / Equality of two domestic powers / Breed scrupulous faction: the hated, grown to strength, / Are newly grown to love: the condemn'd Pompey, / Rich in his father's honour, creeps apace / Into the hearts of such as have not thriv'd / Upon the present state, whose numbers threaten; / And quietness, grown sick of rest, would purge / By any desperate change. My more particular, / And that which most with you should safe my going, / Is Fulvia's death.

Listen to me, queen. The urgent needs of the moment require my service for a while, but my whole heart stays here with you. Italy is glittering with the swords of civil war. Sextus Pompeius is advancing on Rome itself. When two powers at home are equally matched, petty factions grow. Those who were hated, now they're strong, are suddenly loved. Pompey, though condemned, is rich in his father's fame and is quickly winning the hearts of those who haven't done well under the present government, and there are enough of them to be a threat. And peace, sick of too much quiet, wants to cure itself with any desperate change. My more personal reason, and the one that should most reassure you about my going, is Fulvia's death.
Though age from folly could not give me freedom, / It does from childishness:--can Fulvia die?
Though age hasn't freed me from foolishness, it has freed me from childishness. Can Fulvia die?
She's dead, my queen. / Look here, and, at thy sovereign leisure, read / The garboils she awak'd; at the last, best. / See when and where she died.
She's dead, my queen. Look here, and when you have time, read about the trouble she stirred up. Last of all, and best, see when and where she died.
O most false love! / Where be the sacred vials thou shouldst fill / With sorrowful water? Now I see, I see, / In Fulvia's death how mine receiv'd shall be.
Oh, most false love! Where are the sacred bottles you should fill with sad tears? Now I see, I see, from how you take Fulvia's death, how mine will be received.

Quarrel no more, but be prepar'd to know / The purposes I bear; which are, or cease, / As you shall give the advice. By the fire / That quickens Nilus' slime, I go from hence / Thy soldier, servant, making peace or war / As thou affect'st.

Stop quarrelling, and be ready to hear my plans, which will go ahead or stop as you advise. By the sun's fire that brings the Nile's mud to life, I leave here as your soldier and servant, making peace or war as you wish.
Cut my lace, Charmian, come;-- / But let it be: I am quickly ill and well, / So Antony loves.
Cut my corset laces, Charmian, come! No, never mind. I'm quickly ill and quickly well again, just as Antony loves.
My precious queen, forbear; / And give true evidence to his love, which stands / An honourable trial.
My precious queen, stop it. Trust my love, which will stand up to any honourable test.

So Fulvia told me. / I pr'ythee, turn aside and weep for her; / Then bid adieu to me, and say the tears / Belong to Egypt: good now, play one scene / Of excellent dissembling; and let it look / Like perfect honour.

That's what Fulvia was told. Please, turn away and weep for her, then say goodbye to me and say the tears are for Egypt. Go on, act one scene of excellent pretending, and make it look like perfect honour.
You'll heat my blood: no more.
You'll make me angry. No more.
You can do better yet; but this is meetly.
You can do better than that, but this is fairly good.
And target.--Still he mends; / But this is not the best:--look, pr'ythee, Charmian, / How this Herculean Roman does become / The carriage of his chafe.
And shield. He's getting better, but this isn't his best. Look, please, Charmian, how well this Herculean Roman acts out his rage.

Courteous lord, one word. / Sir, you and I must part,--but that's not it; / Sir, you and I have lov'd,--but there's not it; / That you know well: something it is I would,-- / O, my oblivion is a very Antony, / And I am all forgotten.

Courteous lord, one word. Sir, you and I must part, but that's not it. Sir, you and I have loved, but that's not it either; you know that well. There's something I want to say... Oh, my memory is just like Antony: it deserts me, and I'm completely forgotten.
But that your royalty / Holds idleness your subject, I should take you / For idleness itself.
If you weren't a queen who rules over idleness itself, I'd take you for Idleness in person.

'Tis sweating labour / To bear such idleness so near the heart / As Cleopatra this. But, sir, forgive me; / Since my becomings kill me, when they do not / Eye well to you: your honour calls you hence; / Therefore be deaf to my unpitied folly, / And all the gods go with you! upon your sword / Sit laurel victory! and smooth success / Be strew'd before your feet!

It's hard work carrying idleness like this so close to my heart. But, sir, forgive me, since my moods kill me when you don't like them. Your honour calls you away, so don't listen to my foolishness, which nobody pities. May all the gods go with you! May victory crown your sword with laurel, and may easy success be scattered at your feet!
Let us go. Come; / Our separation so abides, and flies, / That thou, residing here, goes yet with me, / And I, hence fleeting, here remain with thee. / Away!
Let's go. Come. Our parting is such that it both stays and goes: you, staying here, go with me, and I, leaving here, stay with you. Away!

You may see, Lepidus, and henceforth know, / It is not Caesar's natural vice to hate / Our great competitor. From Alexandria / This is the news:--he fishes, drinks, and wastes / The lamps of night in revel: is not more manlike / Than Cleopatra, nor the queen of Ptolemy / More womanly than he: hardly gave audience, or / Vouchsaf'd to think he had partners: you shall find there / A man who is the abstract of all faults / That all men follow.

You can see, Lepidus, and know from now on, that it isn't my nature to hate our great partner. This is the news from Alexandria: he goes fishing, drinks, and wastes the night in partying. He's no more manly than Cleopatra, and she, Ptolemy's widow, is no more womanly than he is. He hardly received our messengers, or bothered to remember he has partners. You'll find there a man who sums up every fault that men have.

I must not think there are / Evils enow to darken all his goodness: / His faults in him seem as the spots of heaven, / More fiery by night's blackness; hereditary / Rather than purchas'd; what he cannot change / Than what he chooses.

I can't believe there are enough faults to darken all his goodness. His faults are like the stars in the sky, shining brighter against night's darkness. They're inborn rather than acquired; things he can't change rather than things he chooses.

You are too indulgent. Let's grant it is not / Amiss to tumble on the bed of Ptolemy; / To give a kingdom for a mirth; to sit / And keep the turn of tippling with a slave; / To reel the streets at noon, and stand the buffet / With knaves that smell of sweat: say this becomes him,-- / As his composure must be rare indeed / Whom these things cannot blemish,--yet must Antony / No way excuse his foils when we do bear / So great weight in his lightness. If he fill'd / His vacancy with his voluptuousness, / Full surfeits and the dryness of his bones / Call on him for't: but to confound such time / That drums him from his sport, and speaks as loud / As his own state and ours,--'tis to be chid / As we rate boys, who, being mature in knowledge, / Pawn their experience to their present pleasure, / And so rebel to judgment.

You're too kind. Let's agree it isn't wrong to roll around in bed with Ptolemy's queen, to give away a kingdom for a joke, to take turns drinking with a slave, to stagger through the streets at noon and trade punches with rogues who stink of sweat. Say this suits him, though he'd have to be a rare man indeed not to be stained by such things. Even so, Antony can't excuse his failings when we have to carry so much weight because of his frivolity. If he filled his free time with pleasure, upset stomachs and diseased bones would make him pay for it. But to waste time that drums him back to duty, and that matters so much to his position and ours, deserves a scolding, the way we scold boys who know better but trade what they've learned for pleasure, and so rebel against good sense.

Thy biddings have been done; and every hour, / Most noble Caesar, shalt thou have report / How 'tis abroad. Pompey is strong at sea; / And it appears he is belov'd of those / That only have fear'd Caesar: to the ports / The discontents repair, and men's reports / Give him much wrong'd.

Your orders have been carried out, and every hour, noble Caesar, you'll get reports of what's happening. Pompey is strong at sea, and it seems he's loved by those who only feared you. The discontented flock to the ports, and people say he's been badly treated.

I should have known no less: / It hath been taught us from the primal state / That he which is was wish'd until he were; / And the ebb'd man, ne'er lov'd till ne'er worth love, / Comes dear'd by being lack'd. This common body, / Like to a vagabond flag upon the stream, / Goes to and back, lackeying the varying tide, / To rot itself with motion.

I should have expected that. History has taught us from the very beginning that the man in power was wanted only until he got power, and the man who's fallen, never loved until he's no longer worth loving, becomes dear by being missed. The common people are like a loose reed on a river, drifting back and forth, following the changing tide like a servant, until it rots from all the motion.

Caesar, I bring thee word / Menecrates and Menas, famous pirates, / Make the sea serve them, which they ear and wound / With keels of every kind: many hot inroads / They make in Italy; the borders maritime / Lack blood to think on't, and flush youth revolt: / No vessel can peep forth but 'tis as soon / Taken as seen; for Pompey's name strikes more / Than could his war resisted.

Caesar, I bring you news that Menecrates and Menas, famous pirates, are making the sea their servant, ploughing and cutting it with all kinds of ships. They make many fierce raids on Italy. The people on the coast turn pale at the thought, and hot-blooded young men are rebelling. No ship can set out without being captured as soon as it's seen. Pompey's name does more damage than his army could if it were fought.

Antony, / Leave thy lascivious wassails. When thou once / Was beaten from Modena, where thou slew'st / Hirtius and Pansa, consuls, at thy heel / Did famine follow; whom thou fought'st against, / Though daintily brought up, with patience more / Than savages could suffer: thou didst drink / The stale of horses, and the gilded puddle / Which beasts would cough at: thy palate then did deign / The roughest berry on the rudest hedge; / Yea, like the stag when snow the pasture sheets, / The barks of trees thou browsed'st; on the Alps / It is reported thou didst eat strange flesh, / Which some did die to look on: and all this,-- / It wounds thine honour that I speak it now,-- / Was borne so like a soldier that thy cheek / So much as lank'd not.

Antony, give up your lustful partying. When you were defeated at Modena, where you killed the consuls Hirtius and Pansa, famine followed close behind you. You fought it, though you'd been raised in luxury, with more endurance than savages could. You drank horses' urine and slimy puddles that animals would choke on. Your taste then accepted the hardest berry on the roughest hedge. Yes, like a stag when snow covers the pasture, you ate the bark off trees. In the Alps, they say, you ate strange meat that killed some men just to look at. And all this (it hurts your honour that I mention it now) you endured so like a soldier that your face didn't even get thinner.
Let his shames quickly / Drive him to Rome; 'tis time we twain / Did show ourselves i' the field; and to that end / Assemble we immediate council: Pompey / Thrives in our idleness.
Let his shame drive him quickly back to Rome. It's time the two of us took the field, and for that we should call a council at once. Pompey grows stronger while we sit idle.
To-morrow, Caesar, / I shall be furnish'd to inform you rightly / Both what by sea and land I can be able / To front this present time.
Tomorrow, Caesar, I'll be able to tell you exactly what forces I can raise on sea and land to face this situation.
Till which encounter / It is my business too. Farewell.
Until we meet, that will be my business too. Goodbye.
Farewell, my lord: what you shall know meantime / Of stirs abroad, I shall beseech you, sir, / To let me be partaker.
Goodbye, my lord. If you hear of any developments in the meantime, I beg you, sir, to share them with me.
Doubt not, sir; / I knew it for my bond.
Don't worry, sir. I know it's my duty.
Ha, ha!-- / Give me to drink mandragora.
Ha, ha! Give me mandrake to drink.
That I might sleep out this great gap of time / My Antony is away.
So I can sleep through this huge stretch of time while my Antony is away.
You think of him too much.
You think about him too much.
Not now to hear thee sing; I take no pleasure / In aught an eunuch has; 'tis well for thee / That, being unseminar'd, thy freer thoughts / May not fly forth of Egypt. Hast thou affections?
Not to hear you sing now. I take no pleasure in anything a eunuch has. It's lucky for you that, being castrated, your thoughts can't fly out of Egypt after anyone. Do you have desires?
Not in deed, madam; for I can do nothing / But what indeed is honest to be done: / Yet have I fierce affections, and think / What Venus did with Mars.
Not in deed, madam, because I can't do anything except what's decent. But I do have fierce desires, and think about what Venus did with Mars.

O Charmian, / Where think'st thou he is now? Stands he or sits he? / Or does he walk? or is he on his horse? / O happy horse, to bear the weight of Antony! / Do bravely, horse! for wott'st thou whom thou mov'st? / The demi-Atlas of this earth, the arm / And burgonet of men.--He's speaking now, / Or murmuring 'Where's my serpent of old Nile?' / For so he calls me.--Now I feed myself / With most delicious poison:--think on me, / That am with Phoebus' amorous pinches black, / And wrinkled deep in time? Broad-fronted Caesar, / When thou wast here above the ground I was / A morsel for a monarch: and great Pompey / Would stand and make his eyes grow in my brow; / There would he anchor his aspect and die / With looking on his life.

Oh, Charmian, where do you think he is now? Is he standing or sitting? Or is he walking? Or is he on his horse? Oh, happy horse, to carry Antony's weight! Do well, horse! Do you know who you're carrying? The half-Atlas who holds up the world, the arm and helmet of mankind. He's speaking now, or murmuring, 'Where's my serpent of old Nile?' That's what he calls me. Now I'm feeding myself the most delicious poison. Think of me, who am tanned black by the sun's loving pinches and deeply wrinkled with age? Julius Caesar, with your broad forehead, when you were alive I was a dish fit for a king. And great Pompey would stand and fix his eyes on my face; he'd anchor his gaze there and die looking at what he lived for.
How much unlike art thou Mark Antony! / Yet, coming from him, that great medicine hath / With his tinct gilded thee.-- / How goes it with my brave Mark Antony?
How unlike Mark Antony you are! Yet, coming from him, his great magic has gilded you with its colour. How is my brave Mark Antony?
Last thing he did, dear queen, / He kiss'd,--the last of many doubled kisses,-- / This orient pearl: his speech sticks in my heart.
The last thing he did, dear queen, was kiss this precious pearl, the last of many repeated kisses. His words are stuck in my heart.
Mine ear must pluck it thence.
My ear must pull them out.

'Good friend,' quoth he / 'Say, the firm Roman to great Egypt sends / This treasure of an oyster; at whose foot, / To mend the petty present, I will piece / Her opulent throne with kingdoms; all the east, / Say thou, shall call her mistress.' So he nodded, / And soberly did mount an arm-girt steed, / Who neigh'd so high that what I would have spoke / Was beastly dumb'd by him.

'Good friend,' he said, 'tell great Egypt that the faithful Roman sends her this treasure from an oyster. At her feet, to make up for this small present, I'll add kingdoms to her rich throne. The whole East, tell her, will call her mistress.' Then he nodded and solemnly mounted a war horse, which neighed so loudly that what I wanted to say was drowned out by the beast.
What, was he sad or merry?
Well, was he sad or happy?
Like to the time o' the year between the extremes / Of hot and cold, he was nor sad nor merry.
Like the time of year between the extremes of hot and cold, he was neither sad nor happy.

O well-divided disposition!--Note him, / Note him, good Charmian; 'tis the man; but note him: / He was not sad,--for he would shine on those / That make their looks by his; he was not merry,-- / Which seem'd to tell them his remembrance lay / In Egypt with his joy; but between both: / O heavenly mingle!--Be'st thou sad or merry, / The violence of either thee becomes, / So does it no man else.--Mett'st thou my posts?

Oh, what a balanced mood! Notice that, notice that, good Charmian. That's the man exactly. Notice it: he wasn't sad, because he wanted to cheer those who copy his looks; he wasn't happy, which seemed to tell them his thoughts were in Egypt with his joy; he was in between. Oh, heavenly mixture! Whether you're sad or happy, the extremes of both suit you as they suit no other man. Did you meet my messengers?
Ay, madam, twenty several messengers. / Why do you send so thick?
Yes, madam, twenty different messengers. Why do you send so many?
Who's born that day / When I forget to send to Antony / Shall die a beggar.--Ink and paper, Charmian.-- / Welcome, my good Alexas.--Did I, Charmian, / Ever love Caesar so?
Anyone born on a day when I forget to send to Antony will die a beggar. Ink and paper, Charmian. Welcome, my good Alexas. Charmian, did I ever love Julius Caesar this much?
Be chok'd with such another emphasis! / Say 'the brave Antony.'
Choke on another word like that! Say 'the brave Antony'.
By Isis, I will give thee bloody teeth / If thou with Caesar paragon again / My man of men.
By Isis, I'll give you a bloody mouth if you compare Caesar with my man of men again.
By your most gracious pardon, / I sing but after you.
With your gracious pardon, I'm only repeating what you used to say.

My salad days, / When I was green in judgment:--cold in blood, / To say as I said then!--But come, away; / Get me ink and paper: he shall have every day / A several greeting, / Or I'll unpeople Egypt.

That was in my salad days, when I was green in judgement and cold-blooded, to say what I said then! But come, let's go. Get me ink and paper. He'll have a separate greeting every day, even if I have to empty Egypt of people to send them.
If the great gods be just, they shall assist / The deeds of justest men.
If the great gods are fair, they'll help the actions of the fairest men.
Know, worthy Pompey, / That what they do delay they not deny.
Remember, worthy Pompey, that what they delay they don't refuse.
Whiles we are suitors to their throne, decays / The thing we sue for.
While we're begging at their throne, the very thing we're asking for is wasting away.
We, ignorant of ourselves, / Beg often our own harms, which the wise powers / Deny us for our good; so find we profit / By losing of our prayers.
We don't know ourselves, so we often pray for things that would harm us, and the wise gods refuse them for our own good. So we benefit from having our prayers turned down.

I shall do well; / The people love me, and the sea is mine; / My powers are crescent, and my auguring hope / Says it will come to the full. Mark Antony / In Egypt sits at dinner, and will make / No wars without doors: Caesar gets money where / He loses hearts: Lepidus flatters both, / Of both is flatter'd; but he neither loves / Nor either cares for him.

I'll do well. The people love me, and the sea is mine. My power is growing like the new moon, and my hopes predict it will be full. Mark Antony sits at dinner in Egypt and won't fight any wars outside. Caesar raises money but loses people's love. Lepidus flatters both of them and is flattered by both, but he loves neither, and neither cares for him.
Caesar and Lepidus / Are in the field: a mighty strength they carry.
Caesar and Lepidus are in the field with a huge army.
Where did you hear that? It's not true.

He dreams: I know they are in Rome together, / Looking for Antony. But all the charms of love, / Salt Cleopatra, soften thy wan'd lip! / Let witchcraft join with beauty, lust with both! / Tie up the libertine in a field of feasts, / Keep his brain fuming; Epicurean cooks / Sharpen with cloyless sauce his appetite; / That sleep and feeding may prorogue his honour / Even till a Lethe'd dullness.

He's dreaming. I know they're in Rome together, waiting for Antony. Lustful Cleopatra, may all the charms of love sweeten your faded lips! Let witchcraft join with beauty, and lust with both! Keep the pleasure-seeker tied up in a world of feasts and keep his brain fogged with wine. May gourmet cooks sharpen his appetite with sauces that never sicken him, so that sleeping and eating put off his sense of honour until he forgets it completely.
This is most certain that I shall deliver:-- / Mark Antony is every hour in Rome / Expected: since he went from Egypt 'tis / A space for further travel.
What I'm about to tell you is certain: Mark Antony is expected in Rome any hour. He left Egypt long enough ago to have travelled further.

I could have given less matter / A better ear.--Menas, I did not think / This amorous surfeiter would have donn'd his helm / For such a petty war; his soldiership / Is twice the other twain: but let us rear / The higher our opinion, that our stirring / Can from the lap of Egypt's widow pluck / The ne'er lust-wearied Antony.

I'd have been happier to hear less important news. Menas, I didn't think this overfed lover would put on his helmet for such a small war. As a soldier he's worth twice the other two. But it should make us think more highly of ourselves that our rising has torn the never-tired-of-lust Antony from the lap of Egypt's widow.
I cannot hope / Caesar and Antony shall well greet together: / His wife that's dead did trespasses to Caesar; / His brother warr'd upon him; although, I think, / Not mov'd by Antony.
I can't believe Caesar and Antony will get on well. Antony's dead wife wronged Caesar, and his brother made war on him, though I don't think Antony urged him to.

I know not, Menas, / How lesser enmities may give way to greater. / Were't not that we stand up against them all, / 'Twere pregnant they should square between themselves; / For they have entertained cause enough / To draw their swords: but how the fear of us / May cement their divisions, and bind up / The petty difference, we yet not know. / Be't as our gods will have't! It only stands / Our lives upon to use our strongest hands. / Come, Menas.

I don't know, Menas, how smaller quarrels may give way to bigger ones. If we weren't standing up against all of them, it's likely they'd fight among themselves, because they've got enough reasons to draw their swords. But we don't yet know how far fear of us may patch up their divisions and heal their petty differences. Let it be as the gods want! Our lives depend on using all our strength. Come, Menas.
Good Enobarbus, 'tis a worthy deed, / And shall become you well, to entreat your captain / To soft and gentle speech.
Good Enobarbus, it would be a worthy thing, and it would suit you, to ask your captain to speak calmly and gently.

I shall entreat him / To answer like himself: if Caesar move him, / Let Antony look over Caesar's head, / And speak as loud as Mars. By Jupiter, / Were I the wearer of Antonius' beard, / I would not shave't to-day.
I'll ask him to answer like himself. If Caesar provokes him, let Antony look down on Caesar from above and speak as loudly as Mars. By Jupiter, if I had Antony's beard, I wouldn't shave it today.
'Tis not a time / For private stomaching.
This isn't the time for personal grudges.
Every time / Serves for the matter that is then born in't.
Any time is right for the business that comes up in it.
But small to greater matters must give way.
But small matters must give way to bigger ones.
Not if the small come first.
Not if the small ones came first.
Your speech is passion: / But, pray you, stir no embers up. Here comes / The noble Antony.
You're speaking with emotion. But please, don't stir up the embers. Here comes noble Antony.
If we compose well here, to Parthia; / Hark, Ventidius.
If we reach an agreement here, then on to Parthia. Listen, Ventidius.
I do not know, / Maecenas; ask Agrippa.
I don't know, Maecenas. Ask Agrippa.

Noble friends, / That which combin'd us was most great, and let not / A leaner action rend us. What's amiss, / May it be gently heard: when we debate / Our trivial difference loud, we do commit / Murder in healing wounds: then, noble partners,-- / The rather for I earnestly beseech,-- / Touch you the sourest points with sweetest terms, / Nor curstness grow to the matter.

Noble friends, what united us was very great, so don't let a smaller matter tear us apart. Whatever is wrong, let it be heard calmly. When we argue loudly over petty differences, we kill the patient while trying to heal the wound. So, noble partners (and all the more because I'm begging you sincerely), deal with the sorest points in the kindest words, and don't let bad temper make things worse.
'Tis spoken well. / Were we before our armies, and to fight, / I should do thus.
Well said. Even if we stood before our armies about to fight, I'd do the same.
I learn you take things ill which are not so, / Or being, concern you not.
I hear you're offended by things that aren't offensive, or if they are, they don't concern you.

I must be laugh'd at / If, or for nothing or a little, I / Should say myself offended, and with you / Chiefly i' the world; more laugh'd at that I should / Once name you derogately, when to sound your name / It not concern'd me.

I'd deserve to be laughed at if I said I was offended over nothing or very little, especially with you of all people. And I'd be laughed at even more if I spoke badly of you when it was none of my business to mention you at all.
My being in Egypt, Caesar, / What was't to you?
What was my being in Egypt to you, Caesar?
No more than my residing here at Rome / Might be to you in Egypt: yet, if you there / Did practise on my state, your being in Egypt / Might be my question.
No more than my living here in Rome was to you in Egypt. But if you were plotting against my position from there, then your being in Egypt might well concern me.
You may be pleas'd to catch at mine intent / By what did here befall me. Your wife and brother / Made wars upon me; and their contestation / Was theme for you, you were the word of war.
You can work out what I mean from what happened to me here. Your wife and brother made war on me, and their fight was in your name; you were their battle cry.

You do mistake your business; my brother never / Did urge me in his act: I did inquire it; / And have my learning from some true reports / That drew their swords with you. Did he not rather / Discredit my authority with yours; / And make the wars alike against my stomach, / Having alike your cause? Of this my letters / Before did satisfy you. If you'll patch a quarrel / As matter whole you have not to make it with, / It must not be with this.

You've got it wrong. My brother never used my name in what he did. I looked into it, and I heard from reliable men who fought on your side. Didn't he undermine my authority as much as yours, and make war against my wishes, since your cause was the same as mine? My letters already proved this to you. If you want to patch together a quarrel, and you've no real material to make one from, it can't be with this.
You praise yourself / By laying defects of judgment to me; but / You patch'd up your excuses.
You praise yourself by blaming my judgement, but you've only patched together excuses.

Not so, not so; / I know you could not lack, I am certain on't, / Very necessity of this thought, that I, / Your partner in the cause 'gainst which he fought, / Could not with graceful eyes attend those wars / Which 'fronted mine own peace. As for my wife, / I would you had her spirit in such another: / The third o' the world is yours; which with a snaffle / You may pace easy, but not such a wife.

Not so, not so. I'm certain you must have realised that I, your partner in the cause he was fighting against, couldn't look kindly on wars that threatened my own peace. As for my wife, I wish you had a wife with spirit like hers. A third of the world is yours, and you can control it easily with a light bridle, but not a wife like that.
Would we had all such wives, that the men / Might go to wars with the women.
I wish we all had wives like that, so the men could go to war with the women.

So much uncurbable, her garboils, Caesar, / Made out of her impatience,--which not wanted / Shrewdness of policy too,--I grieving grant / Did you too much disquiet: for that you must / But say I could not help it.

Her wild troubles, Caesar, came from her impatience, though there was some cunning in it too. I'm sorry to admit they caused you too much trouble. As for that, you'll just have to accept that I couldn't help it.
I wrote to you / When rioting in Alexandria; you / Did pocket up my letters, and with taunts / Did gibe my missive out of audience.
I wrote to you while you were partying in Alexandria. You put my letters in your pocket and sent my messenger away with jeers.

Sir, / He fell upon me ere admitted: then / Three kings I had newly feasted, and did want / Of what I was i' the morning: but next day / I told him of myself; which was as much / As to have ask'd him pardon. Let this fellow / Be nothing of our strife; if we contend, / Out of our question wipe him.

Sir, he burst in on me before he was let in. I'd just been feasting three kings and wasn't quite the man I am in the morning. But the next day I told him myself, which was as good as asking his pardon. Let's keep that fellow out of our quarrel. If we argue, let's leave him out of it.
You have broken / The article of your oath; which you shall never / Have tongue to charge me with.
You've broken a term of your oath, which you'll never be able to accuse me of doing.
No; Lepidus, let him speak. / The honour is sacred which he talks on now, / Supposing that I lack'd it.--But on, Caesar; / The article of my oath.
No, Lepidus, let him speak. The honour he's talking about is sacred, if he's suggesting I lack it. But go on, Caesar: the term of my oath.
To lend me arms and aid when I requir'd them; / The which you both denied.
To lend me weapons and help when I asked for them. You refused both.

Neglected, rather; / And then when poison'd hours had bound me up / From mine own knowledge. As nearly as I may, / I'll play the penitent to you: but mine honesty / Shall not make poor my greatness, nor my power / Work without it. Truth is, that Fulvia, / To have me out of Egypt, made wars here; / For which myself, the ignorant motive, do / So far ask pardon as befits mine honour / To stoop in such a case.

Neglected, rather, and at a time when poisoned hours had made me forget myself. As far as I can, I'll apologise to you. But my honesty won't make my greatness smaller, and my power won't act without honesty. The truth is that Fulvia made war here to get me out of Egypt. Since I was the unknowing cause, I ask pardon as far as my honour allows me to stoop in such a case.
If it might please you to enforce no further / The griefs between ye: to forget them quite / Were to remember that the present need / Speaks to atone you.
If you'd agree not to press your grievances any further, and forget them completely, you'd be remembering that the present emergency calls on you to make peace.
Or, if you borrow one another's love for the instant, you may, / when you hear no more words of Pompey, return it again: you shall / have time to wrangle in when you have nothing else to do.
Or, if you borrow each other's love for now, you can give it back when you hear no more about Pompey. You'll have time to squabble when you've nothing else to do.
Thou art a soldier only: speak no more.
You're only a soldier. Say no more.
That truth should be silent I had almost forgot.
I'd almost forgotten that truth should keep quiet.
You wrong this presence; therefore speak no more.
You're being disrespectful to this company. So say no more.
Go to, then; your considerate stone!
All right, then. I'll be your thoughtful stone.

I do not much dislike the matter, but / The manner of his speech; for't cannot be / We shall remain in friendship, our conditions / So differing in their acts. Yet if I knew / What hoop should hold us stanch, from edge to edge / O' the world, I would pursue it.

I don't object so much to what he says as to how he says it. We can't stay friends when we behave so differently. Yet if I knew of a hoop that would hold us firmly together, I'd search for it from one end of the world to the other.
Thou hast a sister by the mother's side, / Admir'd Octavia: great Mark Antony / Is now a widower.
You have a sister on your mother's side, the admired Octavia. Great Mark Antony is now a widower.
Say not so, Agrippa: / If Cleopatra heard you, your reproof / Were well deserv'd of rashness.
Don't say that, Agrippa. If Cleopatra heard you, you'd deserve her rebuke for being so rash.
I am not married, Caesar: let me hear / Agrippa further speak.
I'm not married, Caesar. Let me hear more from Agrippa.

To hold you in perpetual amity, / To make you brothers, and to knit your hearts / With an unslipping knot, take Antony / Octavia to his wife; whose beauty claims / No worse a husband than the best of men; / Whose virtue and whose general graces speak / That which none else can utter. By this marriage / All little jealousies, which now seem great, / And all great fears, which now import their dangers, / Would then be nothing: truths would be tales, / Where now half tales be truths: her love to both / Would each to other, and all loves to both, / Draw after her. Pardon what I have spoke; / For 'tis a studied, not a present thought, / By duty ruminated.

To keep you friends forever, to make you brothers and tie your hearts with a knot that won't slip, let Antony take Octavia as his wife. Her beauty deserves nothing less than the best of men as a husband, and her virtue and graces say more than anyone else could. With this marriage, all the small suspicions that now seem great, and all the great fears that now seem dangerous, would come to nothing. True stories would be dismissed as gossip, where now half-truths are believed. Her love for both of you would draw you to each other, and draw everyone's love to you both. Forgive what I've said. It's a considered idea, not a sudden one, thought over out of duty.
Not till he hears how Antony is touch'd / With what is spoke already.
Not until he hears how Antony feels about what's already been said.
What power is in Agrippa, / If I would say 'Agrippa, be it so,' / To make this good?
What power does Agrippa have to make this happen, if I said, 'Agrippa, let it be so'?
The power of Caesar, and / His power unto Octavia.
Caesar's power, and his power over Octavia.

May I never / To this good purpose, that so fairly shows, / Dream of impediment!--Let me have thy hand: / Further this act of grace; and from this hour / The heart of brothers govern in our loves / And sway our great designs!

May I never dream of any obstacle to this good plan, which looks so promising! Give me your hand. Help this gracious deal along, and from this hour may brotherly hearts rule our love and guide our great plans!
There is my hand. / A sister I bequeath you, whom no brother / Did ever love so dearly: let her live / To join our kingdoms and our hearts; and never / Fly off our loves again!
There's my hand. I give you a sister, loved more dearly than any brother ever loved a sister. Let her live to join our kingdoms and our hearts, and may our friendship never fall apart again!

I did not think to draw my sword 'gainst Pompey; / For he hath laid strange courtesies and great / Of late upon me. I must thank him only, / Lest my remembrance suffer ill report; / At heel of that, defy him.

I didn't expect to draw my sword against Pompey, because he's recently done me great and unusual kindnesses. I must thank him first, so that I'm not called ungrateful. Right after that, I'll challenge him.
Time calls upon's: / Of us must Pompey presently be sought, / Or else he seeks out us.
Time is pressing us. We must go after Pompey immediately, or he'll come after us.
What is his strength / By land?
How strong is he on land?
Great and increasing; but by sea / He is an absolute master.
Strong and growing. But at sea he's in complete control.
So is the fame. / Would we had spoke together! Haste we for it: / Yet, ere we put ourselves in arms, despatch we / The business we have talk'd of.
So they say. I wish we'd talked earlier! Let's hurry. But before we arm ourselves, let's settle the business we've discussed.
With most gladness; / And do invite you to my sister's view, / Whither straight I'll lead you.
Very gladly. And I invite you to meet my sister. I'll take you to her right away.
Let us, Lepidus, / Not lack your company.
Lepidus, don't deny us your company.
Noble Antony, / Not sickness should detain me.
Noble Antony, not even sickness would keep me away.
Half the heart of Caesar, worthy Maecenas!--my honourable friend, / Agrippa!--
Half of Caesar's heart, worthy Maecenas! My honourable friend, Agrippa!
We have cause to be glad that matters are so well digested. You / stay'd well by it in Egypt.
We have reason to be glad that things have been so well settled. You had a good time of it in Egypt.
Ay, sir; we did sleep day out of countenance, and made the night / light with drinking.
Yes, sir. We slept all day till the daylight was embarrassed, and lit up the night with drinking.
Eight wild boars roasted whole at a breakfast, and but twelve / persons there. Is this true?
Eight wild boars roasted whole for breakfast, and only twelve people there. Is that true?
This was but as a fly by an eagle: we had much more monstrous / matter of feast, which worthily deserved noting.
That was like a fly next to an eagle. We had far more amazing feasts, really worth talking about.
She's a most triumphant lady, if report be square to her.
She's a magnificent lady, if the stories about her are accurate.
When she first met Mark Antony she pursed up his heart, upon the / river of Cydnus.
When she first met Mark Antony, on the river Cydnus, she put his heart in her purse.
There she appeared indeed; or my reporter devised well for her.
That's where she really showed herself, or else whoever told me made it up nicely for her.

I will tell you. / The barge she sat in, like a burnish'd throne, / Burn'd on the water: the poop was beaten gold; / Purple the sails, and so perfumed that / The winds were love-sick with them; the oars were silver, / Which to the tune of flutes kept stroke, and made / The water which they beat to follow faster, / As amorous of their strokes. For her own person, / It beggar'd all description: she did lie / In her pavilion,--cloth-of-gold of tissue,-- / O'er-picturing that Venus where we see / The fancy out-work nature: on each side her / Stood pretty dimpled boys, like smiling Cupids, / With divers-colour'd fans, whose wind did seem / To glow the delicate cheeks which they did cool, / And what they undid did.

I'll tell you. The barge she sat in shone like a polished throne and seemed to burn on the water. The stern was beaten gold. The sails were purple and so perfumed that the winds were lovesick for them. The oars were silver and kept time to the music of flutes, making the water they struck follow faster, as if it were in love with their strokes. As for her, she was beyond all description. She lay in her tent, made of gold cloth, looking more beautiful than a painting of Venus in which imagination outdoes nature. On each side of her stood pretty, dimpled boys, like smiling Cupids, with many-coloured fans whose breeze seemed to make her delicate cheeks glow even as it cooled them, undoing what it did.
Oh, what a sight for Antony!

Her gentlewomen, like the Nereids, / So many mermaids, tended her i' the eyes, / And made their bends adornings: at the helm / A seeming mermaid steers: the silken tackle / Swell with the touches of those flower-soft hands / That yarely frame the office. From the barge / A strange invisible perfume hits the sense / Of the adjacent wharfs. The city cast / Her people out upon her; and Antony, / Enthron'd i' the market-place, did sit alone, / Whistling to the air; which, but for vacancy, / Had gone to gaze on Cleopatra too, / And made a gap in nature.

Her ladies, like sea nymphs, like so many mermaids, waited on her every look, and made their bows look graceful. A woman like a mermaid steered at the helm. The silk ropes swelled at the touch of those flower-soft hands that handled them so skilfully. A strange, invisible perfume drifted from the barge and filled the senses of everyone on the nearby wharves. The whole city poured out its people to see her, and Antony, sitting on a throne in the market-place, was left alone, whistling to the air. The air itself would have gone to gaze at Cleopatra too, except that would have left an empty space in nature.

Upon her landing, Antony sent to her, / Invited her to supper: she replied / It should be better he became her guest; / Which she entreated: our courteous Antony, / Whom ne'er the word of 'No' woman heard speak, / Being barber'd ten times o'er, goes to the feast, / And, for his ordinary, pays his heart / For what his eyes eat only.

When she landed, Antony sent to her and invited her to supper. She replied that it would be better if he became her guest, and she begged him to. Our polite Antony, who's never said 'No' to a woman, had himself shaved ten times over and went to the feast. And for his meal he paid with his heart, for what only his eyes ate.
Royal wench! / She made great Caesar lay his sword to bed: / He ploughed her, and she cropp'd.
Royal hussy! She made great Julius Caesar put his sword to bed. He ploughed her, and she bore his child.
I saw her once / Hop forty paces through the public street; / And, having lost her breath, she spoke and panted, / That she did make defect perfection, / And, breathless, power breathe forth.
I saw her once hop forty paces through the public street. She ran out of breath, and spoke and panted so charmingly that she made a fault seem perfect, and, breathless, breathed out power.
Now Antony must leave her utterly.
Now Antony will have to leave her completely.

Never; he will not: / Age cannot wither her, nor custom stale / Her infinite variety: other women cloy / The appetites they feed; but she makes hungry / Where most she satisfies: for vilest things / Become themselves in her; that the holy priests / Bless her when she is riggish.

Never. He won't. Age can't wither her, and familiarity can't make her endless variety go stale. Other women satisfy the appetites they feed until you're sick of them, but she makes you hungry the more she satisfies you. Even the most shameful things become attractive in her, so that the holy priests bless her when she's being lustful.
If beauty, wisdom, modesty, can settle / The heart of Antony, Octavia is / A blessed lottery to him.
If beauty, wisdom and modesty can settle Antony's heart, Octavia is a blessed prize for him.
Let us go.-- / Good Enobarbus, make yourself my guest / Whilst you abide here.
Let's go. Good Enobarbus, be my guest while you're staying here.
The world and my great office will sometimes / Divide me from your bosom.
The world and my great duties will sometimes take me away from your arms.
All which time / Before the gods my knee shall bow my prayers / To them for you.
All that time, I'll kneel before the gods and pray to them for you.
Good night, sir.--My Octavia, / Read not my blemishes in the world's report: / I have not kept my square; but that to come / Shall all be done by the rule. Good night, dear lady.--
Good night, sir. My Octavia, don't judge me by what the world says about my faults. I haven't always kept to the rules, but from now on everything will be done properly. Good night, dear lady.
Now, sirrah, you do wish yourself in Egypt?
Now, fellow, do you wish you were in Egypt?
Would I had never come from thence, nor you / Thither!
I wish I'd never come from there, and that you'd never gone there!
Tell me why, if you can.
I see it in my motion, have it not in my tongue; but yet / Hie you to Egypt again.
I feel it in my mind but can't put it into words. But hurry back to Egypt.
Say to me, / Whose fortunes shall rise higher, Caesar's or mine?
Tell me, whose fortunes will rise higher, Caesar's or mine?

Caesar's. / Therefore, O Antony, stay not by his side: / Thy demon, that thy spirit which keeps thee, is / Noble, courageous, high, unmatchable, / Where Caesar's is not; but near him thy angel / Becomes a fear, as being o'erpower'd: therefore / Make space enough between you.

Caesar's. So, oh Antony, don't stay near him. Your guardian spirit, which protects you, is noble, brave, lofty and unmatched where Caesar's isn't. But near him your angel becomes fearful, as if overpowered. So keep plenty of distance between you.

To none but thee; no more but when to thee. / If thou dost play with him at any game, / Thou art sure to lose; and of that natural luck / He beats thee 'gainst the odds: thy lustre thickens / When he shines by: I say again, thy spirit / Is all afraid to govern thee near him; / But, he away, 'tis noble.

To nobody but you, and only to you. If you play any game with him, you're sure to lose. His natural luck beats you against the odds. Your brightness dims when he shines nearby. I say again: your spirit is afraid to guide you near him, but when he's away, it's noble.
Get thee gone: / Say to Ventidius I would speak with him:--
Go away. Tell Ventidius I want to speak to him.

He shall to Parthia.--Be it art or hap, / He hath spoken true: the very dice obey him;-- / And in our sports my better cunning faints / Under his chance: if we draw lots, he speeds; / His cocks do win the battle still of mine, / When it is all to nought; and his quails ever / Beat mine, inhoop'd, at odds. I will to Egypt: / And though I make this marriage for my peace, / I' the East my pleasure lies.

He'll go to Parthia. Whether by skill or luck, the fortune-teller's right. Even the dice obey Caesar, and in our games my greater skill gives way to his luck. If we draw lots, he wins. His fighting cocks always beat mine, even when the odds are all against him, and his quails always beat mine in the ring. I'll go to Egypt. Though I'm making this marriage for peace, my pleasure lies in the East.
O, come, Ventidius, / You must to Parthia: your commission's ready; / Follow me and receive it.
Oh, come, Ventidius. You must go to Parthia. Your orders are ready. Follow me and collect them.
Trouble yourselves no further: pray you, hasten / Your generals after.
Don't trouble yourselves any further. Please, hurry after your generals.
Sir, Mark Antony / Will e'en but kiss Octavia, and we'll follow.
Sir, Mark Antony will just kiss Octavia goodbye, and then we'll follow.
Till I shall see you in your soldier's dress, / Which will become you both, farewell.
Until I see you in your soldiers' uniforms, which will suit you both, goodbye.
We shall, / As I conceive the journey, be at the mount / Before you, Lepidus.
As I understand the journey, we'll be at the mountain before you, Lepidus.
Your way is shorter; / My purposes do draw me much about. / You'll win two days upon me.
Your route is shorter. My plans take me a long way round. You'll get there two days before me.
Give me some music,--music, moody food / Of us that trade in love.
Give me some music. Music is the sad food of us who deal in love.
Let it alone; let's to billiards: / Come, Charmian.
Forget it. Let's play billiards. Come, Charmian.
My arm is sore; best play with Mardian.
My arm's sore. Better play with Mardian.
As well a woman with an eunuch play'd / As with a woman.--Come, you'll play with me, sir?
A woman might as well play with a eunuch as with a woman. Come, will you play with me, sir?
As well as I can, madam.
As well as I can, madam.

And when good will is show'd, though't come too short, / The actor may plead pardon. I'll none now:-- / Give me mine angle,--we'll to the river. There, / My music playing far off, I will betray / Tawny-finn'd fishes; my bended hook shall pierce / Their slimy jaws; and as I draw them up / I'll think them every one an Antony, / And say 'Ah ha! You're caught.'

And when someone shows good will, even if he falls short, the player can be forgiven. I won't play now. Give me my fishing rod. We'll go to the river. There, with my music playing in the distance, I'll trick the golden-finned fish. My curved hook will pierce their slimy jaws, and as I pull them up I'll imagine every one is an Antony, and say, 'Aha! You're caught.'
'Twas merry when / You wager'd on your angling; when your diver / Did hang a salt fish on his hook, which he / With fervency drew up.
It was funny when you made a bet on your fishing and your diver hung a salted fish on his hook, which he pulled up so eagerly.

That time?--O times!-- / I laughed him out of patience; and that night / I laugh'd him into patience: and next morn, / Ere the ninth hour, I drunk him to his bed; / Then put my tires and mantles on him, whilst / I wore his sword Philippan.

That time? Oh, those times! I laughed him out of his patience, and that night I laughed him back into it. And the next morning, before nine o'clock, I drank him under the table, then dressed him in my headdresses and cloaks while I wore his sword from Philippi.
O! from Italy!-- / Ram thou thy fruitful tidings in mine ears, / That long time have been barren.
Oh! From Italy! Cram your rich news into my ears, which have been empty for so long.

Antony's dead!-- / If thou say so, villain, thou kill'st thy mistress; / But well and free, / If thou so yield him, there is gold, and here / My bluest veins to kiss,--a hand that kings / Have lipp'd, and trembled kissing.

Antony's dead! If you say so, villain, you'll kill your mistress. But if you tell me he's well and free, here's gold, and here are my bluest veins for you to kiss, a hand that kings have kissed and trembled as they kissed it.
Why, there's more gold. / But, sirrah, mark, we use / To say the dead are well: bring it to that, / The gold I give thee will I melt and pour / Down thy ill-uttering throat.
Why, there's more gold. But, fellow, listen: we often say the dead are 'well'. If that's what you mean, I'll melt the gold I gave you and pour it down your evil-speaking throat.

Well, go to, I will; / But there's no goodness in thy face: if Antony / Be free and healthful,--why so tart a favour / To trumpet such good tidings! If not well, / Thou shouldst come like a fury crown'd with snakes, / Not like a formal man.

Well, go on, I will. But there's nothing good in your face. If Antony is free and healthy, why such a sour look to announce such good news? If he isn't well, you should come like a Fury crowned with snakes, not looking like a normal man.
Will you please listen to me?

I have a mind to strike thee ere thou speak'st: / Yet, if thou say Antony lives, is well, / Or friends with Caesar, or not captive to him, / I'll set thee in a shower of gold, and hail / Rich pearls upon thee.
I feel like hitting you before you speak. Yet if you say Antony's alive and well, or friends with Caesar, or not his prisoner, I'll shower you with gold and rain rich pearls on you.
Caesar and he are greater friends than ever.
Caesar and he are greater friends than ever.
Make thee a fortune from me.

I do not like 'but yet', it does allay / The good precedence; fie upon 'but yet'! / 'But yet' is as a gaoler to bring forth / Some monstrous malefactor. Pr'ythee, friend, / Pour out the pack of matter to mine ear, / The good and bad together: he's friends with Caesar; / In state of health, thou say'st; and, thou say'st, free.

I don't like 'but yet'. It spoils the good news that came before it. Curse 'but yet'! 'But yet' is like a jailer bringing out some monstrous criminal. Please, friend, empty the whole bag of news into my ear, good and bad together. He's friends with Caesar, he's healthy, you say, and, you say, free.
Free, madam! no; I made no such report: / He's bound unto Octavia.
Free, madam? No. I never said that. He's bound to Octavia.
Bound to do her what favour?
For the best turn i' the bed.
The most infectious pestilence upon thee! / [Strikes him down.]
May the most infectious plague strike you! [She knocks him down.]
What say you?--Hence, / [Strikes him again.] / Horrible villain! or I'll spurn thine eyes / Like balls before me; I'll unhair thy head:
What did you say? [She hits him again.] Get out, horrible villain, or I'll kick your eyes in front of me like balls! I'll pull out your hair!
Thou shalt be whipp'd with wire and stew'd in brine, / Smarting in ling'ring pickle.
You'll be whipped with wire, and soaked in salt water, stinging in the slow-burning pickle!
Gracious madam, / I that do bring the news made not the match.
Gracious madam, I only bring the news. I didn't arrange the marriage.

Say 'tis not so, a province I will give thee, / And make thy fortunes proud: the blow thou hadst / Shall make thy peace for moving me to rage; / And I will boot thee with what gift beside / Thy modesty can beg.
Say it isn't so, and I'll give you a province and make you rich. The blow you had will make up for making me angry, and I'll give you any other gift you're modest enough to ask for.
Rogue, thou hast liv'd too long. / [Draws a dagger.]
Rogue, you've lived too long. [She draws a dagger.]
Nay, then I'll run.-- / What mean you, madam? I have made no fault.
No, then I'll run. What do you mean, madam? I've done nothing wrong.
Good madam, keep yourself within yourself: / The man is innocent.
Good madam, control yourself. The man is innocent.
Some innocents scape not the thunderbolt.-- / Melt Egypt into Nile! and kindly creatures / Turn all to serpents!--Call the slave again:-- / Though I am mad, I will not bite him:--call!
Some innocent people don't escape the lightning. Let Egypt melt into the Nile, and let all gentle creatures turn into snakes! Call the slave back. Even though I'm mad, I won't bite him. Call him!
These hands do lack nobility, that they strike / A meaner than myself; since I myself / Have given myself the cause.
These hands lack nobility, hitting someone lower than me, when I brought this on myself.
Come hither, sir. / Though it be honest, it is never good / To bring bad news: give to a gracious message / An host of tongues; but let ill tidings tell / Themselves when they be felt.
Come here, sir. Even when it's honest, it's never good to bring bad news. Give good news a whole crowd of tongues, but let bad news announce itself when it's felt.
Is he married? / I cannot hate thee worser than I do / If thou again say 'Yes.'
Is he married? I can't hate you more than I already do if you say 'Yes' again.
The gods confound thee! dost thou hold there still!
May the gods destroy you! Do you still stick to that?

O, I would thou didst, / So half my Egypt were submerg'd, and made / A cistern for scal'd snakes! Go, get thee hence: / Hadst thou Narcissus in thy face, to me / Thou wouldst appear most ugly. He is married?
Oh, I wish you would, even if half my Egypt were flooded and made a tank for scaly snakes! Go, get out of here. Even if you had the face of Narcissus, you'd look ugly to me. He's married?
