Take no offence that I would not offend you: / To punish me for what you make me do / Seems much unequal: he's married to Octavia.
Don't be offended that I don't want to offend you. To punish me for what you make me do seems very unfair. He's married to Octavia.

O, that his fault should make a knave of thee / That art not what tho'rt sure of!--Get thee hence: / The merchandise which thou hast brought from Rome / Are all too dear for me: lie they upon thy hand, / And be undone by 'em!

Oh, that his crime should make a villain of you, when you're not guilty of the news you're so sure of! Get out of here. The goods you've brought from Rome are too expensive for me. Keep them, and may they ruin you!
In praising Antony I have disprais'd Caesar.
In praising Antony, I've criticised Julius Caesar.

I am paid for't now. / Lead me from hence; / I faint:--O Iras, Charmian!--'tis no matter.-- / Go to the fellow, good Alexas; bid him / Report the feature of Octavia, her years, / Her inclination; let him not leave out / The colour of her hair:--bring me word quickly.

Now I'm paying for it. Lead me away. I'm going to faint. Oh, Iras, Charmian! It doesn't matter. Go to the man, good Alexas. Ask him to describe Octavia's looks, her age, her personality. Don't let him leave out the colour of her hair. Bring me word quickly.

Let him for ever go:--let him not, Charmian-- / Though he be painted one way like a Gorgon, / T'other way he's a Mars.--[To Mardian] Bid you Alexas / Bring me word how tall she is.--Pity me, Charmian, / But do not speak to me.--Lead me to my chamber.

Let him go for ever. No, don't, Charmian. Though he looks like a Gorgon from one side, from the other he's a Mars. [To Mardian] Tell Alexas to find out how tall she is. Pity me, Charmian, but don't speak to me. Take me to my room.
Your hostages I have, so have you mine; / And we shall talk before we fight.
I have your hostages, and you have mine. Let's talk before we fight.

Most meet / That first we come to words; and therefore have we / Our written purposes before us sent; / Which, if thou hast consider'd, let us know / If 'twill tie up thy discontented sword, / And carry back to Sicily much tall youth / That else must perish here.

It's right that we talk first, and so we've sent you our proposals in writing. If you've considered them, tell us whether they'll put away your discontented sword and take many fine young men back to Sicily who would otherwise die here.

To you all three, / The senators alone of this great world, / Chief factors for the gods,--I do not know / Wherefore my father should revengers want, / Having a son and friends; since Julius Caesar, / Who at Philippi the good Brutus ghosted, / There saw you labouring for him. What was't / That mov'd pale Cassius to conspire; and what / Made the all-honour'd, honest Roman, Brutus, / With the arm'd rest, courtiers of beauteous freedom, / To drench the Capitol, but that they would / Have one man but a man? And that is it / Hath made me rig my navy; at whose burden / The anger'd ocean foams; with which I meant / To scourge the ingratitude that despiteful Rome / Cast on my noble father.

To all three of you, the only rulers of this great world, the gods' chief agents: I don't see why my father should lack avengers, since he has a son and friends, when Julius Caesar, whose ghost appeared to good Brutus at Philippi, saw you fighting for him there. What made pale Cassius plot? And what made the honoured, honest Roman Brutus, with the other armed lovers of sweet freedom, soak the Capitol in blood, except that they wanted a man to be only a man, not a king? That's why I've rigged up my navy, whose weight makes the angry ocean foam. With it I meant to punish the ingratitude that spiteful Rome showed to my noble father.
Thou canst not fear us, Pompey, with thy sails; / We'll speak with thee at sea: at land thou know'st / How much we do o'er-count thee.
You can't frighten us with your ships, Pompey. We'll meet you at sea. On land, you know how much we outnumber you.
At land, indeed, / Thou dost o'er-count me of my father's house: / But, since the cuckoo builds not for himself, / Remain in't as thou mayst.
On land, it's true, you've outdone me by taking my father's house. But since the cuckoo doesn't build its own nest, stay in it while you can.
Be pleas'd to tell us,-- / For this is from the present,--how you take / The offers we have sent you.
Please tell us (since this is off the point) what you think of the offers we've sent you.
Which do not be entreated to, but weigh / What it is worth embrac'd.
Don't be begged into it. Weigh up what it's worth to accept.
And what may follow, / To try a larger fortune.
And what might happen if you try for more.

You have made me offer / Of Sicily, Sardinia; and I must / Rid all the sea of pirates; then to send / Measures of wheat to Rome; this 'greed upon, / To part with unhack'd edges and bear back / Our targes undinted.

You've offered me Sicily and Sardinia, and I must clear the sea of pirates and send loads of wheat to Rome. If we agree to this, we part with our swords unscratched and take our shields home undented.

Know, then, / I came before you here a man prepar'd / To take this offer: but Mark Antony / Put me to some impatience:--though I lose / The praise of it by telling, you must know, / When Caesar and your brother were at blows, / Your mother came to Sicily, and did find / Her welcome friendly.

Know, then, that I came here ready to accept this offer. But Mark Antony made me a bit impatient. Though I lose the credit by telling it, you should know that when Caesar and your brother were fighting, your mother came to Sicily and was made very welcome.
I have heard it, Pompey, / And am well studied for a liberal thanks / Which I do owe you.
I've heard about it, Pompey, and I've prepared to give you the generous thanks I owe you.
Let me have your hand: / I did not think, sir, to have met you here.
Give me your hand. I didn't expect to meet you here, sir.
The beds i' the East are soft; and, thanks to you, / That call'd me, timelier than my purpose, hither; / For I have gained by it.
The beds in the East are soft. And thanks to you for calling me here sooner than I planned, because I've gained by it.
Since I saw you last / There is a change upon you.
You've changed since I last saw you.
Well, I know not / What counts harsh fortune casts upon my face; / But in my bosom shall she never come / To make my heart her vassal.
Well, I don't know what lines harsh fortune has drawn on my face, but she'll never get inside my heart to make it her slave.
I hope so, Lepidus.--Thus we are agreed: / I crave our composition may be written, / And seal'd between us.
I hope so, Lepidus. So, we're agreed. I want our agreement written down and sealed between us.
That's the next thing to do.
We'll feast each other ere we part; and let's / Draw lots who shall begin.
Let's entertain each other with feasts before we part, and draw lots for who goes first.
No, Antony, take the lot: but, first / Or last, your fine Egyptian cookery / Shall have the fame. I have heard that Julius Caesar / Grew fat with feasting there.
No, Antony, take your chance with the lots. But whether first or last, your fine Egyptian cooking will win the prize. I've heard that Julius Caesar grew fat feasting there.
Then so much have I heard; / And I have heard Apollodorus carried,--
Well, that's what I've heard. And I've heard that Apollodorus carried...
No more of that:--he did so.
No more of that. He did.
A certain queen to Caesar in a mattress.
Carried a certain queen to Caesar rolled up in a mattress.
I know thee now: how far'st thou, soldier?
Now I know you. How are you, soldier?
Well; / And well am like to do; for I perceive / Four feasts are toward.
Well. And likely to do well, because I see four feasts coming up.
Let me shake thy hand; / I never hated thee: I have seen thee fight, / When I have envied thy behaviour.
Let me shake your hand. I never hated you. I've seen you fight and envied your courage.
Sir, / I never lov'd you much; but I ha' prais'd ye / When you have well deserv'd ten times as much / As I have said you did.
Sir, I never liked you much, but I've praised you when you deserved ten times more than I said.
Enjoy thy plainness; / It nothing ill becomes thee.-- / Aboard my galley I invite you all: / Will you lead, lords?
Enjoy your plain speaking. It suits you. I invite you all aboard my ship. Will you lead the way, lords?
[Aside.] Thy father, Pompey, would ne'er have made this treaty.-- / You and I have known, sir.
[Aside] Your father, Pompey, would never have made this treaty. [To Enobarbus] We've met before, sir.
You have done well by water.
I will praise any man that will praise me; though it cannot be / denied what I have done by land.
I'll praise any man who praises me, though no one can deny what I've done on land.
Nor what I have done by water.
Nor what I've done at sea.
Yes, something you can deny for your own safety: you have been a / great thief by sea.
Yes, there's something you'd better deny for your own safety: you've been a great thief at sea.
There I deny my land service. But give me your hand, Menas: if / our eyes had authority, here they might take two thieves kissing.
Then I deny my service on land. But give me your hand, Menas. If our eyes were police, they could arrest two thieves kissing.
All men's faces are true, whatsome'er their hands are.
All men's faces are honest, whatever their hands are.
But there is never a fair woman has a true face.
But no beautiful woman has an honest face.
That's no slander. They steal hearts.
We came hither to fight with you.
We came here to fight you.
For my part, I am sorry it is turn'd to a drinking. Pompey doth / this day laugh away his fortune.
For my part, I'm sorry it's turned into a drinking party. Today Pompey is laughing away his fortune.
If he do, sure he cannot weep it back again.
If he is, he certainly can't cry it back again.
You have said, sir. We look'd not for Mark Antony here: pray you, / is he married to Cleopatra?
You're right, sir. We didn't expect Mark Antony here. Please tell me, is he married to Cleopatra?
True, sir; she was the wife of Caius Marcellus.
True, sir. She was the wife of Caius Marcellus.
But she is now the wife of Marcus Antonius.
But now she's the wife of Marcus Antonius.
Then is Caesar and he for ever knit together.
Then Caesar and he are tied together for ever.
If I were bound to divine of this unity, I would not prophesy so.
If I had to predict the future of this union, I wouldn't say so.
I think the policy of that purpose made more in the marriage than / the love of the parties.
I think politics had more to do with this marriage than love.
I think so too. But you shall find the band that seems to tie / their friendship together will be the very strangler of their / amity:  Octavia is of a holy, cold, and still conversation.
I think so too. But you'll find that the bond which seems to tie their friendship together will be the very thing that strangles it. Octavia is pious, cold and quiet.
Who would not have his wife so?
Who wouldn't want a wife like that?

Not he that himself is not so; which is Mark Antony. He will to / his Egyptian dish again: then shall the sighs of Octavia blow the / fire up in Caesar; and, as I said before, that which is the / strength of their amity shall prove the immediate author of their / variance. Antony will use his affection where it is: he married / but his occasion here.

A man who isn't like that himself, which is Mark Antony. He'll go back to his Egyptian dish. Then Octavia's sighs will fan the flames of Caesar's anger, and, as I said, what now strengthens their friendship will be the direct cause of their quarrel. Antony will give his love where it really is. He only married for convenience here.
And thus it may be. Come, sir, will you aboard? I have a health / for you.
That may well be. Come, sir, will you come aboard? I want to drink your health.
I shall take it, sir: we have used our throats in Egypt.
I'll accept, sir. We've trained our throats in Egypt.
Here they'll be, man. Some o' their plants are ill-rooted / already; the least wind i' the world will blow them down.
Here they come, man. Some of their plants are already badly rooted; the slightest wind in the world will blow them over.
Lepidus is red in the face.
They have made him drink alms-drink.
They've made him drink the leftovers for them.
As they pinch one another by the disposition, he cries out 'no / more'; reconciles them to his entreaty and himself to the drink.
Whenever they needle each other, he shouts 'No more!', makes them make up, and has another drink himself.
But it raises the greater war between him and his discretion.
But that starts a bigger war between him and his good sense.
Why, this it is to have a name in great men's fellowship: I had / as lief have a reed that will do me no service as a partizan I / could not heave.
That's what comes of being named as one of the great men's company. I'd rather have a reed that's no use to me than a spear I can't lift.
To be called into a huge sphere, and not to be seen to move in't, / are the holes where eyes should be, which pitifully disaster the / cheeks.
To be called up into a great position and not be seen to do anything there is like having empty holes where eyes should be, which ruin the face.

[To Caesar.] Thus do they, sir: they take the flow o' the Nile / By certain scales i' the pyramid; they know / By the height, the lowness, or the mean, if dearth / Or foison follow: the higher Nilus swells / The more it promises; as it ebbs, the seedsman / Upon the slime and ooze scatters his grain, / And shortly comes to harvest.

[To Caesar] This is how they do it, sir. They measure the rise of the Nile by marks on the pyramid. They know from how high, low or medium it is whether famine or plenty will follow. The higher the Nile rises, the better the harvest promises. As it goes down, the farmer scatters his seed on the mud and slime, and soon harvests it.
Your serpent of Egypt is bred now of your mud by the operation of / your sun: so is your crocodile.
Your Egyptian serpent is born from your mud by the power of your sun. So is your crocodile.
Sit --and some wine!--A health to Lepidus!
Sit down, and some wine! A toast to Lepidus!
I am not so well as I should be, but I'll ne'er out.
I'm not as well as I should be, but I'll never drop out.
Not till you have slept; I fear me you'll be in till then.
Not until you've slept. I'm afraid you'll be in it till then.
Nay, certainly, I have heard the Ptolemies' pyramises are very / goodly things; without contradiction I have heard that.
No, certainly, I've heard the Ptolemies' pyramids are very fine things. Without contradiction, I've heard that.
[Aside to Menas.] Say in mine ear: what is't?
[Aside to Menas] Whisper in my ear. What is it?
[Aside to Pompey.] Forsake thy seat, I do beseech thee, captain, / And hear me speak a word.
[Aside to Pompey] Leave your seat, I beg you, captain, and listen to me.
[Aside to Menas.] Forbear me till anon-- / This wine for Lepidus!
[Aside to Menas] Wait till later. This wine for Lepidus!
What manner o' thing is your crocodile?
What sort of thing is your crocodile?

It is shaped, sir, like itself; and it is as broad as it hath / breadth: it is just so high as it is, and moves with it own / organs: it lives by that which nourisheth it, and the elements / once out of it, it transmigrates.

It's shaped, sir, like itself, and it's as broad as it is wide. It's exactly as tall as it is, and moves with its own organs. It lives on what feeds it, and when its elements leave it, its soul passes into another body.
'Tis so. And the tears of it are wet.
It is. And its tears are wet.
With the health that Pompey gives him, else he is a very epicure.
Along with the toast Pompey's giving him. Otherwise he's a real glutton.
[Aside to Menas.] Go, hang, sir, hang! Tell me of that! away! / Do as I bid you.--Where's this cup I call'd for?
[Aside to Menas] Go hang yourself, sir! Talk to me about that? Go away! Do as I say. Where's the cup I asked for?
[Aside to Pompey.] If for the sake of merit thou wilt hear me, / Rise from thy stool.
[Aside to Pompey] If you'll listen to me for the sake of my service, get up from your stool.
[Aside to Menas.] I think thou'rt mad.
[Aside to Menas] I think you're mad.
I have ever held my cap off to thy fortunes.
I've always taken my hat off to your fortunes.
Thou hast serv'd me with much faith. / What's else to say?-- / Be jolly, lords.
You've served me very faithfully. What else? Be merry, lords.
These quicksands, Lepidus, / Keep off them, for you sink.
Keep away from these quicksands, Lepidus, or you'll sink.
Wilt thou be lord of all the world?
Do you want to be lord of the whole world?
Wilt thou be lord of the whole world? / That's twice.
Do you want to be lord of the whole world? That's twice I've asked.
But entertain it, / And though you think me poor, I am the man / Will give thee all the world.
Just consider it, and though you think me poor, I'm the man who'll give you the whole world.
No, Pompey, I have kept me from the cup. / Thou art, if thou dar'st be, the earthly Jove: / Whate'er the ocean pales or sky inclips / Is thine, if thou wilt have't.
No, Pompey, I've stayed away from the cup. If you dare, you can be Jupiter on earth. Whatever the ocean encloses or the sky embraces is yours, if you want it.
These three world-sharers, these competitors, / Are in thy vessel: let me cut the cable; / And when we are put off, fall to their throats: / All then is thine.
These three sharers of the world, these partners, are on your ship. Let me cut the anchor cable, and when we're out at sea, cut their throats. Then everything is yours.

Ah, this thou shouldst have done, / And not have spoke on't! In me 'tis villainy: / In thee't had been good service. Thou must know / 'Tis not my profit that does lead mine honour: / Mine honour it. Repent that e'er thy tongue / Hath so betray'd thine act: being done unknown, / I should have found it afterwards well done; / But must condemn it now. Desist, and drink.

Ah, you should have done this and not told me! For me it's villainy; for you it would have been good service. You must understand that my profit doesn't lead my honour; my honour leads it. Regret that your tongue gave away what you were going to do. If you'd done it without my knowing, I'd have approved afterwards. But now I must condemn it. Stop, and drink.
[Aside.] For this, / I'll never follow thy pall'd fortunes more. / Who seeks, and will not take when once 'tis offer'd, / Shall never find it more.
[Aside] Because of this, I'll never follow your faded fortunes again. Whoever looks for something and won't take it when it's offered will never find it again.
Bear him ashore. I'll pledge it for him, Pompey.
Carry him ashore. I'll drink his toast for him, Pompey.
Fill till the cup be hid.
Fill the cup till it overflows.
'A bears the third part of the world, man; see'st not?
He's carrying a third of the world, man. Can't you see?
The third part, then, is drunk; would it were all, / That it might go on wheels!
Then a third of the world is drunk. I wish the whole of it were, so it could go round on wheels!
Drink, then. Make it spin faster.
This is not yet an Alexandrian feast.
This isn't an Alexandrian feast yet.
It ripens towards it.--Strike the vessels, ho!-- / Here is to Caesar!
It's getting there. Clink the cups! Here's to Caesar!
I could well forbear't. / It's monstrous labour when I wash my brain / And it grows fouler.
I'd rather not. It's hard work when I wash my brain and it only gets dirtier.
Be a child o' the time.
Possess it, I'll make answer: / But I had rather fast from all four days / Than drink so much in one.
'Be master of the times', I'd answer. But I'd rather fast for four days than drink so much in one.
[To Antony.] Ha, my brave emperor! / Shall we dance now the Egyptian Bacchanals / And celebrate our drink?
[To Antony] Ha, my brave commander! Shall we dance the Egyptian Bacchanals now and celebrate our drinking?
Come, let's all take hands, / Till that the conquering wine hath steep'd our sense / In soft and delicate Lethe.
Come, let's all hold hands, until the conquering wine has soaked our senses in soft, sweet forgetfulness.

All take hands.-- / Make battery to our ears with the loud music:-- / The while I'll place you: then the boy shall sing; / The holding every man shall bear as loud / As his strong sides can volley. / [Music plays. Enobarbus places them hand in hand.] / Come, thou monarch of the vine, / Plumpy Bacchus with pink eyne! / In thy fats our cares be drown'd, / With thy grapes our hairs be crown'd: / Cup us, till the world go round, / Cup us, till the world go round!

Everyone hold hands. Batter our ears with loud music, while I put you in place. Then the boy will sing, and every man will roar the chorus as loudly as his strong lungs can. [Music plays. Enobarbus places them hand in hand.] SONG: Come, you king of the vine, chubby Bacchus with pink eyes! Let our troubles be drowned in your vats, let our hair be crowned with your grapes. Fill our cups till the world spins round, fill our cups till the world spins round!

What would you more?--Pompey, good night. Good brother, / Let me request you off: our graver business / Frowns at this levity.--Gentle lords, let's part; / You see we have burnt our cheeks: strong Enobarb / Is weaker than the wine; and mine own tongue / Splits what it speaks: the wild disguise hath almost / Antick'd us all. What needs more words. Good night.-- / Good Antony, your hand.

What more do you want? Pompey, good night. Good brother, let me ask you to leave. Our serious business frowns at this frivolity. Gentle lords, let's part. You see we've all gone red in the face. Strong Enobarbus is weaker than the wine, and my own tongue trips over its words. This wild disguise has almost turned us all into clowns. Why say more? Good night. Good Antony, your hand.
I'll try you on the shore.
I'll take you on, on the shore.
And shall, sir: give's your hand.
So you will, sir. Give me your hand.
O Antony, / You have my father's house,--but, what? we are friends. / Come, down into the boat.
Oh Antony, you have my father's house. But what does it matter? We're friends. Come down into the boat.
No, to my cabin.-- / These drums!--these trumpets, flutes! what!-- / Let Neptune hear we bid a loud farewell / To these great fellows: sound and be hang'd, sound out!
No, come to my cabin. These drums! These trumpets, flutes! Let Neptune hear us say a loud farewell to these great men. Play, and be hanged, play loud!
Hooray! he says. There goes my cap.

Now, darting Parthia, art thou struck; and now / Pleas'd fortune does of Marcus Crassus' death / Make me revenger.--Bear the king's son's body / Before our army.--Thy Pacorus, Orodes, / Pays this for Marcus Crassus.

Now, Parthia, you who shoot your darts, you've been struck. And now kind fortune makes me the avenger of Marcus Crassus's death. Carry the king's son's body in front of our army. Orodes, your son Pacorus pays this price for Marcus Crassus.

Noble Ventidius, / Whilst yet with Parthian blood thy sword is warm / The fugitive Parthians follow; spur through Media, / Mesopotamia, and the shelters whither / The routed fly: so thy grand captain Antony / Shall set thee on triumphant chariots, and / Put garlands on thy head.

Noble Ventidius, while your sword is still warm with Parthian blood, chase the fleeing Parthians. Ride hard through Media, Mesopotamia and every hiding place the beaten army runs to. Then your great commander Antony will set you in a victory chariot and put garlands on your head.

O Silius, Silius, / I have done enough: a lower place, note well, / May make too great an act; for learn this, Silius,-- / Better to leave undone, than by our deed / Acquire too high a fame when him we serve's away. / Caesar and Antony have ever won / More in their officer, than person: Sossius, / One of my place in Syria, his lieutenant, / For quick accumulation of renown, / Which he achiev'd by the minute, lost his favour. / Who does i' the wars more than his captain can / Becomes his captain's captain; and ambition, / The soldier's virtue, rather makes choice of loss / Than gain which darkens him. / I could do more to do Antonius good, / But 'twould offend him; and in his offence / Should my performance perish.

Oh Silius, Silius, I've done enough. Remember, a man of lower rank can achieve too much. Learn this, Silius: better leave a thing undone than win too great a fame by it while the man we serve is away. Caesar and Antony have always won more through their officers than in person. Sossius, who held my post in Syria as Antony's lieutenant, lost his favour because he piled up glory too quickly. Whoever does more in war than his commander becomes his commander's commander. And ambition, a soldier's virtue, would rather accept a loss than a gain that puts him in the shade. I could do more to help Antony, but it would offend him, and once he was offended, all my achievements would count for nothing.
Thou hast, Ventidius, that / Without the which a soldier and his sword / Grants scarce distinction. Thou wilt write to Antony?
Ventidius, you have that good sense without which a soldier is hard to tell apart from his sword. Will you write to Antony?

I'll humbly signify what in his name, / That magical word of war, we have effected; / How, with his banners, and his well-paid ranks, / The ne'er-yet-beaten horse of Parthia / We have jaded out o' the field.

I'll humbly tell him what we've achieved in his name, that magic word in war: how, with his banners and his well-paid troops, we've driven the never-beaten Parthian cavalry from the field until they were exhausted.
He purposeth to Athens: whither, with what haste / The weight we must convey with's will permit, / We shall appear before him.--On, there; pass along!
He's heading for Athens. We'll appear before him there, as fast as the heavy loads we must carry allow. March on!

They have despatch'd with Pompey; he is gone; / The other three are sealing. Octavia weeps / To part from Rome: Caesar is sad; and Lepidus, / Since Pompey's feast, as Menas says, is troubled / With the green sickness.

They've finished with Pompey; he's gone. The other three are sealing the agreement. Octavia is weeping to leave Rome; Caesar is sad; and Lepidus, according to Menas, has been suffering from a lovesick young girl's illness since Pompey's feast.
A very fine one: O, how he loves Caesar!
A very fine one. Oh, how he loves Caesar!
Nay, but how dearly he adores Mark Antony!
Yes, but how dearly he adores Mark Antony!
Caesar? Why he's the Jupiter of men.
Caesar? Why, he's the Jupiter of men.
What's Antony? The god of Jupiter.
What's Antony? The god of Jupiter.
Spake you of Caesar? How! the nonpareil!
Did you mention Caesar? What! The one without equal!
O, Antony! O thou Arabian bird!
Oh, Antony! Oh, you phoenix, unique bird of Arabia!
Would you praise Caesar, say 'Caesar'--go no further.
If you want to praise Caesar, just say 'Caesar'. That's enough.
Indeed, he plied them both with excellent praises.
Really, he showered them both with excellent praise.

But he loves Caesar best;--yet he loves Antony: / Hoo! hearts, tongues, figures, scribes, bards, poets, cannot / Think, speak, cast, write, sing, number--hoo!-- / His love to Antony. But as for Caesar, / Kneel down, kneel down, and wonder.

But he loves Caesar best. Yet he loves Antony. Wow! Hearts, tongues, numbers, writers, bards and poets can't think, speak, calculate, write, sing or count his love for Antony. Wow! But as for Caesar, kneel down, kneel down and be amazed.
They are his shards, and he their beetle.
They're his wings, and he's their beetle.
So,-- / This is to horse.--Adieu, noble Agrippa.
So. That's the call to mount up. Goodbye, noble Agrippa.
Good fortune, worthy soldier; and farewell.
Good luck, worthy soldier, and goodbye.

You take from me a great part of myself; / Use me well in't.--Sister, prove such a wife / As my thoughts make thee, and as my furthest band / Shall pass on thy approof.--Most noble Antony, / Let not the piece of virtue which is set / Betwixt us as the cement of our love, / To keep it builded, be the ram to batter / The fortress of it; for better might we / Have lov'd without this mean if on both parts / This be not cherish'd.

You're taking a great part of me away. Treat me well in her. Sister, be the kind of wife I think you are, the kind I'd stake my life on. Most noble Antony, don't let this model of virtue, who is set between us as the cement that holds our friendship together, become the battering ram that knocks it down. It would be better to have stayed friends without her if she isn't cherished by both of us.
Make me not offended / In your distrust.
Don't offend me by distrusting me.
I've said what I wanted to.
You shall not find, / Though you be therein curious, the least cause / For what you seem to fear: so, the gods keep you, / And make the hearts of Romans serve your ends! / We will here part.
However closely you look, you won't find the slightest cause for what you seem to fear. So, may the gods protect you, and make the hearts of Romans serve your purposes! We'll part here.
Farewell, my dearest sister, fare thee well: / The elements be kind to thee, and make / Thy spirits all of comfort! Fare thee well.
Goodbye, my dearest sister, goodbye. May the weather be kind to you and fill your spirits with comfort! Goodbye.
The April's in her eyes: it is love's spring, / And these the showers to bring it on.--Be cheerful.
There's April in her eyes. It's the spring of love, and these are the showers that bring it on. Cheer up.
Sir, look well to my husband's house; and--
Sir, look after my husband's house, and...
I'll tell you in your ear.
Her tongue will not obey her heart, nor can / Her heart inform her tongue,--the swan's down feather, / That stands upon the swell at the full of tide, / And neither way inclines.
Her tongue won't obey her heart, and her heart can't instruct her tongue. She's like a swan's feather floating on the high tide, leaning neither way.
[Aside to Enobarbus.] He has a cloud in's face.
[Aside to Enobarbus] There's a cloud over his face.
[Aside to Agrippa.] He were the worse for that, were he a horse; / So is he, being a man.
[Aside to Agrippa] That would be a fault in a horse, and it's a fault in a man too.
[Aside to Enobarbus.] Why, Enobarbus, / When Antony found Julius Caesar dead, / He cried almost to roaring; and he wept / When at Philippi he found Brutus slain.
[Aside to Enobarbus] Why, Enobarbus, when Antony found Julius Caesar dead, he cried until he was almost roaring. And he wept when he found Brutus dead at Philippi.
[Aside to Agrippa.] That year, indeed, he was troubled with a / rheum; / What willingly he did confound he wail'd: / Believe't till I weep too.
[Aside to Agrippa] That year he certainly had a bad cold. He wept over what he'd been glad to destroy. Believe it when you see me crying too.
No, sweet Octavia, / You shall hear from me still; the time shall not / Out-go my thinking on you.
No, sweet Octavia, you'll keep hearing from me. Time won't run faster than my thoughts of you.
Come, sir, come; / I'll wrestle with you in my strength of love: / Look, here I have you; thus I let you go, / And give you to the gods.
Come, sir, come. I'll wrestle with you in a contest of love. Look, I have you here; now I let you go, and give you to the gods.
Let all the number of the stars give light / To thy fair way!
May every star light your way!
Good majesty, / Herod of Jewry dare not look upon you / But when you are well pleas'd.
Good majesty, even Herod of Judea doesn't dare look at you unless you're in a good mood.
That Herod's head / I'll have: but how? when Antony is gone, / Through whom I might command it?--Come thou near.
I'll have Herod's head. But how, when Antony is gone, through whom I could order it? Come closer.
Madam, in Rome / I look'd her in the face, and saw her led / Between her brother and Mark Antony.
Madam, in Rome. I looked her in the face, and saw her walking between her brother and Mark Antony.
Is she as tall as me?
Is she as tall as me?
Didst hear her speak? is she shrill-tongu'd or low?
Did you hear her speak? Is her voice shrill or low?
Madam, I heard her speak:  she is low-voic'd.
Madam, I heard her speak. She has a low voice.
That's not so good:--he cannot like her long.
That's not so good. He can't like her for long.
Like her! Oh Isis, it's impossible.
I think so, Charmian: dull of tongue and dwarfish!-- / What majesty is in her gait? Remember, / If e'er thou look'dst on majesty.
I think so, Charmian. Dull-voiced and dwarfish! Is there any majesty in the way she walks? Think back, if you've ever seen majesty.
She creeps,-- / Her motion and her station are as one; / She shows a body rather than a life, / A statue than a breather.
She creeps. Moving or standing still, she's the same. She seems more like a body than a living thing, a statue rather than someone who breathes.
It is, or I can't observe anything.
Three in Egypt / Cannot make better note.
There aren't three people in Egypt who could judge better.
He's very knowing; / I do perceive't:--there's nothing in her yet:-- / The fellow has good judgment.
He knows a lot, I can see that. There's nothing special about her yet. The fellow has good judgement.
Guess at her years, I pr'ythee.
And I do think she's thirty.
Bear'st thou her face in mind? is't long or round?
Do you remember her face? Is it long or round?
Round, to the point of being a fault.
For the most part, too, they are foolish that are so.-- / Her hair, what colour?
People with round faces are mostly foolish, too. Her hair, what colour is it?
Brown, madam: and her forehead / As low as she would wish it.
Brown, madam. And her forehead is as low as she could wish it to be.
There's gold for thee. / Thou must not take my former sharpness ill:-- / I will employ thee back again; I find thee / Most fit for business:--go make thee ready; / Our letters are prepar'd.
Here's gold for you. Don't hold my earlier harshness against me. I'll send you back again; I find you very good at this work. Go and get ready. Our letters are prepared.
Indeed, he is so: I repent me much / That so I harried him. Why, methinks, by him, / This creature's no such thing.
Indeed he is. I'm very sorry I treated him so roughly. Why, according to him, this woman is nothing special.
The man hath seen some majesty, and should know.
The man has seen some majesty, so he should know.
Hath he seen majesty? Isis else defend, / And serving you so long!
Has he seen majesty? Isis forbid that he hasn't, after serving you so long!
I have one thing more to ask him yet, good Charmian: / But 'tis no matter; thou shalt bring him to me / Where I will write. All may be well enough.
I've one more thing to ask him, good Charmian. But it doesn't matter. Bring him to me where I'll be writing. Everything may turn out well enough.
I promise you it will, madam.

Nay, nay, Octavia, not only that,-- / That were excusable, that and thousands more / Of semblable import--but he hath wag'd / New wars 'gainst Pompey; made his will, and read it / To public ear: / Spoke scandy of me: when perforce he could not / But pay me terms of honour, cold and sickly / He vented them: most narrow measure lent me; / When the best hint was given him, he not took't, / Or did it from his teeth.

No, no, Octavia, not just that. That would be forgivable, that and thousands more things like it. But he's started new wars against Pompey, made his will and read it out in public. He spoke slightingly of me. When he couldn't avoid praising me, he did it coldly and grudgingly and gave me as little credit as possible. When he had the best opportunity, he didn't take it, or he spoke through gritted teeth.

O my good lord, / Believe not all; or if you must believe, / Stomach not all. A more unhappy lady, / If this division chance, ne'er stood between, / Praying for both parts: / Sure the good gods will mock me presently / When I shall pray 'O, bless my lord and husband!' / Undo that prayer by crying out as loud / 'O, bless my brother!' Husband win, win brother, / Prays and destroys the prayer; no mid-way / 'Twixt these extremes at all.

Oh my good lord, don't believe everything, or if you must believe it, don't resent all of it. If this split happens, there was never a more unhappy lady standing between two sides, praying for both. The good gods will surely mock me when I pray, 'Oh, bless my lord and husband!' and then cancel that prayer by crying just as loudly, 'Oh, bless my brother!' 'Husband win' and 'brother win': each prayer destroys the other. There's no middle way between these extremes.

Gentle Octavia, / Let your best love draw to that point which seeks / Best to preserve it: if I lose mine honour, / I lose myself: better I were not yours / Than yours so branchless. But, as you requested, / Yourself shall go between's: the meantime, lady, / I'll raise the preparation of a war / Shall stain your brother: make your soonest haste; / So your desires are yours.

Gentle Octavia, let your love go to whoever tries hardest to keep it. If I lose my honour, I lose myself. It would be better for me not to be yours at all than to be yours with my branches cut off. But as you asked, you can go between us. Meanwhile, lady, I'll get ready for a war that will put your brother in the shade. Go as quickly as you can. You have what you wanted.

Thanks to my lord. / The Jove of power make me, most weak, most weak, / Your reconciler! Wars 'twixt you twain would be / As if the world should cleave, and that slain men / Should solder up the rift.
Thank you, my lord. May Jupiter, god of power, make me, so weak, so weak, the one who reconciles you! War between you two would be as if the world split apart and dead men had to fill the crack.

When it appears to you where this begins, / Turn your displeasure that way; for our faults / Can never be so equal that your love / Can equally move with them. Provide your going; / Choose your own company, and command what cost / Your heart has mind to.

When you see who started this, turn your anger that way. Our faults can never be so equal that your love can be shared equally between us. Get ready to go. Choose your own companions, and spend whatever you like.
Caesar and Lepidus have made wars upon Pompey.
Caesar and Lepidus have made war on Pompey.
This is old: what is the success?
That's old news. What's the outcome?

Caesar, having made use of him in the wars 'gainst Pompey, / presently denied him rivality; would not let him partake in the / glory of the action: and not resting here, accuses him of letters / he had formerly wrote to Pompey; upon his own appeal, seizes him: / so the poor third is up, till death enlarge his confine.

Caesar used Lepidus in the war against Pompey, then immediately refused to treat him as an equal. He wouldn't let him share in the glory of the victory. And not stopping there, he accuses him of letters he once wrote to Pompey, and on his own accusation has arrested him. So the poor third partner is locked up until death sets him free.
Then, world, thou hast a pair of chaps, no more; / And throw between them all the food thou hast, / They'll grind the one the other. Where's Antony?
Then, world, you have only one pair of jaws now. Throw all the food you have between them, and they'll grind against each other. Where's Antony?
He's walking in the garden--thus; and spurns / The rush that lies before him; cries 'Fool Lepidus!' / And threats the throat of that his officer / That murder'd Pompey.
He's walking in the garden, like this, kicking the rushes in front of him and shouting 'Lepidus, you fool!' And he's threatening to cut the throat of the officer who murdered Pompey.
For Italy and Caesar. More, Domitius; / My lord desires you presently: my news / I might have told hereafter.
For Italy and Caesar. And another thing, Domitius: my lord wants to see you at once. I could have told you my news later.
'Twill be naught; / But let it be.--Bring me to Antony.
It'll come to nothing. But never mind. Take me to Antony.

Contemning Rome, he has done all this, and more, / In Alexandria. Here's the manner of't:-- / I' the market-place, on a tribunal silver'd, / Cleopatra and himself in chairs of gold / Were publicly enthron'd: at the feet sat / Caesarion, whom they call my father's son, / And all the unlawful issue that their lust / Since then hath made between them. Unto her / He gave the 'stablishment of Egypt; made her / Of lower Syria, Cyprus, Lydia, / Absolute queen.

Scorning Rome, he's done all this and more in Alexandria. This is how it happened. In the market-place, on a silver platform, Cleopatra and he sat publicly enthroned on golden chairs. At their feet sat Caesarion, whom they call my father's son, and all the illegitimate children their lust has produced since. He gave her the rule of Egypt and made her absolute queen of lower Syria, Cyprus and Lydia.

I' the common show-place, where they exercise. / His sons he there proclaim'd the kings of kings: / Great Media, Parthia, and Armenia, / He gave to Alexander; to Ptolemy he assign'd / Syria, Cilicia, and Phoenicia: she / In the habiliments of the goddess Isis / That day appear'd; and oft before gave audience, / As 'tis reported, so.

In the public stadium where they hold games. There he proclaimed his sons kings of kings. He gave Great Media, Parthia and Armenia to Alexander; to Ptolemy he gave Syria, Cilicia and Phoenicia. That day she appeared dressed as the goddess Isis, and it's said she often received visitors dressed like that before.
Let Rome be told about this.
Who, queasy with his insolence / Already, will their good thoughts call from him.
Rome is already sick of his arrogance and will stop thinking well of him.
The people knows it: and have now receiv'd / His accusations.
The people know about it, and they've now received his accusations.

Caesar: and that, having in Sicily / Sextus Pompeius spoil'd, we had not rated him / His part o' the isle: then does he say he lent me / Some shipping, unrestor'd: lastly, he frets / That Lepidus of the triumvirate / Should be depos'd; and, being, that we detain / All his revenue.

Me. He says that after I took Sicily from Sextus Pompeius, I didn't give him his share of the island. Then he says he lent me some ships that I didn't return. Finally he's angry that Lepidus was removed from the triumvirate, and, having removed him, that we keep all his income.

'Tis done already, and messenger gone. / I have told him Lepidus was grown too cruel; / That he his high authority abus'd, / And did deserve his change: for what I have conquer'd / I grant him part; but then, in his Armenia / And other of his conquer'd kingdoms, I / Demand the like.

It's already done, and the messenger has gone. I've told him Lepidus had become too cruel, abused his great authority and deserved to lose it. I'll give him part of what I've conquered, but in return I demand the same share of his Armenia and his other conquered kingdoms.
Nor must not then be yielded to in this.
Then he mustn't be given what he wants either.
Hail, Caesar, and my lord! hail, most dear Caesar!
Greetings, Caesar, my lord! Greetings, dearest Caesar!
That ever I should call thee castaway!
To think I should ever call you an outcast!
You have not call'd me so, nor have you cause.
You haven't called me that, and you have no reason to.

Why have you stol'n upon us thus? You come not / Like Caesar's sister: the wife of Antony / Should have an army for an usher, and / The neighs of horse to tell of her approach / Long ere she did appear; the trees by the way / Should have borne men; and expectation fainted, / Longing for what it had not; nay, the dust / Should have ascended to the roof of heaven, / Rais'd by your populous troops: but you are come / A market-maid to Rome; and have prevented / The ostentation of our love, which left unshown / Is often left unlov'd; we should have met you / By sea and land; supplying every stage / With an augmented greeting.

Why have you crept up on us like this? You don't arrive like Caesar's sister. The wife of Antony should have an army to announce her, and the neighing of horses telling of her approach long before she appeared. The trees along the road should have been full of people climbing them to see, and the crowds should have fainted with longing to see her. Why, the dust raised by your huge escort should have risen to the roof of heaven. But you've come to Rome like a girl going to market, and prevented us from showing our love, which, when it isn't shown, often goes unfelt. We should have met you by sea and land, greeting you more grandly at every stage.

Good my lord, / To come thus was I not constrain'd, but did it / On my free will. My lord, Mark Antony, / Hearing that you prepar'd for war, acquainted / My grieved ear withal: whereon I begg'd / His pardon for return.

My good lord, I wasn't forced to come like this; I did it of my own free will. My lord, Mark Antony, hearing that you were preparing for war, told me about it, which grieved me. So I begged his permission to come back.
Which soon he granted, / Being an obstruct 'tween his lust and him.
Which he quickly gave, since you stood in the way of him and his lust.
Do not say so, my lord.
I have eyes upon him, / And his affairs come to me on the wind. / Where is he now?
I have spies watching him, and news of what he does reaches me on the wind. Where is he now?

No, my most wronged sister; Cleopatra / Hath nodded him to her. He hath given his empire / Up to a whore; who now are levying / The kings o' the earth for war: he hath assembled / Bocchus, the king of Libya; Archelaus / Of Cappadocia; Philadelphos, king / Of Paphlagonia; the Thracian king, Adallas; / King Manchus of Arabia; King of Pont; / Herod of Jewry; Mithridates, king / Of Comagene; Polemon and Amyntas, / The kings of Mede and Lycaonia, with / More larger list of sceptres.

No, my most wronged sister. Cleopatra has beckoned him to her. He's given his empire to a whore, and now they're gathering the kings of the earth for war. He's collected Bocchus, king of Libya; Archelaus of Cappadocia; Philadelphos, king of Paphlagonia; the Thracian king Adallas; King Manchus of Arabia; the King of Pontus; Herod of Judea; Mithridates, king of Commagene; Polemon and Amyntas, the kings of Media and Lycaonia, and a longer list of kings besides.
Ay me, most wretched, / That have my heart parted betwixt two friends, / That do afflict each other!
Oh, how wretched I am, with my heart divided between two people I love who are hurting each other!

Welcome hither: / Your letters did withhold our breaking forth, / Till we perceiv'd both how you were wrong led / And we in negligent danger. Cheer your heart: / Be you not troubled with the time, which drives / O'er your content these strong necessities; / But let determin'd things to destiny / Hold unbewail'd their way. Welcome to Rome; / Nothing more dear to me. You are abus'd / Beyond the mark of thought: and the high gods, / To do you justice, make their ministers / Of us and those that love you. Best of comfort; / And ever welcome to us.

Welcome here. Your letters held us back from breaking out against him, until we saw how you were misled and how dangerously careless we were being. Cheer up. Don't be troubled by the times, which force these harsh necessities on your happiness. Let what fate has decided go its way without grieving. Welcome to Rome; nothing is dearer to me. You've been wronged beyond belief, and the high gods, to do you justice, are making us and those who love you their agents. Take comfort, and always be welcome here.

Welcome, dear madam. / Each heart in Rome does love and pity you: / Only the adulterous Antony, most large / In his abominations, turns you off, / And gives his potent regiment to a trull / That noises it against us.

Welcome, dear madam. Every heart in Rome loves and pities you. Only adulterous Antony, so enormous in his disgusting behaviour, throws you aside and hands his great power to a slut who stirs it up against us.
Most certain. Sister, welcome: pray you / Be ever known to patience: my dear'st sister!
Quite certain. Sister, welcome. Please always be patient. My dearest sister!
I will be even with thee, doubt it not.
I'll get even with you, don't doubt it.
Thou hast forspoke my being in these wars, / And say'st it is not fit.
You've spoken against my being in these wars and said it isn't right.
If not denounc'd against us, why should not we / Be there in person?
Even if war wasn't declared on me personally, why shouldn't I be there in person?
[Aside.] Well, I could reply:-- / If we should serve with horse and mares together / The horse were merely lost; the mares would bear / A soldier and his horse.
[Aside] Well, I could answer this: if we took stallions and mares to war together, the stallions would be completely useless, because the mares would carry a soldier and his horse.

Your presence needs must puzzle Antony; / Take from his heart, take from his brain, from's time, / What should not then be spar'd. He is already / Traduc'd for levity: and 'tis said in Rome / That Photinus an eunuch and your maids / Manage this war.

Your presence is bound to distract Antony. It will take from his heart, his brain and his time what he can't spare right now. He's already criticised for being frivolous, and in Rome they say that a eunuch called Photinus and your maids are running this war.

Sink Rome, and their tongues rot / That speak against us! A charge we bear i' the war, / And, as the president of my kingdom, will / Appear there for a man. Speak not against it; / I will not stay behind.
Let Rome sink, and let the tongues that speak against us rot! I'm paying for this war, and as the ruler of my kingdom I'll be there like a man. Don't argue against it. I won't stay behind.
Nay, I have done. / Here comes the emperor.
No, I've finished. Here comes the commander.
Is it not strange, Canidius, / That from Tarentum and Brundusium / He could so quickly cut the Ionian sea, / And take in Toryne?--You have heard on't, sweet?
Isn't it strange, Canidius, that he could cross the Ionian Sea so quickly from Tarentum and Brundisium, and capture Toryne? Have you heard about it, sweet?
Celerity is never more admir'd / Than by the negligent.
Speed is never more admired than by people who are slow.
A good rebuke, / Which might have well becom'd the best of men / To taunt at slackness.--Canidius, we / Will fight with him by sea.
A good rebuke, which would have suited the best of men, to mock slackness. Canidius, we'll fight him at sea.
Why will my lord do so?
Why will my lord do that?
For that he dares us to't.
So hath my lord dar'd him to single fight.
And my lord has dared him to fight one to one.
Ay, and to wage this battle at Pharsalia, / Where Caesar fought with Pompey. But these offers, / Which serve not for his vantage, he shakes off; / And so should you.
Yes, and to fight this battle at Pharsalia, where Julius Caesar fought Pompey. But he brushes aside these offers when they don't suit him, and so should you.

Your ships are not well mann'd: / Your mariners are muleteers, reapers, people / Ingross'd by swift impress; in Caesar's fleet / Are those that often have 'gainst Pompey fought: / Their ships are yare; yours heavy: no disgrace / Shall fall you for refusing him at sea, / Being prepar'd for land.

Your ships aren't properly manned. Your sailors are mule-drivers, farm workers, men rounded up by press-gangs. In Caesar's fleet are men who've often fought against Pompey. Their ships are quick to handle; yours are heavy. It's no disgrace to refuse to fight him at sea when you're ready to fight on land.

Most worthy sir, you therein throw away / The absolute soldiership you have by land; / Distract your army, which doth most consist / Of war-mark'd footmen; leave unexecuted / Your own renowned knowledge; quite forgo / The way which promises assurance; and / Give up yourself merely to chance and hazard / From firm security.

Most worthy sir, by doing that you throw away your complete mastery as a soldier on land. You divide your army, which is mostly made up of battle-hardened foot soldiers. You leave your famous skill unused, abandon the way that promises success, and give yourself up entirely to chance and risk instead of firm security.
I have sixty sails, Caesar none better.
I have sixty ships. Caesar has none better.
Our overplus of shipping will we burn; / And, with the rest full-mann'd, from the head of Actium / Beat the approaching Caesar. But if we fail, / We then can do't at land.
We'll burn our extra ships, and with the rest fully manned we'll beat Caesar off the point of Actium as he approaches. But if we fail, we can still fight on land.
The news is true, my lord: he is descried; / Caesar has taken Toryne.
The news is true, my lord. He's been sighted. Caesar has taken Toryne.

Can he be there in person? 'tis impossible-- / Strange that his power should be.--Canidius, / Our nineteen legions thou shalt hold by land, / And our twelve thousand horse.--We'll to our ship: / Away, my Thetis!

Can he be there in person? It's impossible. It's strange enough that his army is. Canidius, you'll command our nineteen legions on land, and our twelve thousand cavalry. We'll go to our ship. Away, my Thetis!

O noble emperor, do not fight by sea; / Trust not to rotten planks: do you misdoubt / This sword and these my wounds? Let the Egyptians / And the Phoenicians go a-ducking: we / Have us'd to conquer standing on the earth / And fighting foot to foot.

Oh noble commander, don't fight at sea. Don't trust rotten planks. Do you doubt this sword and these wounds of mine? Let the Egyptians and the Phoenicians go swimming. We're used to winning standing on the ground and fighting hand to hand.
By Hercules, I think I am i' the right.
By Hercules, I think I'm right.
Soldier, thou art: but his whole action grows / Not in the power on't: so our leader's led, / And we are women's men.
You are, soldier. But his whole campaign isn't being run by the part of the army where his strength lies. So our leader is being led, and we're women's men.
You keep by land / The legions and the horse whole, do you not?
You're keeping the legions and the cavalry all together on land, aren't you?
Marcus Octavius, Marcus Justeius, / Publicola, and Caelius are for sea: / But we keep whole by land. This speed of Caesar's / Carries beyond belief.
Marcus Octavius, Marcus Justeius, Publicola and Caelius are going to sea, but we keep the rest together on land. Caesar's speed is unbelievable.
While he was yet in Rome / His power went out in such distractions as / Beguil'd all spies.
While he was still in Rome, his forces set out in such small groups that they fooled all our spies.
Have you heard who his lieutenant is?
They say a man called Taurus.
The commander is calling for Canidius.
With news the time's with labour; and throes forth / Each minute some.
The times are in labour with news, and give birth to more every minute.
Strike not by land; keep whole; provoke not battle / Till we have done at sea. Do not exceed / The prescript of this scroll: our fortune lies / Upon this jump.
Don't attack on land. Keep your army together. Don't start a battle until we've finished at sea. Don't go beyond the orders in this scroll. Our fortune depends on this gamble.
Set we our squadrons on yon side o' the hill, / In eye of Caesar's battle; from which place / We may the number of the ships behold, / And so proceed accordingly.
Let's put our troops on that side of the hill, in sight of Caesar's army. From there we can count his ships and act accordingly.
Naught, naught, all naught! I can behold no longer: / The Antoniad, the Egyptian admiral, / With all their sixty, fly and turn the rudder: / To see't mine eyes are blasted.
Ruin, ruin, total ruin! I can't watch any longer. The Antoniad, the Egyptian flagship, is turning and running away with all their sixty ships. Seeing it blinds my eyes.
Gods and goddesses, / All the whole synod of them!
Gods and goddesses, the whole council of them!
The greater cantle of the world is lost / With very ignorance; we have kiss'd away / Kingdoms and provinces.
The greater part of the world has been lost through sheer stupidity. We've kissed away kingdoms and provinces.

On our side like the token'd pestilence, / Where death is sure. Yon ribaudred nag of Egypt,-- / Whom leprosy o'ertake!--i' the midst o' the fight, / When vantage like a pair of twins appear'd, / Both as the same, or rather ours the elder,-- / The breese upon her, like a cow in June,-- / Hoists sails and flies.

On our side, like the plague when the spots appear and death is certain. That filthy Egyptian nag (may leprosy take her!), in the middle of the fight, when the advantages on each side were as equal as twins, or ours were greater, like a cow in June stung by a gadfly, raised her sails and ran away.
That I beheld: / Mine eyes did sicken at the sight, and could not / Endure a further view.
I saw that. It made my eyes sick, and I couldn't bear to watch any more.

She once being loof'd, / The noble ruin of her magic, Antony, / Claps on his sea-wing, and, like a doting mallard, / Leaving the fight in height, flies after her: / I never saw an action of such shame; / Experience, manhood, honour, ne'er before / Did violate so itself.

Once she'd turned into the wind, Antony, the noble victim of her magic, spread his sails and, like a lovesick duck, left the battle at its height and flew after her. I've never seen anything so shameful. Experience, manhood and honour have never betrayed themselves like this before.

Our fortune on the sea is out of breath, / And sinks most lamentably. Had our general / Been what he knew himself, it had gone well: / O, he has given example for our flight / Most grossly by his own!

Our fortune at sea is out of breath and sinking miserably. If our general had been the man he knows himself to be, it would have gone well. Oh, he's set us an example of running away, a shameful one, by doing it himself!
Ay, are you thereabouts? / Why, then, good night indeed.
Oh, is that what you're thinking? Then it really is all over.
'Tis easy to't; and there I will attend / What further comes.
It's easy to get there, and I'll wait there to see what happens next.
To Caesar will I render / My legions and my horse; six kings already / Show me the way of yielding.
I'll surrender my legions and cavalry to Caesar. Six kings have already shown me how to give in.
I'll yet follow / The wounded chance of Antony, though my reason / Sits in the wind against me.
I'll still follow Antony's wounded fortunes, though my reason is blowing against me.

Hark! the land bids me tread no more upon't;-- / It is asham'd to bear me.--Friends, come hither: / I am so lated in the world that I / Have lost my way for ever:--I have a ship / Laden with gold; take that; divide it; fly, / And make your peace with Caesar.

Listen! The ground tells me not to walk on it any more. It's ashamed to carry me. Friends, come here. I'm like a traveller caught out after dark; I've lost my way for ever. I have a ship loaded with gold. Take it, share it out, run, and make your peace with Caesar.

I have fled myself, and have instructed cowards / To run and show their shoulders.--Friends, be gone; / I have myself resolv'd upon a course / Which has no need of you; be gone; / My treasure's in the harbour, take it.--O, / I follow'd that I blush to look upon: / My very hairs do mutiny; for the white / Reprove the brown for rashness, and they them / For fear and doting.--Friends, be gone: you shall / Have letters from me to some friends that will / Sweep your way for you. Pray you, look not sad, / Nor make replies of loathness: take the hint / Which my despair proclaims; let that be left / Which leaves itself: to the sea-side straightway: / I will possess you of that ship and treasure. / Leave me, I pray, a little: pray you now:-- / Nay, do so; for indeed I have lost command, / Therefore I pray you:--I'll see you by and by.

I've run away myself, and taught cowards to turn and show their backs. Friends, go. I've decided on a course that doesn't need you. Go. My treasure's in the harbour; take it. Oh, I followed what I'm ashamed to look at. Even my hair is rebelling: the white hairs scold the brown ones for being rash, and the brown ones scold the white for being cowardly and foolish. Friends, go. I'll give you letters to some friends who'll clear your way for you. Please don't look sad or show you're unwilling. Take the hint my despair is giving you. Let what abandons itself be abandoned. Go straight to the shore. I'll give you that ship and the treasure. Please leave me for a while. Please, now. No, do it, because I've lost the right to command you, so I'm asking you. I'll see you soon.
Nay, gentle madam, to him!--comfort him.
No, gentle madam, go to him! Comfort him.
Do it! What else can you do?
Let me sit down. O Juno!
Let me sit down. Oh, Juno!
Do you see who's here, sir?

Yes, my lord, yes;--he at Philippi kept / His sword e'en like a dancer; while I struck / The lean and wrinkled Cassius; and 'twas I / That the mad Brutus ended; he alone / Dealt on lieutenantry, and no practice had / In the brave squares of war: yet now--no matter.

Yes, my lord, yes. At Philippi he kept his sword in its sheath like a dancer, while I struck down the thin, wrinkled Cassius, and it was I who finished off the mad Brutus. He only fought through his officers and had no experience of brave battle formations. And yet now... It doesn't matter.
The queen, my lord, the queen!
The queen, my lord, the queen!
Go to him, madam, speak to him: / He is unqualitied with very shame.
Go to him, madam, speak to him. He's not himself out of pure shame.
Well then, hold me up. Oh!
Most noble sir, arise; the queen approaches: / Her head's declin'd, and death will seize her, but / Your comfort makes the rescue.
Most noble sir, get up. The queen is coming. Her head's drooping, and death will take her unless your comfort rescues her.
I have offended reputation,-- / A most unnoble swerving.
I've damaged my reputation. A most dishonourable lapse.
O, whither hast thou led me, Egypt? See / How I convey my shame out of thine eyes / By looking back, what I have left behind / 'Stroy'd in dishonour.
Oh, where have you led me, Egypt? See how I hide my shame from your eyes by looking back at what I've left behind, destroyed in dishonour.
O my lord, my lord, / Forgive my fearful sails! I little thought / You would have follow'd.
Oh my lord, my lord, forgive my frightened sails! I never thought you'd follow.

Egypt, thou knew'st too well / My heart was to thy rudder tied by the strings, / And thou shouldst tow me after: o'er my spirit / Thy full supremacy thou knew'st, and that / Thy beck might from the bidding of the gods / Command me.

Egypt, you knew too well that my heart was tied to your rudder by its strings, and that you'd pull me along after you. You knew you had complete power over my spirit, and that one nod from you could make me disobey the gods.

Now I must / To the young man send humble treaties, dodge / And palter in the shifts of lowness; who / With half the bulk o' the world play'd as I pleas'd, / Making and marring fortunes. You did know / How much you were my conqueror; and that / My sword, made weak by my affection, would / Obey it on all cause.

Now I must send humble peace offers to that young man, and dodge and shuffle in the tricks of the defeated: I, who played with half the world as I liked, making and breaking fortunes. You knew how completely you'd conquered me, and that my sword, weakened by my love, would obey it whatever the cause.

Fall not a tear, I say; one of them rates / All that is won and lost: give me a kiss; / Even this repays me.--We sent our schoolmaster; / Is he come back?--Love, I am full of lead.-- / Some wine, within there, and our viands!--Fortune knows / We scorn her most when most she offers blows.

Don't let a tear fall, I tell you. One of them is worth everything that's been won and lost. Give me a kiss. Even this repays me. We sent our schoolmaster to Caesar; has he come back? Love, I feel heavy as lead. Some wine, in there, and food! Fortune knows we scorn her most when she hits us hardest.
Let him appear that's come from Antony.-- / Know you him?
Let the man from Antony come in. Do you know him?
Caesar, 'tis his schoolmaster: / An argument that he is pluck'd, when hither / He sends so poor a pinion of his wing, / Which had superfluous kings for messengers / Not many moons gone by.
Caesar, it's his children's tutor. That proves he's been plucked bare, if he sends such a poor feather from his wing, when not many months ago he had kings to spare as messengers.
Such as I am, I come from Antony: / I was of late as petty to his ends / As is the morn-dew on the myrtle leaf / To his grand sea.
Lowly as I am, I come from Antony. Until recently I was as unimportant to his affairs as the morning dew on a myrtle leaf is to the great sea.
So be it. State your business.

Lord of his fortunes he salutes thee, and / Requires to live in Egypt: which not granted, / He lessens his requests; and to thee sues / To let him breathe between the heavens and earth, / A private man in Athens: this for him. / Next, Cleopatra does confess thy greatness; / Submits her to thy might, and of thee craves / The circle of the Ptolemies for her heirs, / Now hazarded to thy grace.

He greets you as the master of his fortunes and asks to live in Egypt. If that isn't allowed, he asks for less, and begs you to let him breathe between heaven and earth as a private citizen in Athens. That's for him. Next, Cleopatra acknowledges your greatness, submits to your power, and asks you to let her heirs keep the crown of the Ptolemies, which now depends on your mercy.

For Antony, / I have no ears to his request. The queen / Of audience nor desire shall fail; so she / From Egypt drive her all-disgraced friend, / Or take his life there: this if she perform, / She shall not sue unheard. So to them both.

As for Antony, I won't listen to his request. The queen will get a hearing and her wishes, provided she drives her disgraced lover out of Egypt or kills him there. If she does this, she won't plead unheard. Tell them both that.

[To Thyreus.] To try thy eloquence, now 'tis time. Despatch; / From Antony win Cleopatra. Promise, / And in our name, what she requires; add more, / From thine invention, offers: women are not / In their best fortunes strong; but want will perjure / The ne'er-touch'd vestal: try thy cunning, Thyreus; / Make thine own edict for thy pains, which we / Will answer as a law.

[To Thyreus] Now's the time to test your skill with words. Hurry. Win Cleopatra away from Antony. Promise her in our name whatever she asks, and invent more offers of your own. Women aren't strong even when things are going well, but need will make even a pure Vestal virgin break her vows. Use your cunning, Thyreus. Name your own reward for your efforts, and we'll honour it as law.
Observe how Antony becomes his flaw, / And what thou think'st his very action speaks / In every power that moves.
Notice how Antony bears his fall, and what you think his behaviour reveals in every move he makes.
Is Antony or we in fault for this?
Is Antony to blame for this, or me?

Antony only, that would make his will / Lord of his reason. What though you fled / From that great face of war, whose several ranges / Frighted each other? why should he follow? / The itch of his affection should not then / Have nick'd his captainship; at such a point, / When half to half the world oppos'd, he being / The mered question; 'twas a shame no less / Than was his loss, to course your flying flags / And leave his navy gazing.

Antony alone, who let his desire rule his reason. So what if you ran from that great face of war, where the ranks of ships terrified each other? Why did he have to follow? The itch of his passion shouldn't have cut into his leadership at a time like that, when half the world was fighting the other half and he was the whole cause of it. It was as shameful as his defeat, to chase after your fleeing ships and leave his navy staring.
The queen shall then have courtesy, so she / Will yield us up.
Then the queen will be treated kindly, if she'll hand us over.
Let her know't.-- / To the boy Caesar send this grizzled head, / And he will fill thy wishes to the brim / With principalities.
Let her know it. Send this grey head to the boy Caesar, and he'll fill your wishes to the brim with kingdoms.

To him again: tell him he wears the rose / Of youth upon him; from which the world should note / Something particular: his coins, ships, legions, / May be a coward's; whose ministers would prevail / Under the service of a child as soon / As i' the command of Caesar: I dare him therefore / To lay his gay comparisons apart, / And answer me declin'd, sword against sword, / Ourselves alone. I'll write it: follow me.

Go back to him. Tell him he has the bloom of youth on him, and the world should expect something special from him. His money, ships and legions could belong to a coward, and his officers might win just as well serving a child as under Caesar's command. So I dare him to put aside these showy advantages and fight me, the older man, sword against sword, just the two of us. I'll write it. Follow me.

Yes, like enough high-battled Caesar will / Unstate his happiness, and be stag'd to the show / Against a sworder.--I see men's judgments are / A parcel of their fortunes; and things outward / Do draw the inward quality after them, / To suffer all alike. That he should dream, / Knowing all measures, the full Caesar will / Answer his emptiness!--Caesar, thou hast subdu'd / His judgment too.

[Aside] Oh yes, very likely high-commanding Caesar will throw away his good fortune and put himself on show fighting a swordsman! I see that men's judgement is part of their fortune, and their outward circumstances drag their inner qualities down with them, so both suffer alike. That he should dream, knowing how things stand, that Caesar, with everything, would answer him, with nothing! Caesar, you've conquered his judgement too.
What, no more ceremony?--See, my women!-- / Against the blown rose may they stop their nose / That kneel'd unto the buds.--Admit him, sir.
What, no more ceremony than that? See, my women! People who knelt to the rosebuds hold their noses at the full-blown rose. Let him in, sir.

[Aside.] Mine honesty and I begin to square. / The loyalty well held to fools does make / Our faith mere folly:--yet he that can endure / To follow with allegiance a fallen lord / Does conquer him that did his master conquer, / And earns a place i' the story.

[Aside] My honesty and I are beginning to quarrel. Loyalty kept up towards fools turns faithfulness into plain foolishness. And yet the man who can bear to stay loyal to a fallen lord conquers the one who conquered his master, and earns a place in history.
There's no one here but friends. Speak boldly.
So, haply, are they friends to Antony.
Then perhaps they're also friends of Antony.
He needs as many, sir, as Caesar has; / Or needs not us. If Caesar please, our master / Will leap to be his friend: for us, you know / Whose he is we are, and that is Caesar's.

He needs as many friends, sir, as Caesar has, or else he doesn't need us. If Caesar wishes, our master will jump at the chance to be his friend. As for us, you know we belong to whoever he belongs to, and that will be Caesar.
So.-- / Thus then, thou most renown'd: Caesar entreats / Not to consider in what case thou stand'st / Further than he is Caesar.
So. Then, most famous queen, Caesar begs you not to worry about your situation, beyond remembering that he is Caesar.
Go on. Very royal of him.
He knows that you embrace not Antony / As you did love, but as you fear'd him.
He knows that you didn't take up with Antony out of love, but out of fear.
The scars upon your honour, therefore, he / Does pity, as constrained blemishes, / Not as deserv'd.
So he pities the scars on your honour, as stains you were forced into, not ones you deserved.
He is a god, and knows / What is most right: mine honour was not yielded, / But conquer'd merely.
He's a god and knows what's right. My honour wasn't given up, just conquered by force.
[Aside.] To be sure of that, / I will ask Antony.--Sir, sir, thou art so leaky / That we must leave thee to thy sinking, for / Thy dearest quit thee.
[Aside] To be sure of that, I'll ask Antony. Sir, sir, you're so leaky we'll have to leave you to sink, because your dearest is deserting you.

Shall I say to Caesar / What you require of him? for he partly begs / To be desir'd to give. It much would please him / That of his fortunes you should make a staff / To lean upon: but it would warm his spirits / To hear from me you had left Antony, / And put yourself under his shroud, who is / The universal landlord.

Shall I tell Caesar what you want from him? He's almost begging to be asked to give. It would please him greatly if you made his fortunes a staff to lean on. But it would warm his heart to hear from me that you'd left Antony and put yourself under his protection, since he's lord of all the world.

Most kind messenger, / Say to great Caesar this:--in deputation / I kiss his conquring hand: tell him I am prompt / To lay my crown at's feet, and there to kneel: / Tell him, from his all-obeying breath I hear / The doom of Egypt.

Most kind messenger, tell great Caesar this: through you, I kiss his conquering hand. Tell him I'm ready to lay my crown at his feet and kneel there. Tell him I'll hear Egypt's fate from his voice, which everyone obeys.
'Tis your noblest course. / Wisdom and fortune combating together, / If that the former dare but what it can, / No chance may shake it. Give me grace to lay / My duty on your hand.
That's your noblest course. When wisdom and fortune fight each other, if wisdom dares only do what it can, nothing can shake it. Allow me to kiss your hand in respect.
Your Caesar's father / Oft, when he hath mus'd of taking kingdoms in, / Bestow'd his lips on that unworthy place, / As it rain'd kisses.
Your Caesar's father, when he was thinking about conquering kingdoms, often put his lips on that unworthy place, as if it were raining kisses.
Favours, by Jove that thunders!-- / What art thou, fellow?
Kisses, by thundering Jupiter! Who are you, fellow?
One that but performs / The bidding of the fullest man, and worthiest / To have command obey'd.
Just someone who carries out the orders of the greatest man, the one most worthy of being obeyed.

Approach there.--Ah, you kite!--Now, gods and devils! / Authority melts from me: of late, when I cried 'Ho!' / Like boys unto a muss, kings would start forth / And cry 'Your will?' Have you no ears? I am / Antony yet.

Come here! Ah, you bird of prey! Now, gods and devils! My authority is melting away. Not long ago, when I shouted 'Hey!', kings would rush forward like boys scrambling for coins and cry, 'What do you want?' Are you deaf? I'm still Antony.
Take hence this Jack and whip him.
Take this nobody away and whip him.
'Tis better playing with a lion's whelp / Than with an old one dying.
It's better to play with a lion cub than with an old lion that's dying.

Moon and stars! / Whip him.--Were't twenty of the greatest tributaries / That do acknowledge Caesar, should I find them / So saucy with the hand of she here,--what's her name / Since she was Cleopatra?--Whip him, fellows, / Till like a boy you see him cringe his face, / And whine aloud for mercy: take him hence.

Moon and stars! Whip him. Even if it were twenty of the greatest kings who pay tribute to Caesar, if I found them so cheeky with the hand of her here (what's her name, since she stopped being Cleopatra?), I'd have them whipped. Whip him, men, until you see him screw up his face like a boy and whine aloud for mercy. Take him away.
Tug him away: being whipp'd, / Bring him again.--This Jack of Caesar's shall / Bear us an errand to him.--
Drag him away. When he's been whipped, bring him back. This lackey of Caesar's will take him a message from us.
You were half blasted ere I knew you.--Ha! / Have I my pillow left unpress'd in Rome, / Forborne the getting of a lawful race, / And by a gem of women, to be abus'd / By one that looks on feeders?
You were half rotten before I met you. Ha! Did I leave my pillow in Rome untouched, give up having lawful children with a jewel of a woman, only to be deceived by someone who flirts with servants?

You have been a boggler ever:-- / But when we in our viciousness grow hard,-- / O misery on't!--the wise gods seal our eyes; / In our own filth drop our clear judgments: make us / Adore our errors; laugh at's while we strut / To our confusion.

You've always been unfaithful. But when we become hardened in our vices (oh, how miserable!), the wise gods blind us, drop our clear judgement in our own filth, make us worship our mistakes, and laugh at us while we strut towards our ruin.
Oh, has it come to this?

I found you as a morsel cold upon / Dead Caesar's trencher; nay, you were a fragment / Of Cneius Pompey's; besides what hotter hours, / Unregist'red in vulgar fame, you have / Luxuriously pick'd out:--for I am sure, / Though you can guess what temperance should be, / You know not what it is.

I found you like a cold leftover on dead Julius Caesar's plate. No, you were a scrap left by Gnaeus Pompey, not to mention the hotter hours, not recorded in common gossip, that you lustfully picked out for yourself. Because I'm sure that though you can guess what self-control is, you don't know what it means.

To let a fellow that will take rewards, / And say 'God quit you!' be familiar with / My playfellow, your hand; this kingly seal / And plighter of high hearts!--O that I were / Upon the hill of Basan, to outroar / The horned herd! for I have savage cause; / And to proclaim it civilly were like / A halter'd neck which does the hangman thank / For being yare about him.

Because you let a fellow who takes tips and says 'God reward you!' get familiar with my playmate, your hand, this royal seal that pledges great hearts! Oh, I wish I were on the hill of Bashan, to roar louder than the horned bulls! I have savage reasons, because I'm a cuckold, and to announce it politely would be like a man with a noose round his neck thanking the hangman for being quick.
Cried he? and begg'd he pardon?
Did he cry? And beg for mercy?

If that thy father live, let him repent / Thou wast not made his daughter; and be thou sorry / To follow Caesar in his triumph, since / Thou hast been whipp'd for following him: henceforth / The white hand of a lady fever thee, / Shake thou to look on't.--Get thee back to Caesar; / Tell him thy entertainment: look thou say / He makes me angry with him; for he seems / Proud and disdainful, harping on what I am, / Not what he knew I was: he makes me angry; / And at this time most easy 'tis to do't, / When my good stars, that were my former guides, / Have empty left their orbs, and shot their fires / Into the abysm of hell. If he mislike / My speech and what is done, tell him he has / Hipparchus, my enfranched bondman, whom / He may at pleasure, whip, or hang, or torture, / As he shall like, to quit me: urge it thou: / Hence with thy stripes, be gone.

If your father's alive, let him regret you weren't born his daughter. And be sorry to follow Caesar in his triumph, since you've been whipped for following him.
