From now on, may a lady's white hand give you a fever, and may you shake to look at one. Go back to Caesar. Tell him how you were treated. Make sure you say he's making me angry with him, because he seems proud and scornful, dwelling on what I am, not what he knew I was. He makes me angry, and right now that's very easy to do, when my lucky stars, which used to guide me, have left their places in the sky and shot their fire into the pit of hell. If he doesn't like what I've said and done, tell him he has Hipparchus, my freed slave, whom he can whip, hang or torture as he likes, to pay me back. Urge him to do it. Go, with your welts. Get out.
Alack, our terrene moon / Is now eclips'd, and it portends alone / The fall of Antony!
Alas, our earthly moon is eclipsed now, and that alone predicts the fall of Antony!
I must wait until his mood passes.
To flatter Caesar, would you mingle eyes / With one that ties his points?
To flatter Caesar, would you make eyes at the man who ties his laces?

Ah, dear, if I be so, / From my cold heart let heaven engender hail, / And poison it in the source; and the first stone / Drop in my neck: as it determines, so / Dissolve my life! The next Caesarion smite! / Till, by degrees, the memory of my womb, / Together with my brave Egyptians all, / By the discandying of this pelleted storm, / Lie graveless,--till the flies and gnats of Nile / Have buried them for prey!

Ah, dear, if I am, let heaven make hail from my cold heart and poison it at the source, and let the first hailstone fall on my neck, and as it melts, may my life melt with it! Let the next one strike Caesarion! Until, one by one, all my children, together with all my brave Egyptians, lie unburied as this storm of hailstones melts, until the flies and gnats of the Nile have buried them by eating them!

I am satisfied. / Caesar sits down in Alexandria; where / I will oppose his fate. Our force by land / Hath nobly held: our sever'd navy to / Have knit again, and fleet, threat'ning most sea-like. / Where hast thou been, my heart?--Dost thou hear, lady? / If from the field I shall return once more / To kiss these lips, I will appear in blood: / I and my sword will earn our chronicle: / There's hope in't yet.

I'm satisfied. Caesar is camped at Alexandria, where I'll fight his destiny. Our land army has held out nobly. Our scattered navy has come together again and floats, looking threatening as a warfleet should. Where have you been, my courage? Do you hear, lady? If I come back from the battlefield once more to kiss these lips, I'll come covered in blood. My sword and I will earn our place in history. There's still hope.

I will be treble-sinew'd, hearted, breath'd, / And fight maliciously: for when mine hours / Were nice and lucky, men did ransom lives / Of me for jests; but now I'll set my teeth, / And send to darkness all that stop me.--Come, / Let's have one other gaudy night: call to me / All my sad captains; fill our bowls; once more / Let's mock the midnight bell.

I'll have three times the strength, courage and breath, and fight savagely. When my days were easy and lucky, men could buy their lives from me with a joke. But now I'll grit my teeth and send everyone who stands in my way to darkness. Come, let's have one more celebration night. Call all my sad captains to me. Fill our bowls. Let's mock the midnight bell once more.
It is my birthday. / I had thought t'have held it poor; but since my lord / Is Antony again I will be Cleopatra.
It's my birthday. I'd thought I'd keep it quietly, but since my lord is Antony again, I'll be Cleopatra.
Call all his noble captains to my lord.
Call all his noble captains to my lord.

Do so; we'll speak to them: and to-night I'll force / The wine peep through their scars.--Come on, my queen; / There's sap in't yet. The next time I do fight / I'll make death love me; for I will contend / Even with his pestilent scythe.

Do it. We'll speak to them. And tonight I'll make the wine shine through their scars. Come on, my queen, there's still life in us. The next time I fight, I'll make death love me, because I'll compete even with his plague-bringing scythe.

Now he'll outstare the lightning. To be furious / Is to be frighted out of fear; and in that mood / The dove will peck the estridge; and I see still / A diminution in our captain's brain / Restores his heart: when valour preys on reason, / It eats the sword it fights with. I will seek / Some way to leave him.

Now he'll try to outstare the lightning. Being furious is being frightened out of fear, and in that mood a dove will peck an ostrich. I keep seeing that as our captain's brain shrinks, his courage grows. When courage feeds on reason, it eats the sword it fights with. I'll look for some way to leave him.

He calls me boy; and chides as he had power / To beat me out of Egypt; my messenger / He hath whip'd with rods; dares me to personal combat, / Caesar to Antony:--let the old ruffian know / I have many other ways to die; meantime / Laugh at his challenge.

He calls me a boy, and scolds me as if he had the power to beat me out of Egypt. He's had my messenger whipped with rods, and challenges me to single combat, Caesar against Antony. Let the old thug know I have plenty of other ways to die. Meanwhile, I laugh at his challenge.
Caesar must think / When one so great begins to rage, he's hunted / Even to falling. Give him no breath, but now / Make boot of his distraction:--never anger / Made good guard for itself.

Caesar should realise that when someone so great starts raging, he's been hunted almost to the point of falling. Give him no breathing space, but take advantage of his frenzy right now. Anger never protected itself well.

Let our best heads / Know that to-morrow the last of many battles / We mean to fight.--Within our files there are / Of those that serv'd Mark Antony but late, / Enough to fetch him in. See it done: / And feast the army; we have store to do't, / And they have earn'd the waste. Poor Antony!

Let our top officers know that tomorrow we mean to fight the last of many battles. Within our ranks there are enough men who served Mark Antony until recently to capture him. See to it. And give the army a feast. We have the supplies for it, and they've earned the extravagance. Poor Antony!
He will not fight with me, Domitius?
He thinks, being twenty times of better fortune, / He is twenty men to one.
He thinks that, since his luck is twenty times better, he's worth twenty men to your one.
To-morrow, soldier, / By sea and land I'll fight; or I will live, / Or bathe my dying honour in the blood / Shall make it live again. Woo't thou fight well?
Tomorrow, soldier, I'll fight by sea and land. Either I'll live, or I'll bathe my dying honour in blood that will bring it back to life. Will you fight well?
I'll strike, and shout 'Winner takes all!'
Well said; come on.-- / Call forth my household servants: let's to-night / Be bounteous at our meal.--
Well said. Come on. Call my household servants. Let's have a generous meal tonight.
Give me thy hand, / Thou has been rightly honest;--so hast thou;-- / Thou,--and thou,--and thou;--you have serv'd me well, / And kings have been your fellows.
Give me your hand. You've been truly honest. And so have you, and you, and you, and you. You've served me well, and kings have been your fellow servants.
[Aside to Enobarbus] What does he mean by this?
[Aside to Cleopatra.] 'Tis one of those odd tricks which sorrow / shoots / Out of the mind.
[Aside to Cleopatra] It's one of those strange moods that sorrow shoots out of the mind.
And thou art honest too. / I wish I could be made so many men, / And all of you clapp'd up together in / An Antony, that I might do you service / So good as you have done.
And you're honest too. I wish I could be turned into as many men as you, and all of you rolled together into one Antony, so I could serve you as well as you've served me.
Well, my good fellows, wait on me to-night: / Scant not my cups; and make as much of me / As when mine empire was your fellow too, / And suffer'd my command.
Well, my good fellows, wait on me tonight. Don't be stingy with my wine, and treat me as well as when my empire was your fellow servant too, and obeyed my orders.
[Aside to Enobarbus.] What does he mean?
[Aside to Enobarbus] What does he mean?
[Aside to Cleopatra.] To make his followers weep.
[Aside to Cleopatra] To make his followers cry.

Tend me to-night; / May be it is the period of your duty: / Haply you shall not see me more; or if, / A mangled shadow: perchance to-morrow / You'll serve another master. I look on you / As one that takes his leave. Mine honest friends, / I turn you not away; but, like a master / Married to your good service, stay till death: / Tend me to-night two hours, I ask no more, / And the gods yield you for't!

Serve me tonight. Maybe it's the end of your service. Perhaps you won't see me again, or if you do, as a mangled ghost. Maybe tomorrow you'll serve another master. I look at you like a man saying goodbye. My honest friends, I'm not dismissing you. Like a master married to your good service, I'll keep you till I die. Serve me for two hours tonight, I ask no more, and may the gods reward you for it!
What mean you, sir, / To give them this discomfort? Look, they weep; / And I, an ass, am onion-ey'd: for shame, / Transform us not to women.
What do you mean, sir, by upsetting them like this? Look, they're crying, and I, like an ass, have eyes watering as if from onions. For shame, don't turn us into women.

Ho, ho, ho! / Now the witch take me, if I meant it thus! / Grace grow where those drops fall! My hearty friends, / You take me in too dolorous a sense; / For I spake to you for your comfort,--did desire you / To burn this night with torches: know, my hearts, / I hope well of to-morrow; and will lead you / Where rather I'll expect victorious life / Than death and honour. Let's to supper; come, / And drown consideration.

Ho, ho, ho! Now may the witch take me if I meant it like that! May grace grow where those tears fall! My dear friends, you take me too gloomily. I spoke to comfort you. I wanted you to light up this night with torches. Know this, my hearts: I have good hopes for tomorrow, and I'll lead you where I expect a victorious life rather than an honourable death. Let's go to supper. Come, and drown our worries.
Brother, good night: to-morrow is the day.
Good night, brother. Tomorrow's the day.
It will determine one way: fare you well. / Heard you of nothing strange about the streets?
It will settle things one way or the other. Goodbye. Have you heard about anything strange in the streets?
Belike 'tis but a rumour. Good night to you.
It's probably just a rumour. Good night.
And you. Good night, good night.
You too. Good night, good night.
Here we: [The third and fourth take their posts.] and if / to-morrow / Our navy thrive, I have an absolute hope / Our landmen will stand up.
Here we are. [The third and fourth take their posts.] If our navy does well tomorrow, I'm absolutely sure our land army will hold out.
'Tis a brave army, / And full of purpose. / [Music as of hautboys under the stage.]
It's a brave army, and very determined. [Music of oboes is heard under the stage.]
It signs well, does it not?
It's a good sign, isn't it?
Peace, I say! / What should this mean?
Quiet, I say! What can this mean?
'Tis the god Hercules, whom Antony lov'd, / Now leaves him.
It's the god Hercules, whom Antony loved, leaving him now.
Walk; let's see if other watchmen / Do hear what we do.
Let's walk. Let's see if the other guards hear what we hear.
[Speaking together.] How now! / How now! Do you hear this?
[Speaking together] What's happening! What's happening! Do you hear this?
Do you hear, masters? do you hear?
Do you hear, friends? Do you hear?
Follow the noise so far as we have quarter; / Let's see how it will give off.
Let's follow the noise as far as our post allows. Let's see how it ends.
No, my chuck.--Eros! Come, mine armour, Eros!
No, my chick. Eros! Come, my armour, Eros!
Come, good fellow, put mine iron on.-- / If fortune be not ours to-day, it is / Because we brave her.--Come.
Come, good fellow, put my iron on. If fortune isn't on our side today, it's because we defy her. Come.
Nay, I'll help too. / What's this for?
No, I'll help too. What's this for?
Ah, let be, let be! Thou art / The armourer of my heart. False, false; this, this.
Ah, leave it, leave it! You're the armourer of my heart. Wrong, wrong; this one, this one.
Sooth, la, I'll help: thus it must be.
Really, I'll help. It must go like this.
Well, well; / We shall thrive now.--Seest thou, my good fellow? / Go put on thy defences.
Well, well, we'll do well now. Do you see, my good fellow? Go and put on your own armour.

Rarely, rarely; / He that unbuckles this, till we do please / To daff't for our repose, shall hear a storm.-- / Thou fumblest, Eros, and my queen's a squire / More tight at this than thou: despatch.--O love, / That thou couldst see my wars to-day, and knew'st / The royal occupation! Thou shouldst see / A workman in't.--

Excellently, excellently. Anyone who unbuckles this before we choose to take it off to rest will face a storm. You're fumbling, Eros, and my queen is a better squire at this than you. Hurry up. Oh love, I wish you could see me fight today and understood this royal trade! You'd see a real craftsman at work.
Good-morrow to thee; welcome: / Thou look'st like him that knows a warlike charge: / To business that we love we rise betime, / And go to't with delight.
Good morning to you. Welcome. You look like a man who knows what a military command is. We get up early for work we love, and go to it with delight.
A thousand, sir, / Early though't be, have on their riveted trim, / And at the port expect you.
A thousand men, sir, early as it is, have put on their armour and are waiting for you at the gate.
The morn is fair.--Good morrow, general.
It's a fine morning. Good morning, general.

'Tis well blown, lads: / This morning, like the spirit of a youth / That means to be of note, begins betimes.-- / So, so; come, give me that: this way; well said.-- / Fare thee well, dame, whate'er becomes of me: / [Kisses her.] / This is a soldier's kiss: rebukeable, / And worthy shameful check it were, to stand / On more mechanic compliment; I'll leave thee / Now like a man of steel.--You that will fight, / Follow me close; I'll bring you to't. Adieu.

That's a fine blast, lads. This morning starts early, like the spirit of a young man who means to make a name for himself. So, so. Come, give me that. This way. Well done. Goodbye, lady, whatever happens to me. [He kisses her.] This is a soldier's kiss. It would deserve to be scolded and shamed if I stood here making ordinary polite speeches. I'll leave you now like a man of steel. Those of you who'll fight, follow me closely. I'll lead you to it. Goodbye.
Please you, retire to your chamber.
Lead me. / He goes forth gallantly. That he and Caesar might / Determine this great war in single fight! / Then, Antony,--but now--Well, on.
Lead me. He goes out bravely. If only he and Caesar could settle this great war in single combat! Then, Antony... But now... Well, go on.
The gods make this a happy day to Antony!
May the gods make this a happy day for Antony!
Would thou and those thy scars had once prevail'd / To make me fight at land!
I wish you and those scars of yours had persuaded me to fight on land!
Hadst thou done so, / The kings that have revolted, and the soldier / That has this morning left thee, would have still / Follow'd thy heels.
If you had, the kings who have deserted you, and the soldier who left you this morning, would still be following at your heels.
Who. / One ever near thee. Call for Enobarbus, / He shall not hear thee; or from Caesar's camp / Say 'I am none of thine.'
Who? Someone always close to you. Call for Enobarbus, and he won't hear you, or he'll answer from Caesar's camp, 'I'm not yours.'
Sir, his chests and treasure / He has not with him.
Sir, he didn't take his chests and treasure with him.

Go, Eros, send his treasure after; do it; / Detain no jot, I charge thee; write to him-- / I will subscribe,--gentle adieus and greetings; / Say that I wish he never find more cause / To change a master.--O, my fortunes have / Corrupted honest men!--Eros, despatch.

Go, Eros, send his treasure after him. Do it. Don't keep back a scrap, I order you. Write to him (I'll sign it) with gentle farewells and greetings. Say I hope he never has reason to change masters again. Oh, my bad fortune has corrupted honest men! Hurry, Eros.
Go forth, Agrippa, and begin the fight: / Our will is Antony be took alive; / Make it so known.
Go out, Agrippa, and start the fight. Our wish is that Antony be taken alive. Make that known.
The time of universal peace is near: / Prove this a prosperous day, the three-nook'd world / Shall bear the olive freely.
The time of world peace is near. If this turns out to be a successful day, the three corners of the world will grow olive branches freely.
Antony / Is come into the field.
Go charge Agrippa / Plant those that have revolted in the van, / That Antony may seem to spend his fury / Upon himself.
Go and order Agrippa to put the deserters in the front line, so that Antony seems to be spending his fury on himself.

Alexas did revolt; and went to Jewry on / Affairs of Antony; there did dissuade / Great Herod to incline himself to Caesar / And leave his master Antony: for this pains / Caesar hath hang'd him. Canidius and the rest / That fell away, have entertainment, but / No honourable trust. I have done ill; / Of which I do accuse myself so sorely / That I will joy no more.

Alexas deserted. He went to Judea on Antony's business, and there persuaded great Herod to side with Caesar and abandon his master Antony. For his trouble, Caesar has hanged him. Canidius and the others who deserted are given work, but not honourable trust. I've done wrong, and I blame myself so bitterly that I'll never be happy again.
Enobarbus, Antony / Hath after thee sent all thy treasure, with / His bounty overplus: the messenger / Came on my guard, and at thy tent is now / Unloading of his mules.
Enobarbus, Antony has sent all your treasure after you, with extra gifts of his own. The messenger came while I was on guard and is at your tent now, unloading his mules.
Mock not, Enobarbus. / I tell you true: best you saf'd the bringer / Out of the host; I must attend mine office, / Or would have done't myself. Your emperor / Continues still a Jove.

Don't joke, Enobarbus. I'm telling the truth. You'd better see the man who brought it safely out of the camp. I must get back to my duty, or I'd have done it myself. Your commander is still like Jupiter.

I am alone the villain of the earth, / And feel I am so most. O Antony, / Thou mine of bounty, how wouldst thou have paid / My better service, when my turpitude / Thou dost so crown with gold! This blows my heart: / If swift thought break it not, a swifter mean / Shall outstrike thought: but thought will do't, I feel. / I fight against thee!--No: I will go seek / Some ditch wherein to die; the foul'st best fits / My latter part of life.

I'm the only villain on earth, and I feel it most of all. Oh Antony, you goldmine of generosity, how would you have paid my better service, when you crown my wickedness with gold! This makes my heart swell. If grief doesn't break it quickly, a quicker means will beat grief to it. But I feel grief will do it. Fight against you? No. I'll go and find some ditch to die in. The filthiest suits the last part of my life best.
Retire, we have engag'd ourselves too far: / Caesar himself has work, and our oppression / Exceeds what we expected.
Retreat! We've gone too far. Caesar himself has his hands full, and the pressure on us is greater than we expected.
O my brave emperor, this is fought indeed! / Had we done so at first, we had driven them home / With clouts about their heads.
Oh my brave commander, this is real fighting! If we'd fought like this at first, we'd have driven them home with bandages on their heads.
I had a wound here that was like a T, / But now 'tis made an H.
I had a wound here like a T, but now it's become an H.
We'll beat'em into bench-holes: I have yet / Room for six scotches more.
We'll beat them into the holes of a toilet bench. I've still got room for six more cuts.
They are beaten, sir; and our advantage serves / For a fair victory.
They're beaten, sir, and our advantage means a clear victory.
Let us score their backs / And snatch 'em up, as we take hares, behind: / 'Tis sport to maul a runner.
Let's slash their backs and grab them from behind, the way we catch hares. It's fun to beat a runner.
I will reward thee / Once for thy sprightly comfort, and tenfold / For thy good valour. Come thee on.
I'll reward you once for your cheerful encouragement, and ten times for your great courage. Come on.

We have beat him to his camp. Run one before / And let the queen know of our gests.--To-morrow, / Before the sun shall see us, we'll spill the blood / That has to-day escap'd. I thank you all; / For doughty-handed are you, and have fought / Not as you serv'd the cause, but as't had been / Each man's like mine; you have shown all Hectors. / Enter the city, clip your wives, your friends, / Tell them your feats; whilst they with joyful tears / Wash the congealment from your wounds and kiss / The honour'd gashes whole.--[To Scarus.] Give me thy hand;

We've beaten him back to his camp. Someone run ahead and tell the queen of our deeds. Tomorrow, before the sun sees us, we'll spill the blood that escaped today. I thank you all. You're brave fighters, and you fought not as if you were serving a cause, but as if it were each man's own, as it is mine. You've all been like Hector. Go into the city, hug your wives and friends, tell them your deeds, while they wash the dried blood from your wounds with tears of joy and kiss the honourable gashes until they heal. [To Scarus] Give me your hand.

To this great fairy I'll commend thy acts, / Make her thanks bless thee. O thou day o' the world, / Chain mine arm'd neck; leap thou, attire and all; / Through proof of harness to my heart, and there / Ride on the pants triumphing.

I'll praise your deeds to this great enchantress and let her thanks bless you. Oh you light of the world, put your arms round my armoured neck. Leap, clothes and all, through my tested armour to my heart, and ride there in triumph on its beating.
Lord of lords! / O infinite virtue, com'st thou smiling from / The world's great snare uncaught?
Lord of lords! Oh endless courage, have you come smiling back from the world's great trap without being caught?

Mine nightingale, / We have beat them to their beds. What, girl! though grey / Do something mingle with our younger brown, yet ha' we / A brain that nourishes our nerves, and can / Get goal for goal of youth. Behold this man; / Commend unto his lips thy favouring hand;-- / Kiss it, my warrior: he hath fought to-day / As if a god, in hate of mankind, had / Destroyed in such a shape.

My nightingale, we've beaten them back to their beds. What, girl! Though some grey hairs mix with our younger brown, we still have a brain that strengthens our muscles and can score goal for goal against youth. Look at this man. Give him your gracious hand to kiss. Kiss it, my warrior. He's fought today as if a god who hated mankind had destroyed it in his shape.
I'll give thee, friend, / An armour all of gold; it was a king's.
Friend, I'll give you a suit of armour made entirely of gold. It belonged to a king.

He has deserv'd it, were it carbuncled / Like holy Phoebus' car.--Give me thy hand: / Through Alexandria make a jolly march; / Bear our hack'd targets like the men that owe them: / Had our great palace the capacity / To camp this host, we all would sup together, / And drink carouses to the next day's fate, / Which promises royal peril.--Trumpeters, / With brazen din blast you the city's ear; / Make mingle with our rattling tabourines; / That heaven and earth may strike their sounds together, / Applauding our approach.

He'd deserve it even if it were studded with rubies like the sun god's chariot. Give me your hand. Let's march merrily through Alexandria, carrying our battered shields like the men who own them. If our great palace could hold this whole army, we'd all have supper together and drink toasts to tomorrow's fate, which promises royal danger. Trumpeters, blast the city's ears with your brass noise, and mix it with our rattling drums, so heaven and earth can echo the sound together, applauding our return.
If we be not reliev'd within this hour, / We must return to the court of guard: the night / Is shiny; and they say we shall embattle / By the second hour i' the morn.
If we're not relieved within the hour, we must go back to the guardroom. The night is bright, and they say we'll be lined up for battle by two in the morning.
This last day was / A shrewd one to's.
Yesterday was a bad day for us.
Keep hidden and listen to him.
Be witness to me, O thou blessed moon, / When men revolted shall upon record / Bear hateful memory, poor Enobarbus did / Before thy face repent!--
Be my witness, oh blessed moon, when deserters are remembered with hatred in the history books, that poor Enobarbus repented in front of you!

O sovereign mistress of true melancholy, / The poisonous damp of night disponge upon me, / That life, a very rebel to my will, / May hang no longer on me: throw my heart / Against the flint and hardness of my fault; / Which, being dried with grief, will break to powder, / And finish all foul thoughts. O Antony, / Nobler than my revolt is infamous, / Forgive me in thine own particular; / But let the world rank me in register / A master-leaver and a fugitive: / O Antony! O Antony! / [Dies.]

Oh moon, queen of true sadness, squeeze the poisonous damp of the night onto me, so that life, which rebels against my will, may stop clinging to me. Throw my heart against the hard flint of my crime. It's so dried up with grief that it will break into powder and end all foul thoughts. Oh Antony, more noble than my desertion is shameful, forgive me yourself, but let the world record me as a deserter of his master and a runaway. Oh Antony! Oh Antony! [He dies.]
Let's hear him, for the things he speaks / May concern Caesar.
Let's listen to him, because what he says may concern Caesar.
Let's do so. But he sleeps.
Let's do that. But he's asleep.
Swoons rather; for so bad a prayer as his / Was never yet fore sleep.
Fainted, more likely, because a prayer as miserable as his never came before sleep.
Awake, sir, awake; speak to us.
Wake up, sir, wake up. Speak to us.
The hand of death hath raught him.
The hand of death has taken him.
Hark! the drums / Do merrily wake the sleepers. Let us bear him / To the court of guard; he is of note: our hour / Is fully out.
Listen! The drums are cheerfully waking the sleepers. Let's carry him to the guardroom. He's an important man. Our watch is over.
Come on, then; / He may recover yet.
Come on, then. He may still recover.
Their preparation is to-day by sea; / We please them not by land.
They're preparing to fight at sea today. We don't suit them on land.
They're preparing for both, my lord.

I would they'd fight i' the fire or i' the air; / We'd fight there too. But this it is; our foot / Upon the hills adjoining to the city / Shall stay with us:--order for sea is given; / They have put forth the haven:--forward now, / Where their appointment we may best discover, / And look on their endeavour.

I wish they'd fight in fire or in the air; we'd fight there too. But here's the plan. Our foot soldiers will stay with us on the hills next to the city. Orders have been given for the navy; they've left the harbour. Let's go forward to where we can best see their positions and watch what they do.
But being charg'd, we will be still by land, / Which, as I take't, we shall; for his best force / Is forth to man his galleys. To the vales, / And hold our best advantage.
Unless we're attacked, we'll stay still on land, which I think we can, because his best troops have gone to man his ships. To the valleys, and hold our best position.
Yet they are not join'd: where yond pine does stand / I shall discover all: I'll bring thee word / Straight how 'tis like to go.
They haven't engaged yet. From where that pine tree stands I'll see everything. I'll bring you word straight away of how it's likely to go.

Swallows have built / In Cleopatra's sails their nests: the augurers / Say they know not,--they cannot tell;--look grimly, / And dare not speak their knowledge. Antony / Is valiant and dejected; and, by starts, / His fretted fortunes give him hope and fear / Of what he has and has not.

Swallows have built their nests in Cleopatra's sails. The fortune-tellers say they don't know, they can't tell. They look grim and don't dare say what they know. Antony is brave and depressed, and his worn-down fortunes keep giving him fits of hope and fear about what he has and what he hasn't.

All is lost; / This foul Egyptian hath betrayed me: / My fleet hath yielded to the foe; and yonder / They cast their caps up, and carouse together / Like friends long lost.--Triple-turn'd whore! 'tis thou / Hast sold me to this novice; and my heart / Makes only wars on thee.--Bid them all fly; / For when I am reveng'd upon my charm, / I have done all.--Bid them all fly; begone.

All is lost. This foul Egyptian has betrayed me. My fleet has surrendered to the enemy, and over there they're throwing their caps in the air and drinking together like long-lost friends. Three-times-unfaithful whore! You've sold me to this beginner, and my heart makes war on you alone. Tell them all to run, because once I've had my revenge on my enchantress, I'm finished. Tell them all to run. Go.

O sun, thy uprise shall I see no more: / Fortune and Antony part here; even here / Do we shake hands.--All come to this!--The hearts / That spaniel'd me at heels, to whom I gave / Their wishes, do discandy, melt their sweets / On blossoming Caesar; and this pine is bark'd / That overtopp'd them all. Betray'd I am: / O this false soul of Egypt! this grave charm, / Whose eye beck'd forth my wars and call'd them home; / Whose bosom was my crownet, my chief end,-- / Like a right gypsy, hath, at fast and loose, / Beguil'd me to the very heart of loss.-- / What, Eros, Eros!

Oh sun, I'll never see you rise again. Fortune and Antony part here; right here we shake hands. Has it all come to this? The hearts that followed at my heels like spaniels, to whom I gave everything they wanted, are melting and dripping their sweetness onto Caesar, who's in full bloom. And this pine tree, which towered over them all, is stripped of its bark. I'm betrayed. Oh, this treacherous soul of Egypt! This deadly enchantress, whose look sent out my wars and called them home, whose breast was my crown and my goal, like a real gypsy has cheated me, with her fast-and-loose tricks, into total ruin. Hey, Eros, Eros!
Why is my lord enrag'd against his love?
Why is my lord so angry with his love?

Vanish, or I shall give thee thy deserving, / And blemish Caesar's triumph. Let him take thee / And hoist thee up to the shouting plebeians: / Follow his chariot, like the greatest spot / Of all thy sex; most monster-like, be shown / For poor'st diminutives, for doits; and let / Patient Octavia plough thy visage up / With her prepared nails.

Vanish, or I'll give you what you deserve, and spoil Caesar's victory parade. Let him take you and hold you up to the cheering crowds. Follow his chariot, like the greatest stain on womankind. Be shown like a freak to the poorest people for pennies, and let patient Octavia plough up your face with her sharpened nails.

'Tis well thou'rt gone, / If it be well to live; but better 'twere / Thou fell'st into my fury, for one death / Might have prevented many.--Eros, ho!-- / The shirt of Nessus is upon me: teach me, / Alcides, thou mine ancestor, thy rage: / Let me lodge Lichas on the horns o' the moon; / And with those hands that grasp'd the heaviest club / Subdue my worthiest self. The witch shall die: / To the young Roman boy she hath sold me, and I fall / Under this plot:--she dies for't.--Eros, ho!

It's good that you've gone, if it's good to live. But it would be better if you'd fallen victim to my fury, because one death might have prevented many. Eros, hey! The shirt of Nessus is burning me. Hercules, my ancestor, teach me your rage. Let me throw Lichas up onto the horns of the moon, and with the hands that held the heaviest club, destroy my noblest self. The witch will die. She's sold me to the young Roman boy, and I'm falling because of her plot. She'll die for it. Eros, hey!
Help me, my women! O, he is more mad / Than Telamon for his shield; the boar of Thessaly / Was never so emboss'd.
Help me, my women! Oh, he's madder than Ajax over the shield. The boar of Thessaly never foamed at the mouth like this.
To the monument! / There lock yourself, and send him word you are dead. / The soul and body rive not more in parting / Than greatness going off.
To the monument! Lock yourself in there, and send him word that you're dead. The soul and body don't tear apart more painfully at death than greatness does when it leaves a man.

To the monument!-- / Mardian, go tell him I have slain myself; / Say that the last I spoke was 'Antony', / And word it, pr'ythee, piteously: hence, Mardian; / And bring me how he takes my death.-- / To the monument!
To the monument! Mardian, go and tell him I've killed myself. Say the last word I spoke was 'Antony', and please say it pitifully. Go, Mardian, and tell me how he takes my death. To the monument!
Eros, can you still see me?

Sometime we see a cloud that's dragonish; / A vapour sometime like a bear or lion, / A tower'd citadel, a pendant rock, / A forked mountain, or blue promontory / With trees upon't, that nod unto the world, / And mock our eyes with air: thou hast seen these signs; / They are black vesper's pageants.

Sometimes we see a cloud that looks like a dragon; a mist sometimes like a bear or a lion, a towered castle, an overhanging rock, a jagged mountain, or a blue headland with trees on it, which nod to the world and fool our eyes with air. You've seen these sights; they're the shows of evening.
That which is now a horse, even with a thought / The rack dislimns; and makes it indistinct, / As water is in water.
What's a horse one moment, the drifting clouds blot out as fast as a thought, and make it shapeless, like water poured into water.

My good knave Eros, now thy captain is / Even such a body: here I am Antony; / Yet cannot hold this visible shape, my knave. / I made these wars for Egypt; and the queen,-- / Whose heart I thought I had, for she had mine; / Which, whilst it was mine, had annex'd unto't / A million moe, now lost,--she, Eros, has / Pack'd cards with Caesar, and false-play'd my glory / Unto an enemy's triumph.-- / Nay, weep not, gentle Eros; there is left us / Ourselves to end ourselves.--

My good lad Eros, your captain is just like that kind of shape now. Here I am, Antony, but I can't keep this visible shape, my lad. I fought these wars for Egypt, and the queen, whose heart I thought I had, because she had mine (and while it was mine, a million other hearts were attached to it, now lost), she, Eros, has stacked the cards with Caesar and cheated my glory into my enemy's victory. No, don't cry, gentle Eros. We still have ourselves to end ourselves.
O, thy vile lady! / She has robb'd me of my sword.
Oh, your wicked lady! She's robbed me of my sword.
No, Antony; / My mistress lov'd thee, and her fortunes mingled / With thine entirely.
No, Antony. My mistress loved you, and her fortunes were completely joined with yours.
Hence, saucy eunuch; peace! / She hath betray'd me, and shall die the death.
Get out, cheeky eunuch, quiet! She's betrayed me, and she'll die for it.

Death of one person can be paid but once, / And that she has discharg'd: what thou wouldst do / Is done unto thy hand: the last she spake / Was 'Antony! most noble Antony!' / Then in the midst a tearing groan did break / The name of Antony; it was divided / Between her heart and lips: she render'd life, / Thy name so buried in her.

A person can only pay the debt of death once, and she's already paid it. What you wanted to do has been done for you. The last thing she said was 'Antony! Most noble Antony!' Then a tearing groan broke the name of Antony in the middle. It was divided between her heart and her lips. She gave up her life with your name buried in her.
Unarm, Eros; the long day's task is done, / And we must sleep.--That thou depart'st hence safe / Does pay thy labour richly; go.
Take off my armour, Eros. The long day's work is done, and we must sleep. [To Mardian] Leaving here alive pays you well for your trouble. Go.

Off, pluck off;-- / The sevenfold shield of Ajax cannot keep / The battery from my heart. O, cleave, my sides! / Heart, once be stronger than thy continent, / Crack thy frail case!--Apace, Eros, apace.-- / No more a soldier.--Bruised pieces, go; / You have been nobly borne.--From me awhile.--

Off, pull it off! Not even the seven-layered shield of Ajax could keep this battering away from my heart. Oh, split open, my sides! Heart, for once be stronger than the body that holds you; crack your fragile case! Quickly, Eros, quickly. No longer a soldier. Battered pieces of armour, go; you've been worn with honour. Leave me for a while.

I will o'ertake thee, Cleopatra, and / Weep for my pardon. So it must be, for now / All length is torture.--Since the torch is out, / Lie down, and stray no further:--now all labour / Mars what it does; yea, very force entangles / Itself with strength: seal then, and all is done.-- / Eros!--I come, my queen.--Eros!--stay for me: / Where souls do couch on flowers, we'll hand in hand, / And with our sprightly port make the ghosts gaze: / Dido and her Aeneas shall want troops, / And all the haunt be ours.--Come, Eros, Eros!

I'll catch up with you, Cleopatra, and weep for your forgiveness. It must be this way, because now any delay is torture. Since the torch is out, lie down and wander no further. Now every effort spoils what it does; yes, strength itself gets tangled in its own strength. Seal it, then, and all is done. Eros! I'm coming, my queen. Eros! Wait for me. Where souls lie on flowers in the afterlife, we'll walk hand in hand and make the ghosts stare at our lively bearing. Dido and her Aeneas will lose their admirers, and all the crowds will be ours. Come, Eros, Eros!

Since Cleopatra died, / I have liv'd in such dishonour that the gods / Detest my baseness. I, that with my sword / Quarter'd the world, and o'er green Neptune's back / With ships made cities, condemn myself to lack / The courage of a woman; less noble mind / Than she which by her death our Caesar tells / 'I am conqueror of myself.' Thou art sworn, Eros, / That, when the exigent should come,--which now / Is come indeed--when I should see behind me / The inevitable prosecution of / Disgrace and horror, that, on my command, / Thou then wouldst kill me: do't; the time is come: / Thou strik'st not me; 'tis Caesar thou defeat'st. / Put colour in thy cheek.

Since Cleopatra died, I've lived in such dishonour that the gods hate my lowness. I, who carved up the world with my sword and built cities of ships on green Neptune's back, accuse myself of having less courage than a woman, a less noble mind than she has, who by her death tells our Caesar, 'I am my own conqueror.' You swore, Eros, that when the emergency came (and now it really has come), when I saw behind me the unavoidable chase of disgrace and horror, you would kill me when I ordered it. Do it. The time has come. You're not striking me; it's Caesar you're defeating. Put some colour in your cheeks.
The gods withhold me! / Shall I do that which all the Parthian darts, / Though enemy, lost aim and could not?
The gods prevent me! Shall I do what all the Parthian arrows, enemies though they were, failed to do because they missed?

Eros, / Wouldst thou be window'd in great Rome and see / Thy master thus with pleach'd arms, bending down / His corrigible neck, his face subdu'd / To penetrative shame; whilst the wheel'd seat / Of fortunate Caesar, drawn before him, branded / His baseness that ensued?

Eros, would you like to stand at a window in great Rome and see your master like this, with his arms folded, bowing his tamed neck, his face lowered in burning shame, while the chariot of lucky Caesar, driven in front of him, branded the humiliation of the man following behind?
I wouldn't want to see it.
Come, then; for with a wound I must be cur'd. / Draw that thy honest sword, which thou hast worn / Most useful for thy country.
Come on, then, because I must be cured by a wound. Draw that honest sword of yours, which you've used so well for your country.
When I did make thee free, swor'st thou not then / To do this when I bade thee? Do it at once; / Or thy precedent services are all / But accidents unpurpos'd. Draw, and come.
When I set you free, didn't you swear then to do this when I told you to? Do it now, or all your past service was just accident without purpose. Draw your sword, and come.
Turn from me then that noble countenance, / Wherein the worship of the whole world lies.
Then turn your noble face away from me, which the whole world worships.
Then let it do at once / The thing why thou hast drawn it.
Then let it do at once what you drew it for.
My dear master, / My captain and my emperor, let me say, / Before I strike this bloody stroke, farewell.
My dear master, my captain and my commander, let me say goodbye before I strike this bloody blow.
Farewell, great chief. Shall I strike now?
Goodbye, great leader. Shall I strike now?
Why, there then [falls on his sword]!--thus do I escape the / sorrow / Of Antony's death. / [Dies.]
Why, there, then! [He falls on his sword.] That's how I escape the sorrow of Antony's death. [He dies.]

Thrice nobler than myself! / Thou teachest me, O valiant Eros, what / I should, and thou couldst not. My queen and Eros / Have, by their brave instruction, got upon me / A nobleness in record: but I will be / A bridegroom in my death, and run into't / As to a lover's bed. Come, then; and, Eros, / Thy master dies thy scholar: to do thus

Three times nobler than me! You teach me, oh brave Eros, what I should do and you could not. My queen and Eros, by their brave example, have won a nobler place in history than me. But I'll be a bridegroom in my death and run into it as into a lover's bed. Come, then. And, Eros, your master dies as your pupil. To do this
I learn'd of thee. How? not dead? not dead?-- / The guard, ho!--O, despatch me!
I learned from you. What? Not dead? Not dead? Guards, hey! Oh, finish me off!
I have done my work ill, friends: O, make an end / Of what I have begun.
I've done my work badly, friends. Oh, finish what I've started.
And time is at his period.
And time has come to its end.
Let him that loves me, strike me dead.
Whoever loves me, strike me dead.
Thy death and fortunes bid thy followers fly. / This sword but shown to Caesar, with this tidings, / Shall enter me with him.
Your death and bad fortune tell your followers to run. If I just show this sword to Caesar with this news, he'll take me into his service.
Lives he? / Wilt thou not answer, man?
Is he alive? Won't you answer, man?
Art thou there, Diomed? Draw thy sword and give me / Sufficing strokes for death.
Is that you, Diomedes? Draw your sword and give me enough blows to kill me.
Most absolute lord, / My mistress Cleopatra sent me to thee.
Most absolute lord, my mistress Cleopatra sent me to you.

Lock'd in her monument. She had a prophesying fear / Of what hath come to pass: for when she saw,-- / Which never shall be found,--you did suspect / She had dispos'd with Caesar, and that your rage / Would not be purg'd, she sent you word she was dead; / But, fearing since how it might work, hath sent / Me to proclaim the truth; and I am come, / I dread, too late.

Locked in her monument. She had a prophetic fear of what has happened. When she saw that you suspected she'd done a deal with Caesar (which will never be proved), and that your rage wouldn't calm down, she sent you word that she was dead. But afraid since then of what it might do, she's sent me to tell you the truth. And I've come, I fear, too late.
Too late, good Diomed.--Call my guard, I pr'ythee.
Too late, good Diomedes. Call my guard, please.
What, ho! the emperor's guard! The guard, what ho! / Come, your lord calls!
Hey! The commander's guard! The guard, hey! Come, your lord is calling!
Bear me, good friends, where Cleopatra bides; / 'Tis the last service that I shall command you.
Carry me, good friends, to where Cleopatra is staying. It's the last service I'll ask of you.
Woe, woe are we, sir, you may not live to wear / All your true followers out.
Woe is us, sir, that you won't live to outlast all your faithful followers.

Nay, good my fellows, do not please sharp fate / To grace it with your sorrows: bid that welcome / Which comes to punish us, and we punish it, / Seeming to bear it lightly. Take me up: / I have led you oft: carry me now, good friends, / And have my thanks for all.

No, my good fellows, don't please cruel fate by honouring it with your sorrow. Welcome what comes to punish us, and we punish it by seeming to bear it lightly. Pick me up. I've often led you; carry me now, good friends, and have my thanks for everything.
O Charmian, I will never go from hence!
Oh Charmian, I'll never leave this place!
No, I will not: / All strange and terrible events are welcome, / But comforts we despise; our size of sorrow, / Proportion'd to our cause, must be as great / As that which makes it.--
No, I won't. Every strange and terrible event is welcome, but we despise comfort. The size of our sorrow, matching its cause, must be as great as what causes it.
What is it? Is he dead?
His death's upon him, but not dead. / Look out o' the other side your monument; / His guard have brought him thither.
Death is on him, but he's not dead. Look out the other side of your monument. His guards have brought him there.

O sun, / Burn the great sphere thou mov'st in!--darkling stand / The varying shore o' the world.--O Antony, / Antony, Antony!--Help, Charmian; help, Iras, help,-- / Help, friends below;--let's draw him hither.

Oh sun, burn up the great sphere you move in! Let the changing shore of the world stand in darkness. Oh Antony, Antony, Antony! Help, Charmian; help, Iras, help. Help, friends down there. Let's pull him up here.
Peace! / Not Caesar's valour hath o'erthrown Antony, / But Antony's hath triumph'd on itself.
Quiet! It wasn't Caesar's courage that overthrew Antony, but Antony's courage that triumphed over itself.
So it should be, that none but Antony / Should conquer Antony; but woe 'tis so!
That's how it should be, that no one but Antony should conquer Antony. But how sad that it's so!
I am dying, Egypt, dying; only / I here importune death awhile, until / Of many thousand kisses the poor last / I lay upon thy lips.
I'm dying, Egypt, dying. I'm only begging death to wait a while, until I lay the poor last of many thousand kisses on your lips.

I dare not, dear,-- / Dear my lord, pardon,--I dare not, / Lest I be taken: not the imperious show / Of the full-fortun'd Caesar ever shall / Be brooch'd with me; if knife, drugs, serpents, have / Edge, sting, or operation, I am safe; / Your wife Octavia, with her modest eyes / And still conclusion, shall acquire no honour / Demuring upon me.--But come, come, Antony,-- / Help me, my women,--we must draw thee up; / Assist, good friends.

I don't dare, dear. My dear lord, forgive me, I don't dare come down, or I'll be captured. The proud victory parade of all-fortunate Caesar will never be decorated with me. If knives, drugs or snakes have edge, sting or power, I'm safe. Your wife Octavia, with her modest eyes and quiet judgement, will never win the honour of looking down primly on me. But come, come, Antony. Help me, my women. We must pull you up. Help, good friends.
O, quick, or I am gone.
Oh, quickly, or I'll be gone.

Here's sport indeed!--How heavy weighs my lord! / Our strength is all gone into heaviness; / That makes the weight: had I great Juno's power, / The strong-wing'd Mercury should fetch thee up, / And set thee by Jove's side. Yet come a little,-- / Wishers were ever fools,--O come, come;

This is a fine game! How heavy my lord is! All our strength has turned into heaviness, and that makes the weight. If I had great Juno's power, strong-winged Mercury would fetch you up and set you beside Jupiter. Yet come up a little. People who only wish were always fools. Oh, come, come.
And welcome, welcome! die where thou hast liv'd: / Quicken with kissing: had my lips that power, / Thus would I wear them out.
And welcome, welcome! Die where you've lived. Come back to life with kisses. If my lips had that power, I'd wear them out like this.
I am dying, Egypt, dying: / Give me some wine, and let me speak a little.
I'm dying, Egypt, dying. Give me some wine, and let me say a few words.
No, let me speak; and let me rail so high / That the false huswife Fortune break her wheel, / Provok'd by my offence.
No, let me speak, and let me curse so loudly that Fortune, that unfaithful housewife, breaks her wheel in anger at my insults.
One word, sweet queen: / Of Caesar seek your honour, with your safety.--O!
One word, sweet queen. Get Caesar to protect your honour as well as your safety. Oh!
Gentle, hear me: / None about Caesar trust but Proculeius.
Gentle one, listen to me. Trust no one around Caesar except Proculeius.
My resolution and my hands I'll trust; / None about Caesar.
I'll trust my own determination and my own hands, not anyone around Caesar.

The miserable change now at my end / Lament nor sorrow at: but please your thoughts / In feeding them with those my former fortunes / Wherein I liv'd, the greatest prince o' the world, / The noblest; and do now not basely die, / Not cowardly put off my helmet to / My countryman, a Roman by a Roman / Valiantly vanquish'd. Now my spirit is going: / I can no more.

Don't grieve or mourn over the miserable change in my fortunes at my end. Instead please your thoughts by feeding them on my earlier fortunes, when I lived as the greatest prince in the world, the noblest. And now I don't die shamefully, or like a coward handing my helmet to my countryman, but as a Roman bravely conquered by a Roman. Now my spirit is leaving. I can't say more.
Noblest of men, woo't die? / Hast thou no care of me? shall I abide / In this dull world, which in thy absence is / No better than a sty?--O, see, my women,
Noblest of men, will you die? Don't you care about me? Must I stay in this dull world, which without you is no better than a pigsty? Oh, look, my women,

The crown o' the earth doth melt.--My lord!-- / O, wither'd is the garland of the war, / The soldier's pole is fallen: young boys and girls / Are level now with men: the odds is gone, / And there is nothing left remarkable / Beneath the visiting moon.

The crown of the earth melts. My lord! Oh, the garland of war has withered. The soldier's standard has fallen. Young boys and girls are now equal with men. All difference is gone, and there's nothing remarkable left under the changing moon.
She is dead too, our sovereign.

No more but e'en a woman, and commanded / By such poor passion as the maid that milks / And does the meanest chares.--It were for me / To throw my sceptre at the injurious gods; / To tell them that this world did equal theirs / Till they had stol'n our jewel. All's but naught; / Patience is sottish, and impatience does / Become a dog that's mad: then is it sin / To rush into the secret house of death / Ere death dare come to us?--How do you, women? / What, what! good cheer! Why, how now, Charmian! / My noble girls!--Ah, women, women, look, / Our lamp is spent, it's out!--Good sirs, take heart:-- / We'll bury him; and then, what's brave, what's noble, / Let's do it after the high Roman fashion, / And make death proud to take us. Come, away: / This case of that huge spirit now is cold: / Ah, women, women!--Come; we have no friend / But resolution, and the briefest end.

No more than a woman, and ruled by the same poor emotions as the girl who milks the cows and does the lowest chores. I should throw my sceptre at the cruel gods and tell them this world was equal to theirs until they stole our jewel. Everything is worthless now. Patience is stupid, and impatience suits a mad dog. So is it a sin to rush into death's secret house before death dares to come to us? How are you, women? What, what! Cheer up! Why, Charmian! My noble girls! Ah, women, women, look, our lamp has burnt out; it's gone out! Good sirs, take heart. We'll bury him. And then, what's brave and noble, let's do it in the high Roman way, and make death proud to take us. Come, let's go. This body that held that huge spirit is cold now. Ah, women, women! Come. We have no friend but courage, and the quickest end.
Go to him, Dolabella, bid him yield; / Being so frustrate, tell him he mocks / The pauses that he makes.
Go to him, Dolabella, and tell him to surrender. Tell him that, beaten as he is, his delays only make him look ridiculous.
Wherefore is that? And what art thou that dar'st / Appear thus to us?
What's that for? And who are you, who dare come before us like this?

I am call'd Dercetas; / Mark Antony I serv'd, who best was worthy / Best to be serv'd: whilst he stood up and spoke, / He was my master, and I wore my life / To spend upon his haters. If thou please / To take me to thee, as I was to him / I'll be to Caesar; if thou pleasest not, / I yield thee up my life.

My name is Dercetas. I served Mark Antony, who was the most worthy of being served. While he stood and spoke, he was my master, and I wore my life to spend against his enemies. If you'll take me into your service, I'll be to you what I was to him. If not, I give you my life.
I say, O Caesar, Antony is dead.
I'm saying, oh Caesar, that Antony is dead.

The breaking of so great a thing should make / A greater crack: the round world / Should have shook lions into civil streets, / And citizens to their dens. The death of Antony / Is not a single doom; in the name lay / A moiety of the world.

The breaking of something so great should make a louder crash. The whole world should have shaken lions into city streets and citizens into lions' dens. The death of Antony isn't the end of just one man. Half the world was in that name.

He is dead, Caesar; / Not by a public minister of justice, / Nor by a hired knife; but that self hand / Which writ his honour in the acts it did / Hath, with the courage which the heart did lend it, / Splitted the heart.--This is his sword; / I robb'd his wound of it; behold it stain'd / With his most noble blood.

He's dead, Caesar. Not killed by a public executioner or a hired knife, but by the same hand that wrote his honour in the deeds it did. With the courage his heart gave it, it split that heart. This is his sword. I stole it from his wound. Look, it's stained with his most noble blood.
Look you sad, friends? / The gods rebuke me, but it is tidings / To wash the eyes of kings.
Do you look sad, friends? The gods can scold me, but this is news to make kings weep.
And strange it is / That nature must compel us to lament / Our most persisted deeds.
And it's strange that nature forces us to grieve over the very things we worked hardest to achieve.
His taints and honours / Weigh'd equal with him.
His faults and his honours were equally balanced in him.
A rarer spirit never / Did steer humanity. But you, gods, will give us / Some faults to make us men. Caesar is touch'd.
A rarer spirit never guided a human being. But you gods give us some faults to make us human. Caesar is moved.
When such a spacious mirror's set before him, / He needs must see himself.
When such a huge mirror is held up in front of him, he can't help seeing himself.

O Antony! / I have follow'd thee to this!--But we do lance / Diseases in our bodies: I must perforce / Have shown to thee such a declining day / Or look on thine; we could not stall together / In the whole world: but yet let me lament, / With tears as sovereign as the blood of hearts, / That thou, my brother, my competitor / In top of all design, my mate in empire, / Friend and companion in the front of war, / The arm of mine own body, and the heart / Where mine his thoughts did kindle,--that our stars, / Unreconciliable, should divide / Our equalness to this.--Hear me, good friends,-- / But I will tell you at some meeter season.

Oh Antony! I've driven you to this! But we cut out diseases in our own bodies. I had no choice: I had to show you a day like this one of my decline, or watch yours. We couldn't both live in the whole world. Yet let me grieve, with tears as precious as heart's blood, that you, my brother, my partner in the highest enterprises, my fellow ruler of the empire, my friend and companion at the front of battle, the arm of my own body, and the heart that set my thoughts alight, that our stars, which could never be reconciled, should have split our equality like this. Listen to me, good friends... But I'll tell you at a better time.
The business of this man looks out of him; / We'll hear him what he says.--Whence are you?
This man's business shows in his face. We'll hear what he has to say. Where are you from?
A poor Egyptian yet. The queen, my mistress, / Confin'd in all she has, her monument, / Of thy intents desires instruction, / That she preparedly may frame herself / To the way she's forc'd to.
A poor Egyptian still. The queen, my mistress, shut up in all she has left, her monument, wants to know your intentions, so she can prepare herself for whatever she's forced to do.
Bid her have good heart: / She soon shall know of us, by some of ours, / How honourable and how kindly we / Determine for her; for Caesar cannot learn / To be ungentle.
Tell her to take heart. She'll soon hear from some of our people how honourably and kindly we've decided to treat her. Caesar can't learn to be unkind.
Then may the gods keep you!

Come hither, Proculeius. Go and say / We purpose her no shame: give her what comforts / The quality of her passion shall require / Lest, in her greatness, by some mortal stroke / She do defeat us; for her life in Rome / Would be eternal in our triumph: go, / And with your speediest bring us what she says, / And how you find her.

Come here, Proculeius. Go and tell her we mean her no shame. Give her whatever comfort her grief needs, in case, in her pride, she kills herself and defeats us. Her being alive in Rome would make our triumph remembered for ever. Go, and as quickly as you can bring us back what she says and how she seems.
Where's Dolabella, to back up Proculeius?

Let him alone, for I remember now / How he's employ'd; he shall in time be ready. / Go with me to my tent; where you shall see / How hardly I was drawn into this war; / How calm and gentle I proceeded still / In all my writings: go with me, and see / What I can show in this.

Never mind; I remember now what he's doing. He'll be ready soon. Come with me to my tent, where you'll see how reluctantly I was drawn into this war, and how calmly and gently I always went about it in all my letters. Come with me and see what I can show you.

My desolation does begin to make / A better life. 'Tis paltry to be Caesar; / Not being Fortune, he's but Fortune's knave, / A minister of her will: and it is great / To do that thing that ends all other deeds; / Which shackles accidents and bolts up change; / Which sleeps, and never palates more the dug, / The beggar's nurse and Caesar's.

My loneliness is starting to make a better life for me. It's worthless to be Caesar. He's not Fortune, just Fortune's servant, carrying out her wishes. And it's a great thing to do the deed that ends all other deeds, that chains up accidents and locks out change, that sleeps and never again tastes the earth's breast that feeds both beggar and Caesar.
Caesar sends greetings to the queen of Egypt; / And bids thee study on what fair demands / Thou mean'st to have him grant thee.
Caesar sends greetings to the Queen of Egypt, and asks you to think about what fair requests you'd like him to grant you.

Antony / Did tell me of you, bade me trust you; but / I do not greatly care to be deceiv'd, / That have no use for trusting. If your master / Would have a queen his beggar, you must tell him / That majesty, to keep decorum, must / No less beg than a kingdom: if he please / To give me conquer'd Egypt for my son, / He gives me so much of mine own as I / Will kneel to him with thanks.

Antony told me about you and said I should trust you. But I don't much mind being deceived, since I've no use for trust any more. If your master wants a queen as his beggar, you must tell him that a queen, to keep up her dignity, can't beg for less than a kingdom. If he's willing to give me conquered Egypt for my son, he'll be giving me so much of what's mine that I'll kneel and thank him.

Be of good cheer; / You are fallen into a princely hand; fear nothing: / Make your full reference freely to my lord, / Who is so full of grace that it flows over / On all that need: let me report to him / Your sweet dependency; and you shall find / A conqueror that will pray in aid for kindness / Where he for grace is kneel'd to.

Cheer up. You've fallen into a prince's hands; don't be afraid. Put yourself completely in my lord's hands. He's so full of grace that it overflows onto everyone in need. Let me tell him how sweetly you depend on him, and you'll find a conqueror who will ask others to help him be kind to you, when you kneel to him for mercy.
Pray you, tell him / I am his fortune's vassal and I send him / The greatness he has got. I hourly learn / A doctrine of obedience; and would gladly / Look him i' the face.
Please tell him I'm the servant of his good fortune, and I acknowledge the greatness he's won. Every hour I'm learning how to obey, and I'd gladly see him face to face.
This I'll report, dear lady. / Have comfort, for I know your plight is pitied / Of him that caus'd it.
I'll tell him that, dear lady. Take comfort, because I know the man who caused your trouble pities you.
You see how easily she may be surpris'd:
You see how easily she can be taken by surprise.
[To Proculeius. and the Guard.] Guard her till Caesar come.
[To Proculeius and the guard] Guard her till Caesar comes.
O Cleopatra! thou art taken, queen!
Quick, quick, good hands. / [Drawing a dagger.]
Quick, quick, good hands. [She draws a dagger.]
Hold, worthy lady, hold; / [Seizes and disarms her.] / Do not yourself such wrong, who are in this / Reliev'd, but not betray'd.
Stop, worthy lady, stop! [He seizes the dagger from her.] Don't do yourself such harm. You've been rescued here, not betrayed.
What, of death too, / That rids our dogs of languish?
Rescued even from death, which puts our dogs out of their misery?
Cleopatra, / Do not abuse my master's bounty by / The undoing of yourself: let the world see / His nobleness well acted, which your death / Will never let come forth.
Cleopatra, don't insult my master's generosity by destroying yourself. Let the world see his nobility in action, which your death would never allow.
Where art thou, death? / Come hither, come! Come, come, and take a queen / Worth many babes and beggars!
Where are you, death? Come here, come! Come, come and take a queen worth many babies and beggars!

Sir, I will eat no meat; I'll not drink, sir; / If idle talk will once be accessary, / I'll not sleep neither: this mortal house I'll ruin, / Do Caesar what he can. Know, sir, that I / Will not wait pinion'd at your master's court; / Nor once be chastis'd with the sober eye / Of dull Octavia. Shall they hoist me up, / And show me to the shouting varletry / Of censuring Rome? Rather a ditch in Egypt / Be gentle grave unto me! rather on Nilus' mud / Lay me stark-nak'd, and let the water-flies / Blow me into abhorring! rather make / My country's high pyramides my gibbet, / And hang me up in chains!

Sir, I won't eat food. I won't drink, sir. And if I have to talk nonsense to stay awake, I won't sleep either. I'll destroy this mortal body, whatever Caesar does. Know this, sir: I won't wait with my arms tied at your master's court, or be punished even once by the solemn look of dull Octavia. Will they hoist me up and show me to the jeering rabble of disapproving Rome? I'd rather have a ditch in Egypt as a gentle grave! I'd rather lie stark naked on the Nile's mud and let the water-flies lay their eggs on me until I'm disgusting! I'd rather make my country's high pyramids my gallows and hang there in chains!
You do extend / These thoughts of horror further than you shall / Find cause in Caesar.
You're taking these horrible thoughts much further than Caesar will give you reason to.
Proculeius, / What thou hast done thy master Caesar knows, / And he hath sent for thee: as for the queen, / I'll take her to my guard.
Proculeius, your master Caesar knows what you've done, and he's sent for you. As for the queen, I'll take her into my care.
So, Dolabella, / It shall content me best: be gentle to her.-- / [To Cleopatra.] To Caesar I will speak what you shall please, / If you'll employ me to him.
Fine, Dolabella, I'm happy with that. Be gentle with her. [To Cleopatra] I'll tell Caesar whatever you want, if you'll make me your messenger to him.
Tell him I want to die.
Most noble empress, you have heard of me?
Most noble empress, have you heard of me?
No matter, sir, what I have heard or known. / You laugh when boys or women tell their dreams; / Is't not your trick?
It doesn't matter, sir, what I've heard or known. You laugh when boys or women tell you their dreams. Isn't that your habit?
I dream'd there was an Emperor Antony:-- / O, such another sleep, that I might see / But such another man!
I dreamt there was an Emperor Antony. Oh, for another sleep like that, so I could see such a man again!
His face was as the heavens; and therein stuck / A sun and moon, which kept their course, and lighted / The little O, the earth.
His face was like the sky, and in it were set a sun and moon, which kept their course and lit up this little O, the earth.

His legs bestrid the ocean; his rear'd arm / Crested the world: his voice was propertied / As all the tuned spheres, and that to friends; / But when he meant to quail and shake the orb, / He was as rattling thunder. For his bounty, / There was no winter in't; an autumn 'twas / That grew the more by reaping: his delights / Were dolphin-like; they show'd his back above / The element they liv'd in: in his livery / Walk'd crowns and crownets; realms and islands were / As plates dropp'd from his pocket.

His legs straddled the ocean; his raised arm was like a crest over the world. His voice had the music of all the singing spheres, and that was for his friends. But when he wanted to terrify and shake the globe, he was like rattling thunder. As for his generosity, there was no winter in it. It was an autumn that grew richer the more it was harvested. His pleasures were like dolphins: they showed his back above the element they lived in. Kings and princes walked among his servants. Kingdoms and islands were like coins dropped from his pocket.
Think you there was or might be such a man / As this I dream'd of?
Do you think there was, or could be, a man like the one I dreamt of?

You lie, up to the hearing of the gods. / But if there be, or ever were, one such, / It's past the size of dreaming: nature wants stuff / To vie strange forms with fancy: yet to imagine / An Antony were nature's piece 'gainst fancy, / Condemning shadows quite.

You lie, loudly enough for the gods to hear. But if there is, or ever was, such a man, he's beyond the size of dreams. Nature usually lacks the material to compete with imagination in creating wonderful shapes. Yet to imagine an Antony was nature's masterpiece against imagination, putting all fantasies to shame.

Hear me, good madam. / Your loss is, as yourself, great; and you bear it / As answering to the weight: would I might never / O'ertake pursu'd success, but I do feel, / By the rebound of yours, a grief that smites / My very heart at root.

Listen to me, good madam. Your loss is as great as you are, and you bear it as its weight deserves. May I never achieve what I'm aiming for if I don't feel, as an echo of your grief, a sorrow that strikes the very root of my heart.
I thank you, sir. / Know you what Caesar means to do with me?
Thank you, sir. Do you know what Caesar plans to do with me?
I am loath to tell you what I would you knew.
I don't want to tell you what I wish you knew.
He'll lead me, then, in triumph?
He'll lead me in his victory parade, then?
Madam, he will; / I know it.
Madam, he will. I know it.
Which is the queen of Egypt?
Which one is the Queen of Egypt?
Arise, you shall not kneel:-- / I pray you, rise; rise, Egypt.
Get up. You shall not kneel. Please, get up. Get up, Egypt.
Sir, the gods / Will have it thus; my master and my lord / I must obey.
Sir, the gods want it this way. I must obey my master and my lord.
Take to you no hard thoughts; / The record of what injuries you did us, / Though written in our flesh, we shall remember / As things but done by chance.
Don't think harshly. Though the record of the injuries you did us is written in our flesh, we'll remember them as things that happened by chance.
Sole sir o' the world, / I cannot project mine own cause so well / To make it clear: but do confess I have / Been laden with like frailties which before / Have often sham'd our sex.
Only lord of the world, I can't present my own case well enough to clear myself. But I confess I've been burdened with the same weaknesses that have often shamed women before.

Cleopatra, know / We will extenuate rather than enforce: / If you apply yourself to our intents,-- / Which towards you are most gentle,--you shall find / A benefit in this change; but if you seek / To lay on me a cruelty, by taking / Antony's course, you shall bereave yourself / Of my good purposes, and put your children / To that destruction which I'll guard them from, / If thereon you rely. I'll take my leave.

Cleopatra, understand that we'll make light of your faults rather than press them. If you go along with our intentions, which are very gentle towards you, you'll benefit from this change. But if you try to make me look cruel by following Antony's example, you'll lose my good intentions, and put your children in the danger I'll protect them from if you rely on me. I'll take my leave.
And may, through all the world: 'tis yours, and we, / Your scutcheons and your signs of conquest, shall / Hang in what place you please. Here, my good lord.
And you may, through the whole world. It's yours, and we, your shields and trophies of conquest, will hang wherever you please. Here, my good lord.
You shall advise me in all for Cleopatra.
You'll advise me on everything to do with Cleopatra.
This is the brief of money, plate, and jewels, / I am possess'd of: 'tis exactly valued; / Not petty things admitted.--Where's Seleucus?
This is the list of money, gold and silver, and jewels I own. It's valued exactly; small things aren't included. Where's Seleucus?
This is my treasurer: let him speak, my lord, / Upon his peril, that I have reserv'd / To myself nothing. Speak the truth, Seleucus.
This is my treasurer. Let him tell you, my lord, on pain of punishment, that I've kept nothing back for myself. Tell the truth, Seleucus.
Madam, / I had rather seal my lips than to my peril / Speak that which is not.
Madam, I'd rather seal my lips than say what isn't true and risk punishment.
Enough to purchase what you have made known.
Enough to buy everything you've listed.
Nay, blush not, Cleopatra; I approve / Your wisdom in the deed.
No, don't blush, Cleopatra. I approve of your good sense in doing it.

See, Caesar! O, behold, / How pomp is follow'd! Mine will now be yours; / And, should we shift estates, yours would be mine. / The ingratitude of this Seleucus does / Even make me wild: O slave, of no more trust / Than love that's hir'd!--What, goest thou back? thou shalt / Go back, I warrant thee; but I'll catch thine eyes / Though they had wings; slave, soulless villain, dog! / O rarely base!

See, Caesar! Oh, look how greatness is followed! My servants will now be yours, and if we swapped places, yours would be mine. This Seleucus's ingratitude makes me wild. Oh slave, no more to be trusted than paid-for love! What, are you backing away? You'll back away, I promise you. But I'll catch your eyes even if they had wings. Slave, soulless villain, dog! Oh, exceptionally low!
Good queen, let us entreat you.
Good queen, let us beg you to stop.

O Caesar, what a wounding shame is this,-- / That thou vouchsafing here to visit me, / Doing the honour of thy lordliness / To one so meek, that mine own servant should / Parcel the sum of my disgraces by / Addition of his envy! Say, good Caesar, / That I some lady trifles have reserv'd, / Immoment toys, things of such dignity / As we greet modern friends withal; and say, / Some nobler token I have kept apart / For Livia and Octavia, to induce / Their mediation;--must I be unfolded / With one that I have bred? The gods! It smites me / Beneath the fall I have. / [To Seleucus.] Pr'ythee go hence; / Or I shall show the cinders of my spirits / Through the ashes of my chance.--Wert thou a man, / Thou wouldst have mercy on me.

Oh Caesar, what a wounding shame this is! That when you condescend to visit me here, honouring someone so humble with your lordly presence, my own servant should add to the sum of my disgraces with his malice! Say, good Caesar, that I have kept back some ladies' trinkets, unimportant toys, the kind of things we give to ordinary friends. And say I've kept some nobler gift aside for Livia and Octavia, to win them to plead for me. Must I be exposed by someone I raised myself? Gods! It strikes me lower than my fall already has. [To Seleucus] Please go away, or I'll show the sparks of my spirit through the ashes of my fortune. If you were a man, you'd have pity on me.
Be it known that we, the greatest, are misthought / For things that others do; and when we fall / We answer others' merits in our name, / Are therefore to be pitied.
Let it be known that we, the greatest, are blamed for things others do. And when we fall, we answer in our own name for others' deeds, so we should be pitied.

Cleopatra, / Not what you have reserv'd, nor what acknowledg'd, / Put we i' the roll of conquest: still be't yours, / Bestow it at your pleasure; and believe / Caesar's no merchant, to make prize with you / Of things that merchants sold. Therefore be cheer'd; / Make not your thoughts your prisons: no, dear queen; / For we intend so to dispose you as / Yourself shall give us counsel. Feed and sleep: / Our care and pity is so much upon you / That we remain your friend; and so, adieu.

Cleopatra, we won't count what you've kept back, or what you've declared, as part of our conquest. Let it stay yours. Give it away as you like, and believe me, Caesar isn't a merchant who'll bargain with you over things merchants sell. So cheer up. Don't make your thoughts your prison. No, dear queen, because we plan to treat you as you yourself advise. Eat and sleep. Our care and pity for you are so great that we remain your friend. And so, goodbye.
He words me, girls, he words me, that I should not / Be noble to myself: but hark thee, Charmian!
He uses words on me, girls, words, so that I won't do the noble thing for myself. But listen, Charmian!
Finish, good lady; the bright day is done, / And we are for the dark.
Finish it, good lady. The bright day is over, and we're bound for the dark.
Hie thee again: / I have spoke already, and it is provided; / Go put it to the haste.
Hurry back. I've already given the order, and it's arranged. Go and speed it up.

Madam, as thereto sworn by your command, / Which my love makes religion to obey, / I tell you this: Caesar through Syria / Intends his journey; and within three days / You with your children will he send before: / Make your best use of this: I have perform'd / Your pleasure and my promise.

Madam, as I swore to you at your command, which my love makes a religious duty to obey, I'm telling you this: Caesar plans to travel through Syria, and within three days he'll send you and your children ahead of him. Make the best use of this. I've done what you wanted and kept my promise.
Dolabella, / I shall remain your debtor.
Dolabella, I'll always be in your debt.
I your servant. / Adieu, good queen; I must attend on Caesar.
And I your servant. Goodbye, good queen. I must go back to Caesar.

Now, Iras, what think'st thou? / Thou, an Egyptian puppet, shall be shown / In Rome as well as I: mechanic slaves, / With greasy aprons, rules, and hammers, shall / Uplift us to the view; in their thick breaths, / Rank of gross diet, shall we be enclouded, / And forc'd to drink their vapour.

Now, Iras, what do you think? You, an Egyptian puppet, will be put on show in Rome as well as me. Working-class slaves in greasy aprons, with rulers and hammers, will lift us up for everyone to see. We'll be wrapped in the clouds of their bad breath, stinking of coarse food, and forced to breathe it in.

Nay, 'tis most certain, Iras:--saucy lictors / Will catch at us like strumpets; and scald rhymers / Ballad us out o' tune: the quick comedians / Extemporally will stage us, and present / Our Alexandrian revels; Antony / Shall be brought drunken forth, and I shall see / Some squeaking Cleopatra boy my greatness / I' the posture of a whore.

No, it's quite certain, Iras. Cheeky officers will grab at us like whores, and lousy poets will sing ballads about us out of tune. Quick-witted comic actors will make up plays about us on the spot and act out our parties in Alexandria. Antony will be brought on stage drunk, and I'll see some squeaky-voiced boy playing Cleopatra, mocking my greatness in the pose of a whore.
I'll never see't; for I am sure mine nails / Are stronger than mine eyes.
I'll never see it, because I'm sure my nails are stronger than my eyes.
Why, that's the way / To fool their preparation and to conquer / Their most absurd intents.
Why, that's the way to make fools of their preparations and defeat their absurd plans.

Now, Charmian!-- / Show me, my women, like a queen.--Go fetch / My best attires;--I am again for Cydnus, / To meet Mark Antony:--sirrah, Iras, go.-- / Now, noble Charmian, we'll despatch indeed; / And when thou hast done this chare, I'll give thee leave / To play till doomsday.--Bring our crown and all.

Now, Charmian! Dress me like a queen, my women. Go and fetch my best clothes. I'm going to Cydnus again, to meet Mark Antony. Go, Iras. Now, noble Charmian, we'll really finish things. And when you've done this job, I'll give you leave to play until doomsday. Bring our crown and everything.
Here is a rural fellow / That will not be denied your highness' presence: / He brings you figs.
There's a country fellow here who won't take no for an answer and insists on seeing your highness. He's brought you figs.

What poor an instrument / May do a noble deed! he brings me liberty. / My resolution's plac'd, and I have nothing / Of woman in me: now from head to foot / I am marble-constant; now the fleeting moon / No planet is of mine.
