What a humble instrument can do a noble deed! He brings me freedom. My mind's made up, and there's nothing of a woman in me now. From head to foot I'm as steady as marble. The changing moon is no longer my planet.
Hast thou the pretty worm of Nilus there / That kills and pains not?
Do you have the pretty serpent of the Nile there, the one that kills without pain?
Truly, I have him. But I would not be the party that should / desire you to touch him, for his biting is immortal; those that / do die of it do seldom or never recover.
I've got him, all right. But I wouldn't want to be the one to tell you to touch him, because his bite is immortal. Those who die of it seldom or never recover.
Remember'st thou any that have died on't?
Do you remember anyone who has died of it?

Very many, men and women too. I heard of one of them no longer / than yesterday: a very honest woman, but something given to lie; / as a woman should not do but in the way of honesty: how she died / of the biting of it, what pain she felt,--truly she makes a very / good report o' the worm; but he that will believe all that they / say shall never be saved by half that they do: but this is most / falliable, the worm's an odd worm.

Lots, men and women too. I heard about one of them only yesterday: a very honest woman, but a bit inclined to lie, which a woman shouldn't do except honestly. She told how she died of the bite and what pain she felt. Truly, she gives the worm a very good report. But anyone who believes everything they say will never be saved by half of what they do. But this is most fallible: the worm's an odd worm.
I wish you all joy of the worm.
I wish you all the joy of the worm.
You must think this, look you, that the worm will do his kind.
You must understand, you see, that the worm will do what it's made to do.
Look you, the worm is not to be trusted but in the keeping of / wise people; for indeed there is no goodness in the worm.
Look, the worm can only be trusted in the care of wise people, because there's really no goodness in the worm.
Take thou no care; it shall be heeded.
Don't worry. We'll be careful with it.
Very good. Give it nothing, I pray you, for it is not worth the / feeding.
Very good. Don't give it anything to eat, please, because it isn't worth feeding.

You must not think I am so simple but I know the devil himself / will not eat a woman: I know that a woman is a dish for the gods, / if the devil dress her not. But truly, these same whoreson devils / do the gods great harm in their women, for in every ten that they / make the devils mar five.

You mustn't think I'm so simple that I don't know the devil himself won't eat a woman. I know that a woman is a dish fit for the gods, if the devil doesn't cook her. But truly, these same rotten devils do the gods great harm with their women, because for every ten the gods make, the devils spoil five.
Yes, forsooth. I wish you joy o' the worm.
Yes, indeed. I wish you joy of the worm.

Give me my robe, put on my crown; I have / Immortal longings in me: now no more / The juice of Egypt's grape shall moist this lip:-- / Yare, yare, good Iras; quick.--Methinks I hear / Antony call; I see him rouse himself / To praise my noble act; I hear him mock / The luck of Caesar, which the gods give men / To excuse their after wrath. Husband, I come: / Now to that name my courage prove my title! / I am fire and air; my other elements / I give to baser life.--So,--have you done? / Come then, and take the last warmth of my lips. / Farewell, kind Charmian;--Iras, long farewell. / [Kisses them. Iras falls and dies.] / Have I the aspic in my lips? Dost fall? / If thus thou and nature can so gently part, / The stroke of death is as a lover's pinch, / Which hurts and is desir'd. Dost thou lie still? / If thou vanishest, thou tell'st the world / It is not worth leave-taking.

Give me my robe, put on my crown. I have immortal longings in me. Now the juice of Egypt's grapes will never wet this lip again. Quick, quick, good Iras, hurry. I think I hear Antony calling. I see him getting up to praise my noble act. I hear him mocking Caesar's luck, which the gods give men to excuse their anger later. Husband, I'm coming. Now let my courage prove my right to that name! I'm fire and air; my other elements, earth and water, I leave to baser life. So, have you finished? Come then, and take the last warmth of my lips. Goodbye, kind Charmian. Iras, a long goodbye. [She kisses them. Iras falls and dies.] Do I have the snake's poison on my lips? Are you falling? If you and life can part so gently, death's blow is like a lover's pinch, which hurts and is wanted. Are you lying still? If you vanish like this, you tell the world it isn't worth saying goodbye to.
Dissolve, thick cloud, and rain; that I may say / The gods themselves do weep!
Dissolve, thick cloud, and rain, so I can say the gods themselves are weeping!

This proves me base: / If she first meet the curled Antony, / He'll make demand of her, and spend that kiss / Which is my heaven to have.--Come, thou mortal wretch, / [To an asp, which she applies to her breast.] / With thy sharp teeth this knot intrinsicate / Of life at once untie: poor venomous fool, / Be angry and despatch. O couldst thou speak, / That I might hear thee call great Caesar ass / Unpolicied!

This makes me look low. If she meets curly-haired Antony first, he'll ask her about me and spend on her the kiss that is my heaven to have. Come, you deadly little wretch, [to an asp, which she puts to her breast] with your sharp teeth untie this tangled knot of life at once. Poor poisonous fool, be angry and get it done. Oh, if you could speak, so I could hear you call great Caesar an ass, outwitted!
Peace, peace! / Dost thou not see my baby at my breast / That sucks the nurse asleep?
Quiet, quiet! Don't you see my baby at my breast, sucking its nurse to sleep?
As sweet as balm, as soft as air, as gentle:-- / O Antony! Nay, I will take thee too:-- / [Applying another asp to her arm.] / What should I stay,-- / [Falls on a bed and dies.]
As sweet as perfume, as soft as air, as gentle... Oh Antony! No, I'll take you too. [She puts another asp to her arm.] Why should I stay... [She falls on a bed and dies.]

In this vile world?--So, fare thee well.-- / Now boast thee, death, in thy possession lies / A lass unparallel'd.--Downy windows, close; / And golden Phoebus never be beheld / Of eyes again so royal! Your crown's awry; / I'll mend it and then play.

...in this vile world? So, goodbye. Now boast, death: you have in your power a girl without equal. Soft eyelids, close, and may golden Apollo the sun never be seen by such royal eyes again! Your crown's crooked. I'll straighten it, and then play.
Too slow a messenger. [She puts an asp to herself.]
O, come apace, despatch: I partly feel thee.
Oh, come quickly, finish it. I can partly feel you.
Approach, ho! all's not well: Caesar's beguil'd.
Come here, hey! Something's wrong. Caesar's been tricked.
There's Dolabella sent from Caesar; call him.
There's Dolabella, sent by Caesar. Call him.
What work is here!--Charmian, is this well done?
What's been done here! Charmian, is this well done?
It is well done, and fitting for a princess / Descended of so many royal kings. / Ah, soldier!
It is well done, and fitting for a princess descended from so many royal kings. Ah, soldier! [She dies.]
Caesar, thy thoughts / Touch their effects in this: thyself art coming / To see perform'd the dreaded act which thou / So sought'st to hinder. / [Within.] A way there, a way for Caesar!
Caesar, your fears have come true. You're coming yourself to see the dreaded act done which you tried so hard to prevent. [Voices offstage] Make way there, make way for Caesar!
O sir, you are too sure an augurer; / That you did fear is done.
Oh sir, you're too accurate a prophet. What you feared has happened.
Bravest at the last, / She levell'd at our purposes, and being royal, / Took her own way.--The manner of their deaths? / I do not see them bleed.
Bravest at the end, she guessed our plans, and being royal, she took her own way. How did they die? I don't see any blood.
A simple countryman that brought her figs. / This was his basket.
A simple countryman who brought her figs. This was his basket.
O Caesar, / This Charmian liv'd but now; she stood and spake: / I found her trimming up the diadem / On her dead mistress; tremblingly she stood, / And on the sudden dropp'd.
Oh Caesar, this Charmian was alive just now. She stood and spoke. I found her straightening the crown on her dead mistress. She stood there trembling, and suddenly dropped.
O noble weakness!-- / If they had swallow'd poison 'twould appear / By external swelling: but she looks like sleep,-- / As she would catch another Antony / In her strong toil of grace.
Oh, noble weakness! If they'd swallowed poison, it would show in swelling on the outside. But she looks as if she's asleep, as if she'd catch another Antony in the strong net of her grace.
Here on her breast / There is a vent of blood, and something blown: / The like is on her arm.
Here on her breast there's a small trickle of blood, and some swelling. The same on her arm.
This is an aspic's trail: and these fig-leaves / Have slime upon them, such as the aspic leaves / Upon the caves of Nile.
This is a snake's trail. And these fig leaves have slime on them, like the slime snakes leave on the caves of the Nile.

Most probable / That so she died; for her physician tells me / She hath pursu'd conclusions infinite / Of easy ways to die. Take up her bed, / And bear her women from the monument:-- / She shall be buried by her Antony: / No grave upon the earth shall clip in it / A pair so famous. High events as these / Strike those that make them; and their story is / No less in pity than his glory which / Brought them to be lamented. Our army shall / In solemn show attend this funeral; / And then to Rome.--Come, Dolabella, see / High order in this great solemnity.

Very likely that's how she died, because her doctor tells me she's carried out endless experiments on easy ways to die. Pick up her bed, and carry her women out of the monument. She'll be buried beside her Antony. No grave on earth will hold such a famous pair. Great events like these strike even those who caused them, and their story is no less pitiful than the glory of the man who brought them to be mourned. Our army will attend this funeral in solemn procession, and then on to Rome. Come, Dolabella, see that this great ceremony is done with dignity.
